skills: Build Riemann sums on data grids and predict whether they over- or underestimate
Reason about integrals without computing them, using sign, symmetry, linearity, and bounds
Integrate piecewise and discontinuous functions by geometry, splitting the region where a formula changes
Describe a region in both orders, find where its boundaries meet, and reverse the order of integration
Find volumes as $\iint_D(\text{top}-\text{bottom})\,dA$ and check them against known formulas
formulas: $\displaystyle\iint_R f\,dA\approx\sum_{i,j}f(x_{ij}^*,y_{ij}^*)\,\Delta A$, with $(x_{ij}^*,y_{ij}^*)$ a sample point in each cell of area $\Delta A$
$\displaystyle\iint_R f\,dA=\int_a^b\!\!\int_c^d f\,dy\,dx=\int_c^d\!\!\int_a^b f\,dx\,dy$ for continuous $f$ on $R=[a,b]\times[c,d]$
Type I region $D$: $a\le x\le b$, $g_1(x)\le y\le g_2(x)$, so $\displaystyle\iint_D f\,dA=\int_a^b\!\!\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)}f\,dy\,dx$
$m\le f\le M$ on $D$ $\Rightarrow$ $m\cdot\text{Area}(D)\le\iint_D f\,dA\le M\cdot\text{Area}(D)$
$\displaystyle V=\iint_D(\text{top}-\text{bottom})\,dA$ when top $\ge$ bottom on $D$

problems.title: Weighing a monsoon storm on a 0.25° grid
problems.context: When monsoon winds from the Arabian Sea hit the Western Ghats, the mountains along India’s west coast, they can drop heavy rain. A gauge measures only the depth of rain at one point. To know the volume of water that fell over a region, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) turns readings from thousands of rain gauges into a grid of 0.25° cells, with one rainfall value per cell. Multiplying each cell’s depth by its area and adding up the results is a Riemann sum. How much water fell on a block of four cells, and how far off is the total if you read each cell’s rain at only one point?
problems.model: The grid spacing, gauge count, and rainfall categories are published by IMD, while the rainfall pattern on the four cells is a model of one heavy-rain day, not data from the archive.
work: Sketch the $2\times2$ block, mark where $d$ is smallest and largest, and explain where $\Delta A\approx730$ km$^2$ comes from.
Before (a): predict whether the upper-right sum over- or underestimates, from how $d$ changes in $x$ and $y$.
Mark both sets of sample points, and classify the four midpoint depths with IMD’s terms.
After (c): say what $A(x)=\int_0^2 d(x,y)\,dy$ measures, draw it as a cross-section under the graph of $d$, and confirm the volume in the other order.
Explain whether the midpoint sum over- or underestimated, using the shape of $d$ in $x$.

questions.prompt: Using the upper-right corner of each cell as its sample point, find the Riemann sum for the rain volume over the block, in millions of cubic meters.
hints: For one cell, depth times area is the volume of rain on it. Sample $d$ at each upper-right corner, add the four depths, and multiply by $\Delta A\approx730$ km$^2$.
The corners are $(1,1)$, $(1,2)$, $(2,1)$, $(2,2)$. Convert: 1 mm of rain on 1 km$^2$ is 1000 m$^3$, or 0.001 million m$^3$.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: Left: the two-by-two block of cells with crosses at the four upper-right corners, labeled (1,1), (1,2), (2,1), and (2,2), and arrows showing that d grows eastward and northward. Right: the rising curve of d along the line y = 1, with a dashed rectangle on each cell whose height is the value at the right end of the cell
hintFigure.caption: Because $d$ grows in both $x$ and $y$, each upper-right corner is the wettest point of its cell; multiply each corner depth by $\Delta A\approx730$ km$^2$.

questions.prompt: Using the midpoint of each cell as its sample point, find the Riemann sum for the rain volume over the block, in millions of cubic meters.
hints: Sample $d$ at the center of each cell instead of a corner.
The midpoints are $(0.5,0.5)$, $(0.5,1.5)$, $(1.5,0.5)$, $(1.5,1.5)$; convert with mm $\times$ km$^2\times0.001=$ million m$^3$.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: Left: the two-by-two block of cells with a dot at the center of each cell, labeled (0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 1.5), (1.5, 0.5), and (1.5, 1.5). Right: a thin slab of water 1 km by 1 km by 1 mm deep, labeled as 1000 cubic meters, or 0.001 million cubic meters
hintFigure.caption: Sample $d$ at the four cell centers, and convert with 1 mm on 1 km$^2$ $=1000$ m$^3=0.001$ million m$^3$.

questions.prompt: Use an iterated integral of $d$ to find the exact rain volume over the block in the model, in millions of cubic meters.
hints: In cell units, integrate $d$ over $[0,2]\times[0,2]$; each unit square of the $(x,y)$-plane is one cell of 730 km$^2$.
Integrate in $y$ first; you will need $\int_0^2x^2\,dx=8/3$. Size check: a few hundred million m$^3$, and below your answer to (a).
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: Left: the block of cells with a vertical segment at a fixed x running from y = 0 to y = 2. Right: the cross-section of the rain solid above that segment, a trapezoid whose height rises linearly from 50 + 30x squared at y = 0 to 90 + 30x squared at y = 2
hintFigure.caption: At fixed $x$, the depth is linear in $y$, so the cross-section $A(x)=\int_0^2 d\,dy$ is a trapezoid; then integrate $A(x)$ from $x=0$ to $2$.

solution: Cell area: a degree of latitude is about 111.2 km, and a degree of longitude is shorter by the factor $\cos(\text{latitude})$. Each cell is $0.25^\circ$ of latitude, $0.25\times111.2\approx27.8$ km, by $0.25^\circ$ of longitude, $27.8\cos19^\circ\approx26.3$ km, so $\Delta A\approx730$ km$^2$. Measuring $x$ and $y$ in cell widths makes one unit square of the $(x,y)$-plane one cell. Since 1 mm of rain on 1 km$^2$ is 1000 m$^3$, a total in mm·cells times 0.73 gives millions of m$^3$.

Prediction check and upper-right sum (a): $d=50+30x^2+20y$ increases in both $x$ and $y$ on the block, so the upper-right corner gives the largest value on every cell, and the upper-right sum must overestimate. Its heights are $d(1,1)=100$, $d(1,2)=120$, $d(2,1)=190$, and $d(2,2)=210$ mm, so the sum is $620\times0.73=452.6$ million m$^3$.
Midpoint sum (b): the midpoint heights are $67.5$, $87.5$, $127.5$, and $147.5$ mm, which IMD would call heavy, heavy, very heavy, and very heavy. The sum is $430\times0.73=313.9$ million m$^3$.

Exact volume (c): the inner integral $A(x)=\int_0^2(50+30x^2+20y)\,dy=140+60x^2$ is the area of the cross-section of the solid at fixed $x$, the rain volume per unit of east–west width. Then $\int_0^2(140+60x^2)\,dx=280+160=440$ mm·cells, so $V=440\times0.73=321.2$ million m$^3$.
Other order: $\int_0^2(50+30x^2+20y)\,dx=180+40y$, and $\int_0^2(180+40y)\,dy=360+80=440$ mm·cells, the same total.

Midpoint error: the midpoint sum is low by $10\times0.73=7.3$ million m$^3$, about 2%. Midpoints integrate the linear $20y$ term exactly, but $30x^2$ is convex, and the average of a convex function over a cell is at least its value at the cell’s midpoint, so the midpoint sum underestimates.

Reconciliation: all three volumes are positive, and the exact $321.2$ million m$^3$ lies between the midpoint and upper-right sums. Spread over four cells, $440$ mm·cells is an average depth of $110$ mm, in IMD’s heavy range, so the size fits a heavy-rain day. The assumption that matters most is the smooth formula for $d$: real rain is patchier, and one sample per cell can miss sharp peaks.
problems.reflection: IMD’s grid stores one value per 0.25° cell, at the grid point in its center. Which Riemann sum is a gridded rainfall product effectively computing, and where would it be most biased?
problems.discussionSolution: It is effectively a midpoint sum, most biased where the rain pattern curves most sharply. One value per cell, taken at the cell’s center, is a midpoint sample. Midpoint sums are exact for rain that varies linearly across a cell, so the bias comes from curvature: they overestimate near a sharp rain peak (concave down) and underestimate in a dip between rain bands (convex). A 0.25° grid is least reliable where rainfall rises or falls sharply within a few cells.

Rain gauges behind the grid (IMD): 6955

Each cell is treated as a flat rectangle of about 27.8 km $\times$ 26.3 km, so $\Delta A\approx730$ km$^2$; across a block this small, the cell width changes by less than 1%.
Rain depth increases eastward toward the mountains and slightly northward, following one smooth formula for one heavy-rain day; real rainfall is patchier than any smooth formula.

$x$ = cell widths east of the block’s west edge, $y$ = cell widths north of its south edge, with $0\le x\le2$ and $0\le y\le2$

problems.title: Is it El Niño? Reading the Niño 3.4 box
problems.context: El Niño, a periodic warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean, shifts rainfall patterns far beyond the Pacific. To decide whether one is under way, NOAA forecasters watch a single number: the sea-surface temperature anomaly (how much warmer than normal the surface water is), averaged over a rectangle of ocean called the Niño 3.4 box. An average of $+0.5$ °C or more signals El Niño conditions. Given three model maps of the anomaly, is the box warm enough on average to call El Niño, and how sure can you be without working out every integral?
problems.model: The box, the $+0.5$ °C threshold, and the ONI values are published by NOAA, while the three anomaly maps are models chosen to illustrate the reasoning, not observed fields.
work: Sketch $B$ in scaled coordinates, and shade where $T_1$ is warm and where it is cold.
Before (a): without integrating, explain the sign of $I_1$ by comparing the warm and cold parts along each line $y=$ constant.
Before (b): explain which terms of $T_2$ integrate to zero over $B$, by pairing $(x,y)$ with $(-x,y)$ or with $(x,-y)$.
Before (c): predict whether the warm pool $T_3$ is an El Niño state.
For (c): with no antiderivative, prove bounds $m\le T_3\le M$ on $B$, conclude $m\le I_3\le M$, and check your prediction.

questions.prompt: For the developing-El Niño snapshot $T_1=1.5(x+0.3)(1-y^2)$, the Niño 3.4 index $I_1$ is
hints: Look along one horizontal line $y=$ constant at a time, and compare the cold piece with the warm piece.
$T_1<0$ only for $x<-0.3$, because the factor $1-y^2$ is never negative on $B$.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: Left: the box B with a horizontal line y = c, cold shading left of x = −0.3 and warm shading to its right. Right: the graph of T1 along that line, a straight line crossing zero at x = −0.3, with a cold region marked minus below the axis from −1 to −0.3 and a warm region marked plus above the axis from −0.3 to 1
hintFigure.caption: Along each line $y=c$, $T_1$ is a straight line that is negative on $-1\le x<-0.3$ and positive on $-0.3<x\le1$; compare the two signed areas.

questions.prompt: For the anomaly map $T_2=0.9+1.6x^3-0.8y+0.6(1-x^2)$, find the index $I_2=\frac14\iint_B T_2\,dA$, in °C.
hints: Over the symmetric box, the $x^3$ and $y$ terms cancel: pair $(x,y)$ with $(-x,y)$, or with $(x,-y)$.
The constant $0.9$ averages to itself; then average $1-x^2$ over $-1\le x\le1$. Size check: since $0\le1-x^2\le1$, the index is between 0.9 and 1.5 °C.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: Left: the box B with a point (x, y), its mirror image (−x, y) across the y-axis, where x cubed flips sign, and its mirror image (x, −y) across the x-axis, where y flips sign. Right: the parabola 1 − x squared over −1 to 1 with the area under it shaded, and a note that its average equals the shaded area divided by 2
hintFigure.caption: Mirror pairs cancel the $1.6x^3$ and $-0.8y$ terms; what remains is the constant $0.9$ plus $0.6$ times the average of $1-x^2$.

questions.prompt: For the warm pool $T_3=3e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}$, find the best constant lower bound: the largest $m$ with $T_3\ge m$ everywhere on the box $B$, in °C.
hints: $T_3$ is smallest where $x^2+y^2$ is largest on the box, at the corners.
On $B$, $-(x^2+y^2)/2\ge-1$, and $e^s$ is increasing in $s$.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: Left: the box B shaded by the warm pool, hottest at the center, with dashed circles of constant x squared plus y squared, the four corners marked, and the distance square root of 2 from the center to a corner. Right: the increasing curve 3e to the s for s from −1 at the corners to 0 at the center
hintFigure.caption: $x^2+y^2$ is largest, $2$, at the corners, so $s=-(x^2+y^2)/2$ runs from $-1$ to $0$ on $B$, and $3e^s$ is smallest where $s$ is smallest.

solution: Setup: in scaled coordinates, $x=$ (degrees east of $145^\circ$W)$/25$ and $y=$ latitude$/5^\circ$, so the box is $B=[-1,1]\times[-1,1]$, with area 4, and $I=\frac14\iint_B T\,dA$. Equal-area weighting is fine, because $\cos(\text{latitude})\ge0.996$ over $\pm5^\circ$ of latitude.

Sign of $I_1$ (a): on each line $y=c$ with $|c|<1$, the cold part $-1\le x<-0.3$ is a triangle of base $0.7$ and depth $1.5(0.7)(1-c^2)$. The warm part $-0.3<x\le1$ is a triangle of base $1.3$ and height $1.5(1.3)(1-c^2)$. The warm triangle is larger on every line, so $I_1>0$. (Exactly, $I_1=1.5(0.3)(2/3)=0.3$ °C, which is positive but still below the $0.5$ °C threshold.)

Symmetry and linearity (b): $1.6x^3$ is odd in $x$ and $-0.8y$ is odd in $y$, and the box is symmetric in both, so these terms integrate to 0. By linearity, $I_2=0.9+0.6\cdot\frac12\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)\,dx=0.9+0.6\cdot\frac23=1.3$ °C.

Bounds (c): on $B$, $0\le x^2+y^2\le2$, so $-1\le-(x^2+y^2)/2\le0$. Because $e^s$ is increasing, $3e^{-1}\le T_3\le3$, so the best lower bound is $m=3e^{-1}\approx1.10$ °C, reached at the corners. Multiplying by the area 4 gives $4(3e^{-1})\le\iint_BT_3\,dA\le12$, so $1.10\le I_3\le3$ °C.
Prediction check: the lower bound alone gives $I_3\ge1.10>0.5$ °C, so the warm pool is an El Niño state, with no antiderivative needed. Numerically, $I_3\approx2.20$ °C.

Reconciliation: all three indices are positive, but only $T_2$ ($1.3$ °C) and $T_3$ (about $2.2$ °C) pass the $0.5$ °C threshold; $T_1$, at $0.3$ °C, is warm on average but below it. The warm pool’s $2.2$ °C is comparable to the published ONI peaks of $2.0$ to $2.6$ °C. The assumption that matters most is the shape of each model map.
problems.reflection: The ONI reached 2.6 °C in Nov–Jan 2015/16. Using $T_1$ as an example, explain how a large positive box average can hide parts of the box that were colder than normal. Why do forecasters still find the average useful?
problems.discussionSolution: A large positive average can hide cold water because the average is a signed integral divided by the area, so warm and cold regions cancel. In $T_1$, the western part of the box ($x<-0.3$) is colder than normal even though the index is positive. Forecasters still use the box average because the atmosphere responds to broad, large-scale warming, and averaging smooths out small eddies that matter little for that response.

data: Niño 3.4 box: $5^\circ$N–$5^\circ$S, $120^\circ$–$170^\circ$W
El Niño threshold: $+0.5$ °C
Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), the 3-month mean anomaly over the box: 2.6 °C (Nov–Jan 2015/16), 2.4 °C (1997/98), 2.0 °C (2023/24)
assume: The index is the plain area average of the anomaly over the box; weighting by latitude would change it by less than 0.4%, because the box lies within 5° of the equator.
The three anomaly maps $T_1,T_2,T_3$ (in °C) are models chosen to show the reasoning, not observed fields, so their indices illustrate methods, not real years.
model: Scaled coordinates: $x=(\text{degrees east of }145^\circ\text{W})/25$ and $y=\text{latitude}/5^\circ$, so the box is $B=[-1,1]\times[-1,1]$
Anomaly $T(x,y)$ (°C): how much warmer than normal the surface water is; negative means colder
Index (°C), the average anomaly over the box of area 4: $I=\dfrac{1}{4}\iint_B T\,dA$

photo.alt: NOAA world map of sea-surface temperature differences from average in November 2015, with a long band of warm water along the equator in the eastern Pacific

figure.alt: Left: a map of the tropical Pacific with the Niño 3.4 box drawn from 170°W to 120°W and from 5°S to 5°N, west of South America. Right: the same box in scaled coordinates from −1 to 1, split by the vertical line x = −0.3 into a narrow cold strip on the left and a wider warm part on the right
figure.caption: Left: the Niño 3.4 box in the tropical Pacific. Right: the box $B$ in scaled coordinates, showing where the snapshot $T_1$ is cold ($x<-0.3$) and warm ($x>-0.3$).

solutionFigures.alt: The graph of T1 along a line y = c: a cold triangle below the axis with base 0.7 and depth 1.5(0.7)(1 − c squared), and a warm triangle above the axis with base 1.3 and height 1.5(1.3)(1 − c squared)
solutionFigures.caption: On every line $y=c$, the warm triangle (base $1.3$) outweighs the cold one (base $0.7$), so $I_1>0$.

solutionFigures.alt: A temperature axis from 0 to 3.2 °C with the El Niño threshold at 0.5 °C dashed and a band for published ONI peaks from 2.0 to 2.6 °C. I1 = 0.3 lies left of the threshold, I2 = 1.3 right of it, and I3 is drawn as the interval from the bound 1.10 to 3, with its value about 2.20 marked
solutionFigures.caption: Only $I_1$ falls short of the $0.5$ °C threshold; the bound $I_3\ge1.10$ °C alone settles the warm pool, and its value is near the published peaks.

problems.title: The Pyramid of the Sun, smooth and stepped
problems.context: The Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan, near Mexico City, rises in four stepped levels. Archaeologists at INAH, Mexico’s national institute of anthropology and history, have published its height, its base, and the volume of its solid body. You will compare three models: a smooth pyramid, a staircase that fits inside it, and a staircase that wraps around it. The staircases are piecewise-constant functions: their height jumps from one flat value to the next, and they show how the integral of such a jumpy function is defined. How much material is in the pyramid, and how much does the answer depend on picturing its sides as smooth or stepped?
problems.model: INAH archaeologists publish the height, base, number of levels, and solid volume, while the square base, flat faces, and equal-height steps with vertical walls are modeling choices.
work: Sketch the base split along its diagonals $y=\pm x$, mark where $h=66$ m and where $h=0$, and say whether $\max(|x|,|y|)$ is $|x|$ or $|y|$ on each piece.
For (a): integrate $h$ over one piece, then check with the tetrahedron with vertices $(0,0,0)$, $(0,0,66)$, $(112,\pm112,0)$.
Before (b): predict the order of the smooth, inscribed, circumscribed, and published volumes.

Before (b): write the inscribed staircase as $h_{\text{low}}=16.5\,\lfloor4(1-\max(|x|,|y|)/112)\rfloor$, sketch its top view, list every discontinuity (do not miss the summit), and explain why $h_{\text{low}}$ is integrable.
After (c): with $n$ equal steps, write (upper sum $-$ lower sum) as a function of $n$, and explain why it tends to 0.

questions.prompt: Find the volume $V=\iint h\,dA$ of the smooth pyramid model, in cubic meters.
hints: By symmetry, the diagonals split the base into 8 congruent triangles; on $0\le y\le x\le112$, $h=66(1-x/112)$.
On that triangle, integrate in $y$ first: the inner integral multiplies the height by the slice length $x$.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: Left: top view of the square base with the triangle 0 ≤ y ≤ x shaded and a vertical segment at a fixed x running from y = 0 up to the diagonal y = x. Right: the slice of the pyramid above that segment, a rectangle of length x and constant height 66(1 − x/112)
hintFigure.caption: On the triangle $0\le y\le x\le112$ the height $66(1-x/112)$ does not depend on $y$, so the inner integral is that height times the slice length $x$.

questions.prompt: Find the volume of the inscribed staircase $h_{\text{low}}$, the four-level model that fits inside the smooth pyramid, in cubic meters.
hints: Treat the staircase as stacked square slabs 16.5 m thick. Level $k$ reaches out to where the smooth face is at height $16.5k$ m, the top of that level.
The levels have sides 168, 112, 56, and 0 m; the top level shrinks to a point.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: Side view of the smooth pyramid with the inscribed four-level staircase inside it. Dotted lines at heights 16.5, 33, 49.5, and 66 m meet the smooth face at the top of each level, and each level is labeled with its side: 168, 112, and 56 m, and 0 for the top level, which shrinks to a point
hintFigure.caption: Each inscribed level is a square slab 16.5 m thick whose side is set where the smooth face reaches the top of that level.

questions.prompt: Find the volume of the circumscribed staircase, the four-level model that wraps around the smooth pyramid, in cubic meters.
hints: Level $k$ now reaches out to where the smooth face is at height $16.5(k-1)$ m, the bottom of that level.
The levels have sides 224, 168, 112, and 56 m. Size check: more than your answer to (a), but less than the $224\times224\times66$ m$^3$ box, about 3.3 million m$^3$.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: Side view of the smooth pyramid with the circumscribed four-level staircase drawn dashed around it. Dotted lines at heights 0, 16.5, 33, and 49.5 m meet the smooth face at the bottom of each level, and each level is labeled with its side: 224, 168, 112, and 56 m
hintFigure.caption: Each circumscribed level is a square slab 16.5 m thick whose side is set where the smooth face is at the bottom of that level.

solution: Setup: with the origin under the summit, $h(x,y)=66\big(1-\max(|x|,|y|)/112\big)$ on $[-112,112]^2$. The diagonals $y=\pm x$ split the square into 8 congruent triangles. On the four where $|y|\le|x|$ (east and west), $\max(|x|,|y|)=|x|$; on the four where $|x|\le|y|$ (north and south), it is $|y|$. On $0\le y\le x\le112$ it is simply $x$.

Tetrahedron check: the piece over $|y|\le x\le112$ is two of these triangles. Its base triangle has area $\frac12(224)(112)=112^2$, so its volume is $\frac13(112^2)(66)=275{,}968=2\times137{,}984$ m$^3$, as expected.

Discontinuities: $h_{\text{low}}$ is piecewise constant. It is $49.5$ m on the square $\max(|x|,|y|)\le28$ (except the summit), $33$ m out to $56$, $16.5$ m out to $84$, and $0$ beyond. It jumps across the square outlines $\max(|x|,|y|)=28,56,84$, and at the single point $(0,0)$, where $\lfloor4\rfloor=4$ gives $66$ m while all nearby values are $49.5$ m.

Integrability and inscribed volume (b): $h_{\text{low}}$ is bounded, and its discontinuities lie on three square outlines and one point, which have zero area, so it is integrable. Its integral is a sum of slabs: $16.5(168^2+112^2+56^2)=724{,}416$ m$^3$.

Circumscribed volume (c): its slabs have sides $224$, $168$, $112$, and $56$ m, so its volume is $16.5(224^2+168^2+112^2+56^2)=1{,}552{,}320$ m$^3$. The two staircases are a lower and an upper sum for $h$. With $n$ equal steps their volumes differ by exactly one slab $224$ m wide and $66/n$ m thick, so upper $-$ lower $=\frac{66}{n}\cdot224^2\to0$, and both staircases converge to the smooth volume.

Prediction check and reconciliation: the volumes come out in the order inscribed ($0.72$), smooth ($1.10$), published ($1.175$), circumscribed ($1.55$ million m$^3$). The published “a little over 1,175,000 m$^3$” lies between the two staircases and about 6% above the smooth pyramid, so the real body is a little fuller than four flat faces meeting at a point. The assumption that matters most is the shape of the sides: the four-level staircases differ from the smooth model by 34% to 41%.
problems.reflection: Published heights for the pyramid range from about 63 m to 75 m. How much does that range change the smooth-model volume, and is the change bigger or smaller than the difference between the smooth and stepped models?
problems.discussionSolution: The height range matters less than the choice between smooth and stepped sides. Volume is proportional to height, so 63 m to 75 m moves the smooth estimate from about 1.05 to 1.25 million m³, a spread of 0.2 million m³. Each four-level staircase differs from the smooth pyramid by more, 0.38 or 0.45 million m³, though the height spread is larger than the 0.07 million m³ gap between the smooth model and the published 1.175 million m³. With many levels, the staircases would close in on the smooth pyramid and the height uncertainty would dominate.

data: Height today: 66.00 m
Base: 224.00 m
Architectural levels: 4
Solid volume: a little over 1,175,000 m³
assume: The base is a square 224 m on a side, centered at the origin under the summit; INAH gives one base length, so both sides use it.
In the smooth model, four flat faces rise from the edges of the base to the summit; this ignores the steps.
In the staircase models, the 4 levels have equal height 16.5 m, the simplest split of 66 m, and vertical walls; one staircase fits inside the smooth pyramid and one wraps around it.
model: Smooth height (m) of the surface above the point $(x,y)$ of the base: $h(x,y)=66\big(1-\max(|x|,|y|)/112\big)$ on $[-112,112]^2$, with $x,y$ in meters; 66 m is the summit height and 112 m is half the base
$\max(|x|,|y|)$ (m), the “square distance” from the center: it is constant on squares centered under the summit
Level $k$ ($k=1,\ldots,4$) of a staircase is a square slab from height $16.5(k-1)$ m to $16.5k$ m
Volume: $V=\iint h\,dA$ (m$^3$)

figure.alt: Left: side profile of the smooth pyramid, 224 m wide and 66 m high, with a solid four-level staircase inside it and a dashed four-level staircase around it. Right: top view of the square base with both diagonals drawn and one of the eight triangles shaded
figure.caption: The models, to scale in meters. Side view: the smooth pyramid between the inscribed and circumscribed four-level staircases. Top view: the base split along its diagonals into 8 triangles, with the triangle $0\le y\le x$ shaded.

solutionFigures.alt: Two rows of squares: the circumscribed slabs with sides 224, 168, 112, and 56 m on top, and the inscribed slabs with sides 168, 112, 56, and 0 below, shifted so that equal squares line up and cancel; only the 224 m square is left over, so upper minus lower is 16.5 times 224 squared cubic meters, and 66/n times 224 squared with n steps
solutionFigures.caption: Each inscribed slab matches the circumscribed slab one level up, so upper $-$ lower is one 224 m slab, $\frac{66}{n}\times224^2$ m$^3$ with $n$ steps.

problems.title: Filling the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam
problems.context: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) on the Blue Nile is 145 m high and feeds a hydropower plant. When full, its lake of flooded valleys holds 74 billion m³ of water. You will describe the lake’s outline in two ways, compute its area and volume, and compare with the published volume. The Blue Nile also carries a substantial sediment load, so you will find the average sediment concentration in the water at the dam, an integral that works in only one order. Can a simple model of the lake’s shape, built from a few published numbers, predict how much water it holds, and how muddy is the water at the dam, on average?
problems.model: The area, volume, and dam height come from ASCE and the depth at the dam and reservoir length are secondary values, while the valley shape and the sediment profile are assumed.
work: Sketch $D$: find where the shoreline curves meet the dam and each other, which curve is on top (use a test point), and where the water is deepest.
Describe $D$ as a Type I region ($x$ outside) and as a Type II region ($y$ outside).
Compute $\iint_D 1\,dA$ and $\iint_D(1-x^2-|y|)\,dA$ in both orders, check that they agree, and say which order was easier, and why.
Before (b): predict whether the model volume is above or below the published 74 km$^3$, and why.
Before (c): explain why integrating $e^{-4z^2}$ over the dam cross-section sounding by sounding (vertical lines, $z$ inside) fails, and reverse the order.

questions.prompt: In the Type II description of $D$ ($y$ outside, $x$ inside), the upper limit for $x$ is a function of $y$. Evaluate it at $y=0.36$: in scaled units (a fraction of $L$), how far upstream does the lake reach along that line?
hints: Solve the shoreline equation $|y|=1-x^2$ for $x$.
Keep the root with $x\ge0$, because the lake lies upstream of the dam.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: Plan view of the lake D between the shorelines y = 1 − x squared and y = −(1 − x squared), with a horizontal segment at y = 0.36 running from the dam at x = 0 to the upper shoreline, where the end point is marked x = ?, next to notes that both shorelines say |y| = 1 − x squared and that x should be kept nonnegative
hintFigure.caption: In the Type II description, a horizontal line at height $y$ runs from the dam $x=0$ to the shoreline $|y|=1-x^2$; solve that for $x$.

questions.prompt: Use the model and the published area of 1,874 km² to estimate the reservoir’s volume $V$, in km³.
hints: The volume is $LWH$ times a scaled integral of the depth profile, so first find $LW$ from the published area.

In scaled units the area integral is $4/3$, so $\frac43LW=1874$ km$^2$; then multiply $LW$ by $H=0.14$ km and by the scaled volume integral. Size check: the depth never exceeds $H$, so $V<1874\times0.14\approx260$ km$^3$.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: Left: plan view of the lake with a vertical segment at a fixed x running from y = −(1 − x squared) to y = 1 − x squared. Right: the depth across that segment, a tent shape that is 0 at y = ±c and peaks at c = 1 − x squared at y = 0
hintFigure.caption: For the Type I volume integral, the depth $1-x^2-|y|$ across a line of fixed $x$ is a tent of height and half-width $c=1-x^2$; use the area to find $LW$ first.

questions.prompt: Find the average of $e^{-4z^2}$ over the water in the dam cross-section $\{(y,z):|y|\le z\le1\}$. This is the mean sediment concentration as a fraction of $c_0$.
hints: Reverse the order: at height $z$, the water spans $-z\le y\le z$.
After the $y$-integral, substitute $u=4z^2$. The cross-section has area 1 in scaled units.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: The V-shaped water cross-section at the dam between the bed z = |y| and the surface z = 1, shaded darker near the bottom, with a horizontal segment at height z running from y = −z to y = z, and a dashed vertical sounding from z = |y| up to 1 labeled as having no antiderivative
hintFigure.caption: Integrate along horizontal lines: at height $z$ the water spans $-z\le y\le z$, and $e^{-4z^2}$ is constant along that line.

solution: Sketch and intersections: the shorelines $y=\pm(1-x^2)$ meet the dam $x=0$ at $y=\pm1$ and meet each other at $x=1$, the upstream tip. At the test point $x=\tfrac12$, the curves give $y=0.75$ and $y=-0.75$, so $y=1-x^2$ is the top curve.

Two descriptions (a): Type I is $0\le x\le1$, $-(1-x^2)\le y\le1-x^2$. Type II is $-1\le y\le1$, $0\le x\le\sqrt{1-|y|}$, because $|y|\le1-x^2\iff x\le\sqrt{1-|y|}$ when $x\ge0$. At $y=0.36$ the upper limit is $\sqrt{0.64}=0.8$, so the lake reaches $0.8L$ upstream along that line.

Both orders: the area is $\int_0^1 2(1-x^2)\,dx=\frac43=2\int_0^1\sqrt{1-y}\,dy$. For the volume factor in Type I, let $c=1-x^2$; then $\int_{-c}^{c}(c-|y|)\,dy=c^2$, and $\int_0^1(1-x^2)^2\,dx=1-\frac23+\frac15=\frac8{15}$. In Type II, $\int_0^{\sqrt{1-y}}(1-y-x^2)\,dx=\frac23(1-y)^{3/2}$ for $y\ge0$, and $2\int_0^1\frac23(1-y)^{3/2}\,dy=\frac8{15}$, which agrees. Type I is easier: it needs only polynomials, with no square roots.

Volume (b): the real area $\frac43LW=1874$ km$^2$ gives $LW=1405.5$ km$^2$, so $V=\frac8{15}LWH=\frac8{15}(1405.5)(0.14)\approx104.9$ km$^3$. Equivalently, $V=\frac25AH$, so the model’s mean depth is $0.4H=56$ m.

Sediment (c): sounding by sounding, $\int_{-1}^1\int_{|y|}^1e^{-4z^2}\,dz\,dy$ needs an antiderivative of $e^{-4z^2}$, which is not elementary. Reversed, $\int_0^1\int_{-z}^{z}e^{-4z^2}\,dy\,dz=\int_0^1 2ze^{-4z^2}\,dz=\frac{1-e^{-4}}4\approx0.245$. The cross-section has area $\int_{-1}^1(1-|y|)\,dy=1$, so the mean concentration is about $0.245\,c_0$: on average, the water at the dam carries about a quarter of the concentration at the deepest point.

Prediction check and reconciliation: the model volume is positive and below the bound $AH\approx262$ km$^3$, but it is above the published 74 km$^3$. That figure means a real mean depth of $74/1874\approx0.0395$ km $=39.5$ m, only $0.28H$, against the model’s $0.4H$. Real reservoirs flood many shallow side valleys that the smooth model ignores, so the model overestimates the volume by about 40%, and the bed shape is the assumption that matters most. The sediment average $0.245$ lies between $e^{-4}\approx0.02$ and $1$, as any average of $e^{-4z^2}$ for $0\le z\le1$ must.
problems.reflection: The model gives about 105 km³, but the published volume is 74 km³. Which assumption is most responsible, and how would you change the bed shape to fix it while keeping the same area and the same depth at the dam?
problems.discussionSolution: The assumed bed shape is most responsible. The smooth bed rises steadily away from the deepest point at the dam, so most of $D$ is fairly deep. Real reservoirs fill branching valleys whose side arms are shallow, so their mean depth is a smaller fraction of the maximum. A depth of $H(1-x^2-|y|)^p$ with $p>1$ keeps the same shoreline $D$, the same area, and the same 140 m at the dam, but makes most of the lake shallower: $p=2$ gives a mean depth of $0.23H\approx32$ m, so $p\approx1.5$ roughly matches the published 74 km³.

data: Reservoir area when full: about 1,874 km² (ASCE)
Storage at full capacity: 74 billion m³ = 74 km³ (ASCE)
Dam height: 145 m (ASCE)
Maximum water depth: about 140 m (secondary), used as the depth at the dam
Reservoir length: up to 246 km (secondary)
assume: Plan coordinates are scaled: $x$ = distance upstream $/L$ and $y$ = distance across the valley $/W$, with the dam on the line $x=0$.
The river bed rises like $x^2$ going upstream and like $|y|$ toward the banks, and the depth at the dam is $H=140$ m $=0.14$ km; this smooth basin ignores the shallow side valleys of the real lake.
At the dam, sediment concentration falls with height above the deepest point of the bed as $c=c_0e^{-(\text{height}/70\text{ m})^2}$; this profile is assumed, because ASCE gives no sediment numbers.
model: $L$, $W$ (km): the lake’s length upstream and its half-width at the dam; $H=0.14$ km: the depth at the deepest point of the dam
Water depth: $H(1-x^2-|y|)$ where this is positive, so $1-x^2-|y|$ is the depth as a fraction of $H$; the lake is $D=\{(x,y):x\ge0,\ |y|\le1-x^2\}$
Area: $A=LW\iint_D1\,dA$; volume: $V=LWH\iint_D(1-x^2-|y|)\,dA$
Dam cross-section, with $z$ = height above the deepest point $/H$: water fills $|y|\le z\le1$, with concentration $c_0e^{-4z^2}$

problems.title: Measuring the Antarctic ozone hole on a grid
problems.context: Every southern spring, a hole opens in the ozone layer over Antarctica. NASA defines the hole as the region where total ozone is 220 Dobson units (DU) or lower; a Dobson unit measures the total amount of ozone in the column of air above a point. NASA reports the hole’s area each day from satellite maps, and on 21 September 2023 it reached its largest area that year, 26.0 million km². A computer finds that area by adding up grid cells, so the answer depends on which cells count. On a coarse grid, how far apart are the smallest and largest areas the cells could give, and how quickly does a finer grid close the gap?
problems.model: NASA publishes the 220 DU definition, the 2023 maximum area, and the 2023 minimum ozone, while the circular hole and the 1000 km square grid are models.
work: Find the radius $r$ of the hole from its area, then draw the circle on a grid of 1000 km cells, with the South Pole at a grid corner.
Shade the cells entirely inside the hole and, in another color, those that touch it.
Explain why the area of the hole, $\iint\chi\,dA$, lies between the two cell counts.
Before (c): predict whether 500 km cells leave about the same gap between the sums, about half, or about a quarter.
Explain where $\chi$ is discontinuous and why the gap must shrink to 0 as the cells shrink.

questions.prompt: With 1000 km cells, find the lower sum: the total area of the cells that lie entirely inside the hole, in million km².
hints: By symmetry, count the cells in one quarter of the grid and multiply by 4.
A cell lies entirely inside when its corner farthest from the pole is within $r\approx2.88$ thousand km of the pole.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: One quarter of the grid, three by three cells of 1000 km, with the 220 DU contour as a quarter circle around the pole. A dot marks the far corner of every cell, and the example cell from 1 to 2 in both directions is highlighted with a dashed line from the pole to its far corner (2, 2); notes give the test (i+1) squared plus (j+1) squared at most r squared, with r squared about 8.28
hintFigure.caption: A cell lies entirely inside the circle exactly when its far corner does; test each far corner against $r^2\approx8.28$.

questions.prompt: With 1000 km cells, find the upper sum: the total area of the cells that meet the hole, even partly, in million km².
hints: A cell meets the hole when its corner nearest the pole is closer than $r$ to the pole. Size check: the upper sum is more than the true area, 26.0 million km$^2$.
In one quarter, even the cell from $(2,2)$ to $(3,3)$ counts, because $2^2+2^2=8<r^2\approx8.28$.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: One quarter of the grid, three by three cells of 1000 km, with the 220 DU contour as a quarter circle around the pole. A dot marks the near corner of every cell, and the example cell from 2 to 3 in both directions is highlighted with a dashed line from the pole to its near corner (2, 2); notes give the test i squared plus j squared less than r squared
hintFigure.caption: A cell meets the hole exactly when its near corner is closer than $r$ to the pole; test each near corner against $r^2\approx8.28$.

questions.prompt: Repeat with 500 km cells, and find (upper sum) $-$ (lower sum), in million km².
hints: Each cell now has area 0.25 million km$^2$. The gap is the total area of the cells that meet the hole but are not entirely inside.
In one quarter, 20 of the 500 km cells lie entirely inside; count the cells that meet the hole with the nearest-corner test.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: One quarter of the grid with 500 km cells and the quarter-circle contour, with three example cells shaded: one entirely inside the circle, one crossed by the circle, and one outside, and a key saying that only the crossed cells count in the upper sum but not the lower sum
hintFigure.caption: The gap between the sums is the area of the cells the contour crosses; count them with the near-corner and far-corner tests, at $0.25$ million km$^2$ each.

solution: Radius: $\pi r^2=26.0$ gives $r=\sqrt{26.0/\pi}\approx2.877$ thousand km, so $r^2\approx8.28$. In the model, $O=99+121(x^2+y^2)/r^2$ DU equals 220 DU exactly when $x^2+y^2=r^2$, so the 220 DU contour is the circle of radius $r$.

1000 km cells: in one quarter, the cell $[i,i+1]\times[j,j+1]$ lies inside when its far corner does, $(i+1)^2+(j+1)^2\le8.28$. That holds for $(i,j)=(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)$, so the lower sum is $4\times4=16$ million km$^2$. The cell meets the hole when its near corner is inside, $i^2+j^2<8.28$, which holds for all 9 cells with $i,j\le2$, so the upper sum is $4\times9=36$ million km$^2$.

500 km cells: one quarter has 20 cells inside and 31 meeting the hole (80 and 124 in all), so the lower and upper sums are $20$ and $31$ million km$^2$, and the gap falls from $20$ to $11$ million km$^2$. The gap is the area of the cells crossed by the 220 DU contour, roughly (perimeter)$\times$(cell size), so it tends to 0 as the cells shrink.

Integrability: $\chi$ is bounded and is discontinuous only on the contour, a curve of zero area, so it is integrable, and every Riemann sum converges to $\pi r^2=26.0$ million km$^2$. A computer’s cell count therefore approaches the true area of the hole as the grid gets finer.

Prediction check and reconciliation: both pairs of sums bracket the true area, $16<26.0<36$ and $20<26.0<31$ million km$^2$. Halving the cell size roughly halved the gap, as (perimeter)$\times$(cell size) predicts, not a quarter as the cell area might suggest. The assumption that matters most for the gap is the shape: a longer, more ragged contour crosses more cells, so a real hole needs a finer grid for the same accuracy.
problems.reflection: NASA’s maps count a cell as “in the hole” when the ozone value reported for that cell is at most 220 DU. Is that more like the lower sum, the upper sum, or a midpoint sum? Why does the choice matter less on a fine grid?
problems.discussionSolution: It is most like a midpoint sum of $\chi$: a cell crossed by the contour counts only when its sample point happens to be inside the hole. Such a sum always lies between the lower and upper sums, and all three differ only on cells crossed by the contour, whose total area shrinks with the cell size. On a fine grid that difference is a small fraction of the 26 million km².

data: Ozone hole: the region with total ozone ≤ 220 DU
2023 maximum hole area: 26.0 million km² (21 September)
2023 minimum ozone: 99 DU (3 October)
assume: The hole is a circle centered on the South Pole, drawn on a flat map; this keeps the published area but not the real shape.
Ozone rises with distance from the pole according to the formula below, which matches the 2023 minimum at the pole and 220 DU at the edge.
The grid is made of square cells, with the pole at a grid corner, so the four quarters of the grid look the same.
model: Ozone (DU), the total ozone above the point $(x,y)$: $O(x,y)=99+121(x^2+y^2)/r^2$, with $x,y$ in thousands of km from the pole
Hole: $O\le220\iff x^2+y^2\le r^2$, where $r$ (thousands of km) is the hole’s radius and $\pi r^2=26.0$ million km$^2$
Area of the hole: $\iint\chi\,dA$, where the indicator $\chi$ is $1$ in the hole and $0$ outside

figure.alt: A circle centered on the South Pole, marked with a plus sign at a grid corner, drawn over a six-by-six grid of 1000 km squares with axes marked from −3 to 3 thousand km; a key beside it names the contour, the pole, and one cell
figure.caption: The model hole: the 220 DU contour, a circle of area 26.0 million km² centered on the South Pole, on a grid of 1000 km cells with the pole at a grid corner.

solutionFigures.alt: Two quarter grids side by side with the quarter-circle contour. With 1000 km cells, 4 cells are entirely inside and 9 meet the hole; with 500 km cells, 20 are entirely inside and 31 meet the hole. Inside cells are green and the crossed cells pink
solutionFigures.caption: Halving the cell size shrinks the pink band of crossed cells, the gap between the sums, from $20$ to $11$ million km$^2$.

weeks.subtitle: Life Is Like a Box of Integrals
skills: Read a region from its limits and reverse the order, including curved (parabolic, cubic, sine) boundaries
Split a region where a boundary formula changes, and combine a sum of integrals into one
Set up triple integrals over boxes and other solids, finding bounds the problem leaves unstated
Project a solid onto each coordinate plane and compare the resulting integrals
Write iterated limits as an inequality chain, and reorder triple integrals that cannot be done as written
formulas: $\displaystyle\iint_D f\,dA=\int_a^b\!\!\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)}f\,dy\,dx=\int_c^d\!\!\int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)}f\,dx\,dy$ for continuous $f$, when $D$ can be described both ways
$\displaystyle\iiint_E f\,dV=\iint_D\Big(\int_{\text{floor}}^{\text{ceiling}}f\,dz\Big)dA$, where $D$ is the shadow of $E$ in the $xy$-plane
Centroid heights: $\bar y=\dfrac1A\displaystyle\iint_D y\,dA$ for a region, $\bar z=\dfrac1V\displaystyle\iiint_E z\,dV$ for a solid

problems.title: The sand mountain of Pilat
problems.context: The Dune du Pilat, on France’s Atlantic coast near Bordeaux, is a wall of sand about 110 m high that creeps 1 to 5 m into the forest every year. The sea wind pushes sand up the dune’s gentle seaward side, the windward face. At the top, the crest, the sand avalanches down the steep forest side, called the slip face. A slice across the dune is a region between two curves. Where is the crest? How much sand lies in each meter of the dune, and how high above the base does that sand sit on average?
problems.model: Width, length, height, and sand volume are published; the parabola-and-line cross-section, its flat base at sea level, and the slip-face angle are model choices.
work: Sketch the cross-section with one horizontal slice (order $dx\,dy$) and one vertical slice (order $dy\,dx$).
After (a): Show the quadratic for the crest, and explain which root you reject.
Check that the slip face slopes at about $34^\circ$, the angle at which dry sand avalanches.
Explain why the order $dy\,dx$ needs two integrals, and where to split.

Before (c): A geologist computes the first moment as \[\int_0^4\!\!\int_0^{\sqrt x/2}y\,dy\,dx+\int_4^{5.5}\!\!\int_0^{(5.5-x)/1.5}y\,dy\,dx.\] Sketch both pieces on one picture, and combine them into one integral in the order $dx\,dy$.
Before (c): Predict: is $\bar y$ above or below $1/3$ unit, the centroid height of the triangle with the same corners?

questions.prompt: Find the crest, where the windward face $x=4y^2$ meets the slip face $x=5.5-1.5y$. Enter $(x,y)$ in model units (1 unit $=110$ m).
hints: The crest is the point that lies on both curves.
Setting $4y^2=5.5-1.5y$ gives $8y^2+3y-11=0$; one root is negative, below the ground.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: The dune cross-section with the windward face x = 4y^2 and the slip face x = 5.5 - 1.5y. The crest, where the two curves meet above the ground, is circled. Dashed extensions of both curves below the ground cross a second time, also circled.
hintFigure.caption: The crest lies on both curves. Extended below the ground (dashed), the same two equations cross a second time, at a root that is not on the dune.

questions.prompt: Find the area $A$ of the cross-section, in square meters. (This is also the volume of sand, in cubic meters, in each meter of dune length.)
hints: In the order $dx\,dy$, a horizontal slice at height $y$ runs from $x=4y^2$ to $x=5.5-1.5y$.
Integrate over $0\le y\le1$, then multiply by $110^2$ to get square meters. Size check: expect more than the triangle with the same three corners, about 33,000 m².
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: The cross-section with one thin horizontal slice at height y, starting on the windward face x = 4y^2 and ending on the slip face x = 5.5 - 1.5y, with thickness dy. An arrow shows y running from the base up to the crest. Heights are drawn twice as tall as widths.
hintFigure.caption: In the order $dx\,dy$, each horizontal slice runs from $x=4y^2$ to $x=5.5-1.5y$, and $y$ runs from the base up to the crest.

questions.prompt: Find the average height of the sand above the base, which is the height $\bar y$ of the cross-section’s centroid, in meters.
hints: The first moment $\iint_D y\,dA$ adds up height × area over thin horizontal strips; the geologist’s sum is this first moment. Divide it by $A$.
Combined, the first moment is $\int_0^1 y\,(5.5-1.5y-4y^2)\,dy$. Divide by $A$ in model units, then convert with 1 unit $=110$ m.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: Top: the cross-section split at x = 4 into two pieces, with a vertical slice in each, matching the geologist’s two integrals. Bottom: the same region with one horizontal slice at height y.
hintFigure.caption: The geologist’s two pieces of vertical slices fill the same region as one stack of horizontal slices. Each horizontal slice at height $y$ adds $y$ times its area to the first moment.

solution: Crest: setting $4y^2=5.5-1.5y$ gives $8y^2+3y-11=0$, which factors as $(y-1)(8y+11)=0$. So $y=1$ or $y=-11/8$. Reject the negative root: it lies below the ground, where the extended curves cross. The crest is $(4,1)$, which is 440 m inland and 110 m high.
Slip-face angle: the slip face drops 1 unit over 1.5 units, so it slopes at $\tan^{-1}(2/3)\approx33.7^\circ$, close to the $34^\circ$ at which dry sand avalanches.

Area in the order $dx\,dy$: a horizontal slice at height $y$ runs from the windward face $x=4y^2$ to the slip face $x=5.5-1.5y$ (test $y=\tfrac12$: $1<4.75$, so the order is right). So \[A=\int_0^1(5.5-1.5y-4y^2)\,dy=5.5-0.75-\tfrac43=\tfrac{41}{12}\] square units. One square unit is $110^2$ m$^2$, so $A\approx41{,}342$ m$^2$: about 41,342 m$^3$ of sand per meter of dune.

Area in the order $dy\,dx$: a vertical slice has top $\min\!\big(\tfrac{\sqrt x}2,\tfrac{5.5-x}{1.5}\big)$, and the formula changes at the crest, $x=4$. So we split there: \[A=\int_0^4\tfrac{\sqrt x}2\,dx+\int_4^{5.5}\tfrac{5.5-x}{1.5}\,dx=\tfrac83+\tfrac34=\tfrac{41}{12},\] the same area.

Combining the geologist’s integrals: the two pieces are the windward and forest-side parts of the same region, so their sum is one integral in the order $dx\,dy$: \[\int_0^1\!\!\int_{4y^2}^{5.5-1.5y}y\,dx\,dy=\int_0^1(5.5y-1.5y^2-4y^3)\,dy=2.75-0.5-1=\tfrac54.\]

Centroid height: $\bar y=\dfrac{5/4}{41/12}=\dfrac{15}{41}\approx0.366$ units, or about 40.2 m above the base. This is above the $1/3$ unit of the triangle with the same three corners. The windward face bulges seaward of the straight line from toe to crest, which adds sand at mid-height and lifts the centroid a little.

Model check: $A$ and $\bar y$ are positive, and $\bar y$ lies between the base and the crest. The model’s base, $5.5$ units $=605$ m, matches the published width of 600 m. But the model holds too much sand: $41{,}342$ m$^2$ times the 2,900 m length is about 120 million m$^3$, more than twice the published 55 million m$^3$. The flat base at sea level matters most: it fills everything below the 110 m crest with sand, but the real dune may rest on higher ground. The real dune also tapers at its ends.
problems.reflection: What if the dune advances 1 m toward the forest in one year, keeping its shape? How much sand must the wind carry over each meter of the crest that year?
problems.discussionSolution: About 110 m³ per meter of crest, far less than the 41,000 m³ of sand in each meter of dune. When the dune shifts 1 m inland, each horizontal slice of sand, at every height from 0 to 110 m, loses a strip 1 m long at its windward end and gains one at its slip-face end. So the slip-face side of the crest gains 1 m × 110 m = 110 m³ per meter of crest, all carried over the crest; only the crest height matters, not the shape of the faces. At the published 1 to 5 m per year, that is about 110 to 550 m³ per meter of crest each year.

data: Width: 600 m
Length: 2,900 m
Height: about 110 m (the brochure rounds all its figures)
Sand volume: 55 million m³
Advance toward the forest: 1 to 5 m per year
assume: The cross-section is the same along the whole length of the dune. This is fair away from the ends, where the real dune tapers.
The dune sits on a flat base at sea level, so sand fills the full 110 m height. If the dune rests on higher ground, the model holds too much sand.
One model unit is 110 m, both across and up, so the picture is to scale.
The windward face is a parabola, gentle near the sea. The slip face is a straight line, because avalanching sand keeps one steady angle.
model: Cross-section $D$: the region bounded by the windward face $x=4y^2$, the slip face $x=5.5-1.5y$, and the base $y=0$
$x$ (model units): distance inland from the dune’s seaward toe; $y$ (model units): height above the base; 1 unit $=110$ m
Average height of the sand: the centroid height $\bar y=\frac1A\iint_D y\,dA$, where $A$ is the area of $D$ and $\iint_D y\,dA$ is the first moment

figure.alt: Cross-section of the dune drawn to scale: a curved windward face rising from the sea side to the crest and a straight, steeper slip face down to the forest side, with one horizontal slice across the region and one vertical slice on each side of the crest
figure.caption: The model cross-section, to scale (1 unit = 110 m). The horizontal slice runs from the windward face to the slip face. The two vertical slices have different tops, one on each side of the crest.

solutionFigures.alt: The cross-section split at the crest x = 4 into a left piece of area 8/3 under y = sqrt(x)/2 and a right piece of area 3/4 under y = (5.5 - x)/1.5. The total is 41/12 square units, about 41,342 square meters. Heights are drawn twice as tall as widths.
solutionFigures.caption: In the order $dy\,dx$, the top changes formula at the crest, so the area splits into $\frac83+\frac34=\frac{41}{12}$ square units.

solutionFigures.alt: The cross-section with the centroid line at y-bar = 15/41, about 0.366 units (40.2 m), just above the line at 1/3 unit (36.7 m) for the triangle with the same corners. The sliver between the curved windward face and the straight edge of the triangle is shaded as extra sand.
solutionFigures.caption: The centroid sits at $\bar y=\frac{15}{41}\approx0.366$ units (40.2 m), a little above the triangle’s $\frac13$ unit (36.7 m): the windward face bulges seaward and adds sand at mid-height.

problems.title: Monterey Bay: a tank, a tide pool, and a hot mussel
problems.context: The Open Sea tank at the Monterey Bay Aquarium holds 1.2 million gallons of seawater. In the model, its water is warmer than a target temperature near the top and cooler near the floor. In the model, mussels live on rocks in the intertidal zone, the strip of shore that the tide covers and uncovers twice a day. NOAA publishes long-term average water levels for Monterey, such as mean tide level and mean high water. Taken as a whole, is the tank’s water warmer or cooler than the target? How many hours is a mussel underwater at each high tide, and how much heat does it build up while the tide is out?
problems.model: The tank’s size and capacity and the Monterey tidal datums are published; the tank’s temperature profile, the sine-shaped tide, and the mussel’s warming rate are assumptions.
work: Sketch the tank from the side; shade where $T-T_0>0$ and where $T-T_0<0$.
After (a): Explain why $\iiint_B1\,dV$ is the tank’s volume, and compare it with the published 1.2 million gallons ($1$ ft$^3\approx7.48$ gal).
Before (b): Predict the sign of $\iiint_B(T-T_0)\,dV$, and explain why all six orders of integration agree.

Before (c): Sketch the region of the band-average integral in the $\theta y$-plane (a mussel at height $y$ is underwater while $\sin\theta>y$), write it in the other order, and explain why the reversed integral is easier.
Prove, by changing the order of integration, that the heat dose is $D=\int_0^\tau(\tau-s)\,r(s)\,ds$. Explain the factor $\tau-s$ in words, and check the identity when $r$ is constant.

questions.prompt: Find the volume $\iiint_B1\,dV$ of the tank model $B$, in cubic feet.
hints: The tank is a box: integrate $1$ over $0\le x\le90$, $0\le y\le52$, $0\le z\le35$ (ft). On a box this is length × width × height.
Size check: the published 1.2 million gallons is about 160,000 ft³.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: Oblique drawing of the tank as a box, 0 to 90 ft in x, 0 to 52 ft in y, and 0 to 35 ft in z, with one small box dV = dx dy dz inside.
hintFigure.caption: Integrating $1$ over $B$ adds up the volume of every small box $dV$; the limits are the three edges of the tank.

questions.prompt: Find the total temperature excess $\iiint_B (T-T_0)\,dV$ of the tank model $B$, in °C·ft³. (It is negative if the water is cooler than $T_0$ overall.)
hints: The integrand depends only on $z$, so the $x$ and $y$ integrals just give a factor of $90\times52$.
Compute $0.1\int_0^{35}(z-20)\,dz$, and check its sign against your prediction.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: Left: side view of the tank with a thin horizontal slab at height z, of area 90 by 52 square feet and thickness dz. Right: the graph of T - T0 = 0.1(z - 20) against height z, positive (shaded warm) above z = 20 ft and negative (shaded cool) below.
hintFigure.caption: $T-T_0$ is the same all across each horizontal slab, so the $x$ and $y$ integrals give the slab area $90\times52$ ft$^2$. The sign of $0.1(z-20)$ changes at $z=20$ ft.

questions.prompt: Mussels are spread evenly in height between mean tide level and mean high water ($0\le y\le1$). Find their average time underwater during one high tide, in hours.
hints: Reverse the order: for $0\le\theta\le\pi/2$, the height runs from $y=0$ to $y=\sin\theta$.
The band has scaled height 1, so the integral is already the average, in radians of phase; 1 rad $=12.42/(2\pi)$ h. Size check: the answer is less than half of the 12.42 h cycle.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: Two copies of the region under y = sin(theta) for theta from 0 to pi/2. Left: a horizontal slice at height y from theta = arcsin y to theta = pi/2. Right: a vertical slice at phase theta from y = 0 up to y = sin(theta).
hintFigure.caption: The same region read two ways. As written, $\theta$ runs from $\arcsin y$ to $\pi/2$; reversed, $y$ runs from $0$ up to $\sin\theta$.

solution: Tank volume: integrating 1 over the box adds up every small volume $dV$, so $\iiint_B1\,dV=90\cdot52\cdot35=163{,}800$ ft$^3$. That is about 1.225 million gallons, within about 2% of the published 1.2 million gallons; the real tank is not a perfect box.

Sign and order: $T-T_0=0.1(z-20)$ is positive above $z=20$ and negative below. The cool layer is 20 ft thick and the warm layer only 15 ft, so predict a negative total. On a box with a continuous integrand, all six orders give the same value (Fubini’s theorem).

Tank integral: the integrand separates, so \[\iiint_B(T-T_0)\,dV=90\cdot52\cdot0.1\int_0^{35}(z-20)\,dz=468(612.5-700)=-40{,}950\] °C·ft$^3$. Dividing by the volume, the water averages 0.25 °C below the target.

Tide setup: the amplitude is $A=(1.412-0.333)/2\approx0.54$ m, and $0.873+0.54\approx1.412$, so $y=1$ is MHW. The tide height is symmetric about $\theta=\pi/2$, so a mussel at height $y$ is underwater for $2\int_{\arcsin y}^{\pi/2}d\theta$ radians per high tide.

Reversing the order: the region is $0\le\theta\le\pi/2$, $0\le y\le\sin\theta$, so \[2\int_0^1\!\!\int_{\arcsin y}^{\pi/2}d\theta\,dy=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\!\!\int_0^{\sin\theta}dy\,d\theta=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin\theta\,d\theta=2\text{ rad}.\] In the original order, the inner integral leaves $\int\arcsin y\,dy$, which needs integration by parts.
In hours: 2 radians of phase is $2\cdot12.42/(2\pi)\approx3.95$ h. On average, a mussel in the band is underwater for about 4 h of each 12.42 h tide cycle.

Heat dose: the region is $0\le s\le t\le\tau$. For fixed $s$, the variable $t$ runs from $s$ to $\tau$, so \[D=\int_0^\tau\!\!\int_s^\tau r(s)\,dt\,ds=\int_0^\tau(\tau-s)\,r(s)\,ds.\] In words: warming at time $s$ keeps the mussel warmer for the remaining $\tau-s$ hours. For constant $r$, both sides give $r\tau^2/2$.

Model check: the tank volume agrees with the published capacity to within about 2%, and the negative total confirms the prediction. The time underwater, about 4 h, is less than half of the 12.42 h cycle, as it must be for mussels above mean tide level. The sine-shaped tide matters most: real tides differ from one high tide to the next, so a single tide can cover a mussel for more or less time than this average.
problems.reflection: Mussels high on the shore spend less time underwater and face longer, hotter low tides. Using the arcsin formula for time underwater, explain why a small step up the rock near mean high water costs much more underwater time than the same step near mean tide level.
problems.discussionSolution: Because the time underwater falls more and more steeply as $y$ approaches 1. The time underwater per tide is $\pi-2\arcsin y$ radians, and its derivative $-2/\sqrt{1-y^2}$ has size 2 at mean tide level ($y=0$) but grows without bound as $y$ approaches mean high water ($y=1$). So near the top of the band, each centimeter higher removes far more underwater time than the same step near mean tide level.

data: Open Sea tank: 90 ft across, 52 ft front to back, 35 ft tall (published dimensions)
Open Sea capacity: 1,200,000 US gallons
MHW (mean high water): 1.412 m above MLLW (mean lower low water), a NOAA long-term average for Monterey
MTL (mean tide level): 0.873 m above MLLW
MLW (mean low water): 0.333 m above MLLW
assume: The tank is a box $B=[0,90]\times[0,52]\times[0,35]$ ft, with $z$ measured up from the floor. The real tank is not a perfect box.

The water temperature $T$ depends only on height: $T-T_0=0.1(z-20)$ °C, where $T_0$ is the target temperature. Warm water floats on cool water, so layers are natural; the straight-line profile is a guess.
The tide is a sine wave about MTL, with amplitude $A=(\text{MHW}-\text{MLW})/2\approx0.54$ m and period 12.42 h. This ignores the differences between one tide and the next.
A mussel is underwater whenever the water level is above it. Waves and splash are ignored.
model: Total temperature excess $\iiint_B(T-T_0)\,dV$ (°C·ft³): positive if the tank is warmer than $T_0$ overall; divided by the volume, it is the average excess
Tide height above MTL: $A\sin\theta$, with phase $\theta$ in radians (1 rad $=12.42/(2\pi)$ h)
Scaled height $y=(\text{height}-\text{MTL})/A$ (no units); the band from MTL to MHW is $0\le y\le1$
Average time underwater in that band, in radians of phase: $2\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\!\int_{\arcsin y}^{\pi/2}d\theta\,dy$

Mussel heat dose after $\tau$ hours out of water: $D=\displaystyle\int_0^\tau\!\!\int_0^t r(s)\,ds\,dt$ (°C·h). Here $r(s)$ (°C/h) is the mussel’s warming rate $s$ hours after the tide leaves it, so the inner integral is its temperature rise after $t$ hours.
