problems.title: Why Greenland looks as big as Africa
problems.context: On the familiar Mercator world map, Greenland looks about as large as Africa. Yet the Democratic Republic of the Congo alone, on the equator, is slightly larger than Greenland. A map projection sends each point of the globe, given by its longitude and latitude, to a point of a flat map. Gerardus Mercator designed his projection so that sailors could steer by straight lines, and that choice stretches areas near the poles. By how much does the Mercator map enlarge areas at Greenland’s latitude, and can a different map keep areas true?
problems.model: The projection formulas and national areas are published values; the spherical Earth and one representative latitude for each country are simplifications.
work: Sketch the Mercator grid near the equator and near $72^\circ$ N (or use the figure), and mark where equal steps in latitude take up more map height.
Decide whether the Mercator map is one-to-one on $(-\pi,\pi)\times(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$, and say what happens to the poles.
Before (b): Explain why (map Jacobian)$/\cos\phi$ is the map’s areal scale factor, using the sphere’s area element $\cos\phi\,d\lambda\,d\phi$.
Before (c): Predict whether Greenland will look larger or smaller than DR Congo on the map, and by roughly what factor.
After (c): Repeat the Jacobian calculation for the cylindrical equal-area map $x=\lambda$, $y=\sin\phi$, and explain its name.

questions.prompt: With $R=1$, enter the Mercator Jacobian $\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(\lambda,\phi)}$ as a function of phi.
hints: $x=\lambda$ does not depend on $\phi$, and $y$ does not depend on $\lambda$, so the Jacobian is $y_\phi$.
Differentiate $\ln\tan(\pi/4+\phi/2)$ with the chain rule, then use $2\sin A\cos A=\sin2A$.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: Left: the longitude-latitude plane with two equal small squares, delta lambda by delta phi, one at latitudes 0 to 10 degrees and one at 60 to 70 degrees. Right: their images on the Mercator map: both keep the width delta lambda, but the one from 60 to 70 degrees is more than twice as tall; each height is labeled approximately y_phi delta phi.
hintFigure.caption: $x=\lambda$ keeps every width, so only heights change: the Jacobian is $y_\phi$, the rate at which map height grows with latitude.

questions.prompt: Using part (a), by what factor does the Mercator map multiply areas at latitude $72^\circ$ N? This areal scale factor is (map area)/(true area) for a small patch, both with $R=1$.
hints: Divide the Jacobian by the sphere’s area factor $\cos\phi$.
The ratio is $\sec^2\phi$; evaluate it at $\phi=72^\circ$. Size check: $\cos72^\circ$ is about 0.3, so expect a factor near 10.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: Left: a globe with parallels and meridians and a small patch near latitude 72 degrees north shaded, labeled area approximately cos phi delta lambda delta phi. Right: the same patch on the Mercator map, a rectangle of width delta lambda and height J delta phi, labeled area approximately J delta lambda delta phi.
hintFigure.caption: The areal scale factor is (map area)/(true area) for the same small patch: divide $J\,\Delta\lambda\,\Delta\phi$ by $\cos\phi\,\Delta\lambda\,\Delta\phi$, then set $\phi=72^\circ$.

questions.prompt: Treat all of Greenland as lying at latitude $72^\circ$ and all of DR Congo at the equator. How many times larger than DR Congo does Greenland appear on the Mercator map?
hints: Multiply each true area by its areal scale factor, then divide.
At the equator the factor is 1.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: Two squares drawn to scale and almost the same size: Greenland, 2,166,086 square kilometers, and DR Congo, 2,344,858 square kilometers. Under Greenland: times the areal scale factor at 72 degrees north. Under DR Congo: times the areal scale factor at the equator.
hintFigure.caption: On the map, each true area is multiplied by the areal scale factor at its own latitude; compare the two products.

solution: Mercator Jacobian: $x_\lambda=1$, $x_\phi=0$, $y_\lambda=0$, and $y_\phi=\dfrac{\tfrac12\sec^2(\pi/4+\phi/2)}{\tan(\pi/4+\phi/2)}=\dfrac{1}{\sin(\pi/2+\phi)}=\sec\phi$, so $J=\sec\phi$.

Areal scale factor: A small patch of Earth has area about $\cos\phi\,\Delta\lambda\,\Delta\phi$, and its image on the map has area about $|J|\,\Delta\lambda\,\Delta\phi$. So the map multiplies areas by $\sec\phi/\cos\phi=\sec^2\phi$, as Snyder states; at $72^\circ$ this is about 10.47. The map is one-to-one on the open rectangle, but $y\to\pm\infty$ at the poles, so the poles never appear on the map.

Greenland versus DR Congo: The apparent ratio is $\dfrac{2{,}166{,}086\times10.47}{2{,}344{,}858\times1}\approx9.7$. This settles the prediction: on the map Greenland looks larger than DR Congo, by a factor of almost ten, although it is about 8% smaller.
Equal-area map: For $y=\sin\phi$, $J=\cos\phi$, exactly the sphere’s factor. The areal scale factor is 1 everywhere, so the map is equal-area, at the price of squashed shapes near the poles.

Model check: The scale factor is positive and grows toward the poles, as the widening gaps between parallels in the figure show. The roughest assumption is the single latitude. Across Greenland’s latitudes, about $60^\circ$ N to $84^\circ$ N, $\sec^2\phi$ runs from 4 to about 90, so 9.7 is a representative value, not a precise one.
problems.reflection: Mercator’s map preserves angles, which made it ideal for navigation. Can a map from the sphere to the plane preserve both angles and areas? What does the Jacobian say?
problems.discussionSolution: No. A map that preserves angles stretches lengths equally in all directions at each point, by some factor k, so it multiplies area by k². Preserving area too would force k = 1, so the map would preserve all lengths. A sphere cannot be flattened without changing lengths, because its curvature is not zero, so every world map must trade shape against area.

data: Surface area of Greenland (UN, land and inland water): $2{,}166{,}086$ km$^2$
Surface area of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (UN, land and inland water): $2{,}344{,}858$ km$^2$
Mercator projection, spherical form (Snyder): $x=R\lambda$, $y=R\ln\tan(\pi/4+\phi/2)$
Cylindrical equal-area projection, spherical form (Snyder): $x=R\lambda$, $y=R\sin\phi$
assume: Earth is a sphere, as in the published spherical formulas. We take $R=1$, which is safe because $R$ cancels from every area ratio we compute.
All of Greenland is treated as lying at latitude $72^\circ$ N, and all of DR Congo at the equator. This is the roughest assumption, since Greenland spans more than $20^\circ$ of latitude.
model: Map $(\lambda,\phi)\mapsto(x,y)$ on $-\pi<\lambda<\pi$, $-\pi/2<\phi<\pi/2$, with longitude $\lambda$ (east positive) and latitude $\phi$ (north positive) in radians
Sphere area element (with $R=1$): $\cos\phi\,d\lambda\,d\phi$; the factor $\cos\phi$ says a patch near the poles is narrower than one at the equator
Areal scale factor: (map area)/(true area) of a small patch at latitude $\phi$

figure.alt: Mercator grid of meridians every 30 degrees and parallels every 15 degrees, from 30 degrees south to about 85 degrees north; the parallels spread farther apart toward the pole. A band for the latitudes of Greenland, about 60 to 84 degrees north, with a dashed line at 72 degrees north, and a band for the latitudes of DR Congo, about 5 degrees north to 13 degrees south, are shaded
figure.caption: Mercator’s map with parallels every $15^\circ$: equal steps in latitude take up more and more map height toward the poles. Shaded: the latitude bands of Greenland and of DR Congo; dashed: latitude $72^\circ$ N.

solutionFigures.alt: Graph of the Mercator areal scale factor sec squared phi against latitude from 0 to 85 degrees, on a log scale, rising from 1 at the equator to 4 at 60 degrees, 10.47 at 72 degrees, and about 92 at 84 degrees; the band of Greenland latitudes, 60 to 84 degrees, is shaded.
solutionFigures.caption: The factor $\sec^2\phi$ is 1 at the equator and $10.47$ at $72^\circ$, but it runs from 4 to about 90 across Greenland’s latitudes.

solutionFigures.alt: Horizontal bars in million square kilometers: Greenland true area 2.17, DR Congo true area 2.34, Greenland on the map 22.68, DR Congo on the map 2.34; an arrow between the two map bars says 9.7 times larger on the map.
solutionFigures.caption: Greenland is about 8% smaller than DR Congo, but after each area is multiplied by its $\sec^2\phi$, Greenland looks $9.7$ times larger on the Mercator map.

solutionFigures.alt: Two map grids side by side, from 15 degrees south to 80 degrees north, with parallels every 15 degrees and meridians every 30 degrees; the bands of Greenland and DR Congo latitudes are shaded. On the Mercator grid the parallels spread apart toward the pole and the Greenland band is tall; on the equal-area grid the parallels crowd together toward the pole and the Greenland band is thin.
solutionFigures.caption: Mercator spreads the parallels apart ($J=\sec\phi$); the equal-area map crowds them together ($J=\cos\phi$), matching the sphere’s own factor $\cos\phi$.

weeks.title: Balance points and blind spots
weeks.subtitle: The Balancing Act
skills: Find centers of mass of planar regions by symmetry, vertex averages, and moments
Predict how a non-uniform density moves the balance point, then compute it
Set up integrals over cones and balls in cylindrical and spherical coordinates, in more than one order
Derive the volume factors r and ρ² sin φ, and use them for volumes, masses, and moments
Evaluate improper integrals by exhaustion, and test power laws for convergence in one, two, and n dimensions
formulas: $\bar x=\dfrac{1}{M}\iint x\,\delta\,dA,\quad \bar y=\dfrac{1}{M}\iint y\,\delta\,dA,\quad M=\iint\delta\,dA$
Cylindrical: $dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz$. Spherical: $x=\rho\sin\phi\cos\theta,\ y=\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta,\ z=\rho\cos\phi$, with $\rho\ge0$ and $0\le\phi\le\pi$ measured down from the positive $z$-axis
For $f\ge0$: $\iint_{\mathbb R^2}f\,dA=\lim_{n\to\infty}\iint_{D_n}f\,dA$ for any regions $D_n$ that exhaust the plane

problems.title: The Gateway Arch balances on thin air
problems.context: The Gateway Arch in St. Louis is a stainless-steel arch 630 feet tall and just as wide. Each leg’s cross-section is an equilateral triangle, widest at the ground and narrowing toward the top. An object’s center of mass is its balance point: the average position of all its mass. For a thin curved band like the arch, that point need not lie in the material at all. Where does the arch balance, and how far down do the thick bases of its legs pull that point?
problems.model: The arch’s width, height, and leg taper are published, while the parabolic outlines and the thickness-weighted density are assumptions.
work: Sketch $A$ and mark where the band is thick and where it is thin. Explain, without integrating, why $\bar x=0$ for both densities.
Locate the centroid of a leg’s cross-section, the equilateral triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(54,0)$, $(27,27\sqrt3)$ (ft), by averaging the vertices, with no integrals.
Before (b): Describe $A$ as (region under the outer parabola) minus (region under the inner parabola), and explain why its mass and moment are differences.
Before (c): Predict whether weighting by leg thickness moves $\bar y$ up or down from part (b). Why?
After (c): Mark both values of $\bar y$ on your sketch, and explain how a body can balance at a point where it has no material.

questions.prompt: Start with one parabolic region of uniform density: the region under $y=h(1-x^2/w^2)$ and above $y=0$, with height $h$ and half-width $w$ in feet. Enter the height $\bar y$ of its center of mass, in feet above the ground, as a function of h and w.
hints: A thin vertical strip at $x$ has area $h(1-x^2/w^2)\,dx$ and balances halfway up, so it adds $\tfrac12h^2(1-x^2/w^2)^2\,dx$ to the moment $M_x$.
The area is $M=\tfrac43hw$. Integrate the strip moments from $x=-w$ to $x=w$ to get $M_x$, then $\bar y=M_x/M$.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: A single parabolic region under y = h(1 - x squared over w squared), from x = -w to x = w, with height h marked. One thin vertical strip at position x, of width dx, is highlighted; its height is h(1 - x squared over w squared), and a dot halfway up the strip marks where the strip balances.
hintFigure.caption: One thin strip at $x$: its area is its height times $dx$, and it balances halfway up, so it adds (area)$\times$(half its height) to $M_x$.

questions.prompt: Using the mass and moment from part (a), find $\bar y$, in feet above the ground, for the uniform arch region $A$.
hints: Subtract the inner region’s mass and moment from the outer region’s, then divide. Size check: the outer region alone balances at $\tfrac25\cdot630=252$ ft, and removing the inner region, which balances lower, should raise that.
Each region has mass $\tfrac43hw$ and moment $\tfrac8{15}h^2w$; use $h=630$, $w=315$ (outer) and $h=613$, $w=261$ (inner).
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: Three small drawings in a row: the outer parabolic region with h = 630 and w = 315, a minus sign, the inner parabolic region with h = 613 and w = 261, an equals sign, and the arch band A that is left over.
hintFigure.caption: The band $A$ is the outer region with the inner region cut out, so its mass and its moment $M_x$ are (outer) minus (inner), each from part (a)’s formulas.

questions.prompt: Now weight the arch by its leg thickness, so it is heavier where the legs are thicker: density $\delta=54-\tfrac{37}{630}y$. Find $\bar y$ for $A$, in feet above the ground.
hints: Let $I_k=\iint_A y^k\,dA$ for $k=0,1,2$. Under $y=h(1-x^2/w^2)$ these integrals are $\tfrac43wh$, $\tfrac8{15}wh^2$, $\tfrac{32}{105}wh^3$; subtract inner from outer.
Then $M=54I_0-\tfrac{37}{630}I_1$ and $M_x=54I_1-\tfrac{37}{630}I_2$, so $\bar y=M_x/M$.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: Left: the arch band shaded by density, darkest at the ground and lightest at the top. Right: a graph with height y up the side and density across, a straight line from 54 at the ground to 17 at the top, y = 630 ft.
hintFigure.caption: The density $\delta=54-\tfrac{37}{630}y$ falls in a straight line from 54 at the ground to 17 at the top, so the low parts of $A$ count more in both $M$ and $M_x$.

solution: Symmetry: the reflection $x\mapsto-x$ maps $A$ to itself and leaves $\delta$ unchanged, because $\delta$ depends only on $y$. So $x\delta$ is odd in $x$, its integral over $A$ is zero, and $\bar x=0$ for both densities. Triangle centroid: averaging the vertices gives $\big(\tfrac{0+54+27}{3},\tfrac{0+0+27\sqrt3}{3}\big)=(27,9\sqrt3)\approx(27,15.6)$ ft, one third of the way up from the base.

One parabolic region: $M=\int_{-w}^{w}h(1-\tfrac{x^2}{w^2})\,dx=\tfrac43hw$ and $M_x=\int_{-w}^{w}\tfrac12h^2(1-\tfrac{x^2}{w^2})^2\,dx=\tfrac{8}{15}h^2w$, so $\bar y=\tfrac25h$, whatever the width $w$.

Arch as a difference: $A$ is the outer region with the inner region removed, so its mass and moment are differences. This gives $M_A=\tfrac43(630\cdot315-613\cdot261)=51{,}276$ ft$^2$ and $M_{x,A}=\tfrac8{15}(630^2\cdot315-613^2\cdot261)\approx1.4372\times10^7$ ft$^3$, so $\bar y\approx280.3$ ft.

Thickness weighting: the legs are thickest at the ground, so the weighting favors low points and $\bar y$ should drop. On each region, $\iint y^k\,dA$ equals $\tfrac43wh,\ \tfrac8{15}wh^2,\ \tfrac{32}{105}wh^3$ for $k=0,1,2$. Subtracting the inner region, $M=\iint_A(54-\tfrac{37}{630}y)\,dA$ and $M_x=\iint_Ay(54-\tfrac{37}{630}y)\,dA$ give $\bar y\approx229.8$ ft, about 50 ft lower than in part (b).

Interpretation: at $x=0$ the steel lies between 613 and 630 ft, so both balance points, $(0,280.3)$ and $(0,229.8)$ ft, sit in the empty space under the arch. The center of mass is an average of positions, and the average of points on a curved band can lie off the band.

Reconciliation: both heights lie between 0 and 630 ft, as an average height must, and the thickness weighting lowered $\bar y$, as the thick bases suggest. The assumption that matters most is how the mass is spread along the band: changing only the density moved $\bar y$ by about 50 ft.
problems.reflection: The NPS also says there is concrete between the skins of the legs up to a height of 300 ft. Would that concrete move the balance point up or down, and why would an arch builder care where the weight is?
problems.discussionSolution: Down. The concrete fills the legs only from the ground up to 300 ft, where the legs are thickest, so its own balance point is well below the arch’s (about 230 to 280 ft in the model), and adding it pulls the combined balance point lower. A lower center of mass makes a structure harder to tip over, which is one reason a builder wants to know where the weight is.

data: Outer width, outside of one leg to outside of the other: $630$ ft
Maximum height: $630$ ft
Leg cross-section: an equilateral triangle
Side of that triangle: $54$ ft at the base and $17$ ft at the top
assume: The arch is a flat band seen from the front, with all its mass in one plane. This ignores the depth of the legs; part (c) puts it back roughly through the density.
The outer edge is the parabola $y=630(1-x^2/315^2)$, which matches the published width and height. The real design curve is different, so the shape is close but not exact.
The inner edge is the parabola $y=613(1-x^2/261^2)$, chosen so the legs are 54 ft wide at the ground and 17 ft thick at the top. In between, the thickness is whatever the two parabolas give.

In part (c), the density is proportional to leg thickness, falling linearly from 54 at $y=0$ to 17 at $y=630$, because a thicker leg has more material behind each square foot of the front view. This is only a rough stand-in for the real taper.
model: The arch is the flat region $A$ between the two parabolas, above $y=0$; $x$ (ft) is the horizontal distance from the arch’s center line and $y$ (ft) is the height above the ground
In part (a), $h$ (ft) is the height and $w$ (ft) the half-width of a single parabolic region
Density $\delta$ (relative units, “the thickness weight”): uniform in part (b); $\delta=54-\tfrac{37}{630}y$ in part (c)

photo.alt: The stainless-steel Gateway Arch against a blue sky, its legs tapering toward the top, with visitors walking on a path beneath it

figure.alt: Front view of the model arch, drawn to scale: a tan band labeled A between two nested parabolas, the outer edge dark and the inner edge teal, 630 ft tall and 630 ft wide, with each leg 54 ft wide at the ground and 17 ft thick at the top. The equations of both edges are printed at the right, above a drawing of a leg’s cross-section at the ground, an equilateral triangle with 54 ft sides.
figure.caption: The model arch $A$, in feet: the band between the outer parabola $y=630(1-x^2/315^2)$ and the inner parabola $y=613(1-x^2/261^2)$. Right: a leg’s cross-section at the ground, an equilateral triangle with 54 ft sides. Notice how much empty space the band encloses.

solutionFigures.alt: Left: the arch band with two mirror-image points at x and -x at the same height, joined by a dashed line, and a note that mirror pairs cancel, so x-bar = 0. Right: the leg’s triangular cross-section with vertices (0,0), (54,0), and (27, 27 root 3), dashed lines from each vertex to the centroid, which is marked at (27, 9 root 3).
solutionFigures.caption: Left: for every bit of mass at $x$ there is a matching bit at $-x$, so $\bar x=0$. Right: the triangle’s centroid is the average of its vertices, $(27,9\sqrt3)$ ft.

solutionFigures.alt: The arch band to scale with two dots on the center line: the uniform balance point at about 280.3 ft and the thickness-weighted balance point at about 229.8 ft. Both dots are in the empty space below the top of the band, where the steel lies between 613 and 630 ft.
solutionFigures.caption: Both balance points, $\bar y\approx280.3$ ft (uniform) and $\bar y\approx229.8$ ft (thickness-weighted), lie in the empty space under the arch, well below the steel at 613 to 630 ft.

problems.title: Weighing Earth’s core without digging
problems.context: No one can dig to the center of Earth, 6371 km below our feet. Yet two numbers measured from outside show that the center is far denser than the surface. One is Earth’s mass. The other is its moment of inertia, which measures how hard it is to change a body’s spin; it is small when the mass sits close to the spin axis. Astronomers find it from how Earth’s spin axis responds to the pull of the Sun and Moon. How dense must Earth’s center be to match both numbers?
problems.model: Earth’s mass, radius, mean density, and moment-of-inertia factor are published, while the smooth quadratic density profile is a model (the real Earth has distinct layers).
work: Sketch a cut through the spin axis, shade where $a-b\rho^2$ is largest, and mark where a kilogram of material adds the most to $I$.

Explain why a small spherical box with sides $\Delta\rho$, $\Delta\phi$, $\Delta\theta$ has edges $\Delta\rho$, $\rho\,\Delta\phi$, and $\rho\sin\phi\,\Delta\theta$, and derive the volume factor $\rho^2\sin\phi$.
Explain why, for a density that depends only on $\rho$, every mass or moment integral over the ball reduces to one $\rho$-integral times an angular factor.
Before (b): Predict whether a ball that is densest at the center has a bigger or smaller $I/(MR^2)$ than a uniform ball. Why?
After (b): Check your prediction: find $I/(MR^2)$ for a uniform ball and compare it with the measured 0.3308. What does that say about where Earth’s mass is?

Check the published data: compute the work per kilogram to lift a mass from the surface to infinity, $\int_R^\infty GM/r^2\,dr$, explain why this improper integral converges, and recover the escape speed.

questions.prompt: Measure distances in Earth radii, so Earth is the ball $\rho\le1$. Enter the mass of the ball with density $\delta=a-b\rho^2$ as a function of a and b (in units of g/cm³ times one Earth radius cubed).
hints: Use spherical coordinates; for a density that depends only on $\rho$, the two angle integrals together give $4\pi$.
With $dV=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$, the radial integral is $\int_0^1(a-b\rho^2)\rho^2\,d\rho$.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: Left: a cross-section of the ball with one thin ring-shaped shell at radius rho highlighted, labeled thickness d rho. Right: a graph of the density a - b rho squared against rho from 0 to 1, starting at a and falling to a - b at the surface.
hintFigure.caption: Cut the ball into thin shells: every point of the shell at radius $\rho$ has the same density $a-b\rho^2$, so only one $\rho$-integral is left after the angles.

questions.prompt: Enter the model’s moment-of-inertia factor $I/(MR^2)$, a pure number, as a function of a and b, where $I$ is the moment of inertia about the spin axis (the $z$-axis) and $R=1$.
hints: The distance to the spin axis is $\rho\sin\phi$, so $I=\iiint(a-b\rho^2)(\rho\sin\phi)^2\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$.
Use $\int_0^\pi\sin^3\phi\,d\phi=\tfrac43$, then divide $I$ by the mass from part (a).
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: A cross-section of the ball through the z-axis. A point at distance rho from the center, at angle phi from the z-axis, is joined to the axis by a horizontal segment labeled rho sin phi, and a dashed circle shows the path the point traces around the axis. Notes say each bit of mass adds delta times (rho sin phi) squared times dV to I.
hintFigure.caption: The moment of inertia weights each bit of mass by its squared distance to the spin axis, $(\rho\sin\phi)^2$, not by $\rho^2$.

questions.prompt: Choose a and b so that the model matches the published mean density, 5513 kg/m³ = 5.513 g/cm³, and the published moment-of-inertia factor, 0.3308. What central density a does the model give, in g/cm³?
hints: The factor depends only on $k=b/a$: solve $\tfrac23(\tfrac15-\tfrac k7)\big/(\tfrac13-\tfrac k5)=0.3308$ for $k$.
The mean density is $M/V=3(\tfrac a3-\tfrac b5)=a(1-\tfrac35k)$. Size check: $a$ is in g/cm$^3$ and must be well above the mean, $5.513$.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: A graph of the factor I over M R squared against k = b over a, from 0 to 1. The curve starts at 0.4 for a uniform ball and falls as k grows. A dashed horizontal line marks the measured 0.3308, and the crossing point is circled with the note: solve for this k.
hintFigure.caption: The factor depends only on $k=b/a$: find where the curve meets the measured $0.3308$, then use the mean density to get $a$.

solution: Volume factor: the box’s edges are a radial step $\Delta\rho$, an arc $\rho\,\Delta\phi$ of a circle of radius $\rho$, and an arc $\rho\sin\phi\,\Delta\theta$ of a circle of radius $\rho\sin\phi$ (the distance to the $z$-axis). Multiplying them gives $dV=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$. For a density that depends only on $\rho$, the angles separate and contribute $\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^\pi\sin\phi\,d\phi\,d\theta=4\pi$.

Mass and moment: $M=4\pi\int_0^1(a-b\rho^2)\rho^2\,d\rho=4\pi(\tfrac a3-\tfrac b5)$. The squared distance to the spin axis is $\rho^2\sin^2\phi$, so $I=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^\pi\!\int_0^1(a-b\rho^2)\rho^4\sin^3\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta=\tfrac{8\pi}{3}(\tfrac a5-\tfrac b7)$, which gives $\dfrac{I}{MR^2}=\dfrac23\cdot\dfrac{a/5-b/7}{a/3-b/5}$.

Uniform check: a uniform ball ($b=0$) gives $I/(MR^2)=0.4$. A ball that is densest at the center keeps more of its mass near the axis, so its factor is smaller, as predicted. Earth’s $0.3308$ is smaller than $0.4$, so its mass is concentrated toward the center.

Fitting the data: with $k=b/a$, the equation $\tfrac23(\tfrac15-\tfrac k7)=0.3308(\tfrac13-\tfrac k5)$ gives $k\approx0.7933$. The mean density is $M/V=a(1-\tfrac35k)$, so $a=5.513/(1-0.6k)\approx10.5$ g/cm$^3$ at the center and $a(1-k)\approx2.2$ g/cm$^3$ at the surface. A center about five times denser than the surface points to a dense core.

Escape check: $\int_R^\infty\dfrac{GM}{r^2}\,dr=\lim_{T\to\infty}\Big[-\dfrac{GM}{r}\Big]_R^T=\dfrac{GM}{R}\approx62.6$ km$^2$/s$^2$, that is, about $6.26\times10^7$ J per kilogram. It is finite because the exponent 2 is greater than 1. Setting $\tfrac12v^2=GM/R$ gives $v=\sqrt{2\times398{,}600/6371}\approx11.19$ km/s, matching NASA’s 11.186 km/s.

Reconciliation: the model matches the mean density and the factor 0.3308 by construction, and the escape integral reproduces NASA’s escape velocity from the published $GM$ and radius. Both the central and surface densities are positive, and the center, about 10.5 g/cm$^3$, is roughly twice the mean. The assumption that matters most is the smooth quadratic: two numbers can fix only two parameters, so a layered profile with the same mass and moment could have a different central density.
problems.reflection: Suppose gravity weakened like 1/r instead of 1/r². Could anything escape Earth? Which one-variable convergence fact decides?
problems.discussionSolution: No. If the pull per kilogram fell like $1/r$, the work to reach distance $T$ would grow like $\ln(T/R)$, without bound, so no finite launch speed would be enough. The deciding fact is that $\int_1^\infty r^{-p}\,dr$ converges exactly when $p>1$; gravity’s $p=2$ is what makes escape possible.

data: Mean radius $R=6371$ km
Mass $M=5.9722\times10^{24}$ kg
Mean density $5513$ kg/m$^3$ (converted: $5.513$ g/cm$^3$)
Moment-of-inertia factor $I/(MR^2)=0.3308$, measured from how Earth’s spin axis responds to the Sun and Moon
Escape velocity $11.186$ km/s
assume: Earth is a ball whose density depends only on the distance $\rho$ from the center. This lets two outside measurements say something about the inside, but it ignores any differences from place to place at the same depth.
The density is a quadratic function of $\rho$, so it has two unknowns that the two measurements can fix. The real Earth has distinct layers, which a smooth quadratic cannot show.
model: Density $\delta(\rho)=a-b\rho^2$ (g/cm$^3$), with $\rho$ the distance from the center in Earth radii ($0\le\rho\le1$); $a$ is the density at the center and $b$ is how much lower it is at the surface, both in g/cm$^3$
$M$ is the mass and $I$ the moment of inertia about the spin axis (the $z$-axis): each bit of mass times its squared distance from the axis, added up
$I/(MR^2)$, the moment-of-inertia factor (no units), compares $I$ with the value it would have if all the mass sat at distance $R$ from the axis

figure.alt: Cross-section of Earth through its spin axis z, shaded green by the model density and darkest at the center. The angle phi is marked from the vertical z-axis, and a small spherical box has edges labeled delta rho and rho delta phi. Notes at the right explain the shading and say that the third edge, rho sin phi delta theta, points out of the page.
figure.caption: Earth cut along its spin axis $z$, as a ball whose density depends only on $\rho$; darker shading means denser. A small spherical box has edges $\Delta\rho$, $\rho\,\Delta\phi$, and $\rho\sin\phi\,\Delta\theta$, with the third edge pointing out of the page.

solutionFigures.alt: A graph of the fitted density against distance from the center in Earth radii. The curve falls from about 10.5 g per cubic centimeter at the center to about 2.2 at the surface. A dashed horizontal line marks NASA’s mean density, 5.513.
solutionFigures.caption: The fitted model $\delta=a(1-k\rho^2)$ with $k\approx0.793$: about 10.5 g/cm$^3$ at the center and 2.2 g/cm$^3$ at the surface, around the published mean of 5.513 g/cm$^3$.

solutionFigures.alt: A graph of the pull per kilogram, GM over r squared, against distance from Earth’s center in thousands of km, starting at about 9.8 times 10 to the minus 3 km per second squared at the surface and falling toward zero. The area under the curve from the surface outward is shaded, with an arrow toward infinity and the note: shaded area = GM/R, about 62.6 km squared per second squared.
solutionFigures.caption: The work per kilogram to escape is the whole area under $GM/r^2$ from $R$ out to infinity. It is finite, $GM/R\approx62.6$ km$^2$/s$^2$, because the pull falls like $r^{-2}$.

problems.title: The radar’s blind cone
problems.context: Finland’s weather radars scan the sky by turning their antennas in full circles, tilting up a little after each turn. The tilt above the horizon is called the elevation angle. In the Finnish schedule the steepest full-circle scan has a 45° elevation, so these scans never sample the air inside an upside-down cone directly above each radar. This blind region is called the cone of silence. How much air does the cone of silence hide, how high is its balance point, and what share of the sky within the radar’s 100 km range is that? Would a different top tilt move the balance point?
problems.model: The 45° top elevation and the 100 km range are published, while the flat ground and straight-line beams are simplifications.
work: Sketch a side view and shade the blind region below height $h$. Describe it in cylindrical coordinates with $r$ innermost, then with $z$ innermost.
After (a): Check your volume against the cone volume $\tfrac13\pi R^2h$, where $R$ is the radius of the cone’s top.
Before (b): Predict whether $\bar z$ lies above or below $h/2$. Why?
After (b): For any top tilt $\alpha$ (cone $z=r\tan\alpha$, $R=h\cot\alpha$), show that $\bar z$ does not depend on $R$.
Before (c): Write the cone $z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ as an equation in $\phi$, and describe the blind region within 100 km in spherical coordinates.
Explain why one radar sample’s volume, $\Delta\rho$ long and $\Delta\phi$ by $\Delta\theta$ wide, grows like $\rho^2$.

questions.prompt: With the 45° top tilt, find the volume of the blind region below height $h$, with $h$ in km. Enter it, in km³, as a function of h.
hints: With a $45^\circ$ top tilt the blind region is $r\le z$, so at height $z$ it is a disk of radius $z$.
Integrate $r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz$ over $0\le r\le z$, $0\le z\le h$, $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: Side view of the blind cone, a V shape opening upward from the radar, with 45 degree sides, cut off at height h. A horizontal slice at height z is drawn as a disk whose radius equals z.
hintFigure.caption: With a $45^\circ$ top tilt, the horizontal slice at height $z$ is a disk $0\le r\le z$; stack the slices from $z=0$ to $z=h$.

questions.prompt: Treat the blind region below height $h$ as a solid of uniform density. Enter the height $\bar z$ of its center of mass, in km, as a function of h.
hints: Slice the region horizontally: the slice at height $z$ is a disk of area $\pi z^2$.
The moment is $\int_0^h z\cdot\pi z^2\,dz$; divide it by the volume from part (a).
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: Left: the blind cone with horizontal slices at four heights, each wider than the one below, and a dashed line at h/2. Right: a graph of slice area pi z squared against height z from 0 to h, rising steeply, with h/2 marked.
hintFigure.caption: The slice area $\pi z^2$ grows with height, so the upper half of the cone holds much more volume than the lower half. Weight each height $z$ by its slice area.

questions.prompt: Within range 100 km, what fraction of the volume of the half-ball of sky above the radar ($\rho\le100$ km, $z\ge0$) lies in the blind cone? Enter a number between 0 and 1.
hints: In spherical coordinates the blind region is $0\le\rho\le100$, $0\le\phi\le\pi/4$, $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.

The half-ball has the same $\rho$ and $\theta$ limits but $0\le\phi\le\pi/2$, so only the $\phi$ integrals differ. Size check: the fraction should be less than one half; can you see why from your sketch?
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: Left: side view of the half-ball of radius 100 km above the radar, with the blind cone between phi = 0 and phi = pi/4 shaded and the ground at phi = pi/2. Right: a graph of sin phi from 0 to pi/2, with the part from 0 to pi/4 shaded for the blind cone and the rest lightly shaded.
hintFigure.caption: Both regions have $0\le\rho\le100$ and $0\le\theta\le2\pi$; only the $\phi$-limits differ. The factor $\sin\phi$ in $dV$ is small near the axis, so the blind cone holds less than its angle suggests.

solution: Blind region: at a $45^\circ$ top tilt the blind region is $z\ge\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, that is, $r\le z$. With $r$ innermost: $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, $0\le z\le h$, $0\le r\le z$. With $z$ innermost: $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, $0\le r\le h$, $r\le z\le h$.
Volume: $V=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^h\!\int_0^z r\,dr\,dz\,d\theta=\tfrac{\pi h^3}{3}$ km$^3$, which matches $\tfrac13\pi R^2h$ with $R=h$.

Center of mass: $\bar z=\dfrac{\int_0^h z\cdot\pi z^2\,dz}{\pi h^3/3}=\dfrac{3h}{4}$, above $h/2$ because the cone widens upward, so most of its volume is high. For a top tilt $\alpha$ the slice at height $z$ has area $\pi z^2\cot^2\alpha$. The factor $\cot^2\alpha$ (equivalently $R^2/h^2$) cancels, so $\bar z=3h/4$ for every $\alpha$ and every $R$.

Spherical description: $z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ becomes $\rho\cos\phi=\rho\sin\phi$, so $\phi=\pi/4$. The blind region within 100 km is $0\le\rho\le100$, $0\le\phi\le\pi/4$, $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, with volume $V=\tfrac{2\pi}{3}100^3(1-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2})\approx6.1\times10^5$ km$^3$. That is a fraction $1-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\approx0.293$ of the half-ball.

Sample volume: a sample has edges $\Delta\rho$, $\rho\,\Delta\phi$, and $\rho\sin\phi\,\Delta\theta$, so its volume is about $\rho^2\sin\phi\,\Delta\rho\,\Delta\phi\,\Delta\theta$. At 100 km a sample is 100 times larger than at 10 km, so the radar averages over far more air at long range.

Reconciliation: every answer is positive, and the fraction lies between 0 and 1. Within 100 km the cone hides about $6.1\times10^5$ km$^3$, nearly 30 percent of the sky above the radar, but below a height of 10 km it holds only $\pi\cdot10^3/3\approx1050$ km$^3$. Flat ground and straight beams matter little this close to the radar; the answers are far more sensitive to the top tilt. For a tilt $\alpha$ the volume below $h$ is $\tfrac13\pi h^3\cot^2\alpha$, so a steeper top scan shrinks the cone quickly, while $\bar z=3h/4$ stays the same.
problems.reflection: Most weather happens below about 10 km. Why does the blind cone matter more for a radar beside a city than for one far from people, and how can a network of overlapping radars fill it?
problems.discussionSolution: Because the blind cone sits directly over the radar, a radar beside a city cannot see the storms right above the city: with a 45° top tilt, the cone is 20 km across at a height of 10 km. Neighboring radars see the same air from the side at low tilts, so radars spaced so that each blind cone lies inside the others’ coverage leave no gap.

data: Highest elevation angle of the full-circle scans in the Finnish schedule: $45^\circ$ (scan group C)
Range of the group C scans: $100$ km
assume: The ground is flat and the beams are straight lines. Near the radar, where the blind cone is, this matters little; it is least accurate far out at low tilts, where Earth’s curve matters.
Each beam is treated as a line with no width. Real radar beams spread out a little, which would make the true blind cone slightly narrower.
model: The radar sits at the origin; $z$ (km) is the height above it, $r$ (km) the horizontal distance from it, and $\theta$ the direction around it
Blind region (cone of silence): the points above the steepest beam, $z\ge\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$; in parts (a) and (b) it is cut off at height $h$ (km)
Part (c): the blind points within range $100$ km of the radar, $\rho\le100$, where $\rho$ (km) is the straight-line distance from the radar

photo.alt: A water tower in Vantaa, Finland, rising above pine trees, with the white dome of a Finnish Meteorological Institute weather radar on its top; a playground in the foreground

figure.alt: Side view, to scale, of the radar with its group C scan beams at elevations of 2, 7, 11, 15, 25, and 45 degrees out to 100 km. The unscanned cone above the 45 degree beams is shaded and labeled cone of silence.
figure.caption: Side view of the Finnish scan group C (tilts 2°–45°, range 100 km). The shaded cone above the steepest, 45° beam is never sampled by these scans; in the model it is $z\ge\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$.

solutionFigures.alt: Two blind cones of the same height h side by side, one with a 45 degree top tilt and one with a 60 degree top tilt, which is narrower. On both, a solid line and dot mark the center of mass at 3h/4, above a dashed line at h/2.
solutionFigures.caption: Whatever the top tilt, the slice areas are proportional to $z^2$, so the balance point is at $\bar z=3h/4$, above $h/2$, for every cone.

solutionFigures.alt: A graph of the blind share of the half-ball, 1 minus sin alpha, against the top tilt alpha from 20 to 90 degrees. The curve rises as the tilt falls. A dot marks the Finnish 45 degree top tilt at 1 - root 2 over 2, about 0.293, below a dotted line at one half.
solutionFigures.caption: The blind share of the half-ball is $1-\cos(\pi/2-\alpha)=1-\sin\alpha$ for a top tilt $\alpha$; at $45^\circ$ it is $1-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\approx0.293$. Steeper top scans shrink it quickly.

problems.title: Starlight and city light at Lick Observatory
problems.context: Lick Observatory, the University of California’s mountain-top observatory near San Jose, needs dark skies. In a 1977 paper, Lick astronomer Merle Walker reported how much the lights of Salinas brightened the night sky at sites at different distances from the city. He found that this sky glow fades with distance $D$ like $D^{-2.5}$. Astronomers also measure a star by adding up all the light in its blurred image on the camera. Both are improper integrals: integrals over a region that never ends, or of a function that blows up. When does adding up light over an endless region give a finite total, and how much does a wider dark zone around the observatory cut the glow?
problems.model: Walker’s Salinas measurements and his $D^{-2.5}$ law are published, while the Gaussian star image and the evenly spread city lights are models.
work: Sketch the dark circle and mark where $(x^2+y^2)^{-b}$ is large and where it is small. Check Walker’s law on his 10.5 km and 16.9 km rows.

After (a): Camera pixels add up light over squares $[-s,s]^2$. Sandwich each square between two disks to show the limit is the same, say why switching exhaustions is legal here, and factor the square integral to find $\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}dx$.
After (b): Redo part (b) on the punctured disk $0<x^2+y^2\le1$. For which $b$ does it converge, and to what? Show that $b=1$ diverges at both ends.

Compare with $\int_0^1x^{-p}dx$ and $\int_1^\infty x^{-p}dx$, and complete: $1/|\mathbf x|^s$ is integrable near the origin of $\mathbb R^n$ exactly when $s<\underline{\quad}$. Does $(x^2+y^2)^{-3/4}$ converge on the punctured disk, outside the unit disk, both, or neither?
Before (c): Predict whether growing the dark zone from 10 km to 40 km in radius cuts the glow by more or less than a factor of 4. Why?

questions.prompt: A star’s image on the camera has brightness $e^{-(x^2+y^2)}$ (arbitrary units, with $x$ and $y$ measured in image widths). Enter the light collected inside a circular aperture of radius $r$ centered on the star, as a function of r.
hints: Use polar coordinates, calling the polar radius $\rho$ because $r$ is the aperture radius: $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^r e^{-\rho^2}\rho\,d\rho\,d\theta$.
Substitute $w=\rho^2$. Check: as $r$ grows, your answer should level off at a finite total.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: Left: the star image, brightest at the center and fading outward, with a circular aperture of radius r and one thin ring at radius rho highlighted. Right: a graph of the ring light, e to the minus rho squared times 2 pi rho, against rho, with the area from 0 up to the aperture edge r shaded.
hintFigure.caption: Add up thin rings: the ring at $\rho$ has area about $2\pi\rho\,d\rho$ and brightness $e^{-\rho^2}$. The light inside the aperture is the shaded area.

questions.prompt: Suppose city lights are spread evenly over the plane outside a dark circle of radius 1 around the observatory, and the glow from lights at distance $D$ is proportional to $D^{-2b}$. For $b>1$, enter $\iint_{x^2+y^2\ge1}(x^2+y^2)^{-b}\,dA$ as a function of b.
hints: In polar coordinates the integrand times the area factor $r$ is $r^{1-2b}$.
Integrate from $r=1$ to $r=T$, then let $T\to\infty$.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: Left: lights spread over the plane outside a white dark circle of radius 1, with one thin ring at radius r highlighted and a dashed circle at radius T. Right: a graph of r to the power 1 - 2b, drawn for b = 1.5, falling from r = 1, with the area from 1 to T shaded.
hintFigure.caption: In polar coordinates each ring at radius $r$ adds $r^{-2b}\cdot2\pi r\,dr$. Integrate from $1$ to $T$, then let $T\to\infty$.

questions.prompt: Use Walker’s law, $2b=2.5$. If the dark zone around the observatory grows from radius 10 km to 40 km, what is the ratio (new glow)/(old glow) for the evenly spread lights?
hints: Redo part (b) with inner radius $a$: the integral is proportional to $a^{2-2b}$.
Here $2-2b=-\tfrac12$. Check: the ratio is a pure number less than 1, because a wider dark zone removes the nearest lights.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: Left: dots for city lights spread evenly around the observatory, with circles at 10 km and 40 km; the dots between the two circles are orange, marking the lights removed when the dark zone grows. Right: a graph of ring glow, proportional to r to the minus 1.5, against ring radius in km, with the area from 10 km on shaded light and the area from 40 km on shaded orange; both tails continue past the edge.
hintFigure.caption: Growing the dark zone removes only the lights between 10 and 40 km; all the lights beyond 40 km still shine. Compare the two tails using part (b) with inner radius $a$.

solution: Data check: Walker’s law predicts the ratio $(16.9/10.5)^{2.5}\approx3.29$ between the two rows, and the table gives $1.91/0.59\approx3.24$, so the law fits these rows well.
Disk exhaustion: $\iint_{D_r}e^{-(x^2+y^2)}dA=2\pi\int_0^re^{-\rho^2}\rho\,d\rho=\pi(1-e^{-r^2})$, which tends to $\pi$ as $r\to\infty$.

Square exhaustion: the square $[-s,s]^2$ contains the disk of radius $s$ and sits inside the disk of radius $\sqrt2s$. Because the integrand is positive, each square integral lies between $\pi(1-e^{-s^2})$ and $\pi(1-e^{-2s^2})$, and both bounds tend to $\pi$. Switching exhaustions is legal because the integrand is positive; for integrands that change sign it can fail. On a square, $\iint e^{-x^2}e^{-y^2}dA=\big(\int_{-s}^se^{-x^2}dx\big)^2$, so $\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}dx=\sqrt\pi$.

Power laws in the plane: outside the unit disk, $2\pi\int_1^Tr^{1-2b}dr=\dfrac{2\pi}{2-2b}(T^{2-2b}-1)$, which tends to $\dfrac{\pi}{b-1}$ for $b>1$ and to $\infty$ for $b<1$. On the punctured disk, $2\pi\int_\varepsilon^1r^{1-2b}dr\to\dfrac{\pi}{1-b}$ for $b<1$ and diverges for $b>1$. At $b=1$ the integrals are $2\pi\ln T$ and $2\pi\ln(1/\varepsilon)$, so they diverge at both ends.

Thresholds: in one variable, $\int x^{-p}dx$ converges near 0 when $p<1$ and at infinity when $p>1$. In $\mathbb R^n$ the volume factor $r^{n-1}$ turns $1/r^s$ into $r^{n-1-s}$, so the threshold is $s<n$ near the origin and $s>n$ at infinity. For $(x^2+y^2)^{-3/4}=r^{-3/2}$, $s=1.5<2$, so the integral converges on the punctured disk (to $4\pi$) but not outside.

Dark zone: with inner radius $a$ the glow is proportional to $\dfrac{\pi}{b-1}a^{2-2b}=4\pi a^{-1/2}$ for $b=1.25$. Going from $a=10$ km to $a=40$ km multiplies it by $(40/10)^{-1/2}=\tfrac12$. Because Walker’s exponent 2.5 is greater than 2, the total glow from all the lights is finite once the observatory has a dark zone; without one ($a\to0$), the nearest lights would make it grow without bound.

Reconciliation: the ratio is positive and less than 1, and the glow falls by only a factor of 2, less than 4. That is a much smaller gain than moving away from a single city: by Walker’s law, a site 4 times farther from Salinas sees $4^{-2.5}=1/32$ of the glow. With lights spread everywhere, the lights just beyond the new edge still shine, so a 4 times wider dark zone only halves the glow. The evenly spread lights are the assumption that matters most.
problems.reflection: If city glow fell only like D⁻², as light spreading through empty space without absorption does, what would happen to the total glow from lights spread over an endless plain, even with a dark zone around the observatory?
problems.discussionSolution: It would be infinite. With exponent 2b = 2 (b = 1), the integral outside the dark zone is 2π ln(T/a), which grows without bound as the plain extends to radius T, so no dark zone could help. Walker’s measured falloff, $D^{-2.5}$, is faster than $D^{-2}$, and that extra half in the exponent is what keeps the total finite and lets distance protect observatories.

data: Walker (1977), published law: sky glow at $45^\circ$ altitude toward Salinas falls with distance as $D^{-2.5}$
Measured visual glow $10.5$ km from Salinas: $1.91$ (natural sky $=1$)
Measured visual glow $16.9$ km from Salinas: $0.59$ (natural sky $=1$)
assume: A star’s image on the camera has brightness $e^{-(x^2+y^2)}$, in units chosen so the image width is 1. This bell shape is an idealization chosen because it can be integrated exactly.

City lights are spread evenly over the plane outside a dark circle of radius $a$ around the observatory, and their glows add. Real lights cluster in towns, so this model shows trends, not exact brightness.
Each patch of lights adds glow that falls off like Walker’s law, as if his measured falloff for a whole city held for every patch.
model: Star: total light $=\iint_{\mathbb R^2}e^{-(x^2+y^2)}\,dA$ (arbitrary units)
Glow at the observatory $\propto\iint_{x^2+y^2\ge a^2}(x^2+y^2)^{-b}\,dA$, where $a$ (km) is the dark-zone radius and $2b$ is the falloff exponent; $2b=2.5$ for Walker’s law

photo.alt: Aerial view looking east from above San Jose over dry, folded hills of the Diablo Range; the white domes of Lick Observatory are tiny specks on the summit of Mount Hamilton near the center

figure.alt: Log-log plot of Walker’s sky-glow measurements toward Salinas against distance from 8 to 36 km, with visual values as filled dots and blue values as open circles, both falling close to a straight line of slope minus 2.5.
figure.caption: Walker’s 1977 measurements of sky glow toward Salinas (filled dots: visual; open circles: blue) on log–log axes, with a line $\propto D^{-2.5}$. On these axes a power law is a straight line, here with slope $-2.5$.

solutionFigures.alt: Left: the star image with three nested outlines: a disk of radius s, the square from -s to s, and a dashed disk of radius root 2 times s. Right: graphs of the light inside each of the three shapes against s; the square curve stays between the two disk curves and all three level off at pi.
solutionFigures.caption: The square $[-s,s]^2$ sits between the disks of radius $s$ and $\sqrt2s$, so its light is squeezed between $\pi(1-e^{-s^2})$ and $\pi(1-e^{-2s^2})$, and all three tend to $\pi$.

solutionFigures.alt: A graph of glow compared with its value at 10 km. A solid curve for a wider dark zone with lights everywhere, (a/10) to the minus one half, falls slowly and reaches one half at 40 km. A dashed curve for moving farther from one city, (D/10) to the minus 2.5, falls fast and reaches 1/32 at 40 km.
solutionFigures.caption: Growing the dark zone from 10 to 40 km only halves the glow, but moving 4 times farther from a single city cuts it to $\tfrac1{32}$, by Walker’s law.

problems.title: The 660-tonne ball inside Taipei 101
problems.context: Taipei 101 is a skyscraper in Taiwan. Near its top, between the 87th and 92nd floors, hangs a 660-tonne steel weight shaped like a ball. It is a tuned mass damper: when strong winds or earthquakes rock the tower, the heavy pendulum swings against the motion and calms it. The weight is built from stacked steel plates, but here we model it as a solid steel ball. How big must a 660-tonne steel ball be, how hard is it to set spinning, and how far below its center does its lower half balance?
problems.model: The 660-tonne mass and the floors are published, while treating the stacked steel plates as a solid ball of uniform steel is an assumption.
work: Sketch the ball with the $z$-axis pointing up, shade its lower half, and mark the steel that adds the most to its moment of inertia about the vertical axis.
Set up the ball’s volume in spherical coordinates.
Set up its moment of inertia about the vertical axis, and explain the extra factor $\sin^2\phi$.
Before (c): Give the spherical limits for the lower half of the ball, and predict whether its center of mass lies more or less than $R/2$ below the center. Why?
After (c): Compare your answer with $R/2$, and explain the difference using the shape of the half-ball.

questions.prompt: Model the damper as a solid steel ball with density 7850 kg/m³. Find the radius, in meters, of a ball with mass 660 t (660,000 kg).
hints: $V=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^R\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta=\tfrac43\pi R^3$.
Set $7850\,V=660{,}000$ kg and solve for $R$. Size check: $R$ should be a few meters.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: Two views of the ball. Side view: the z-axis points up, a radius rho is drawn, and an arc shows phi sweeping from 0 at the top to pi at the bottom. Top view: a circle with an arc showing theta sweeping all the way around, from 0 to 2 pi.
hintFigure.caption: To cover the whole ball, $\rho$ runs from 0 to $R$, $\phi$ from 0 (straight up) to $\pi$ (straight down), and $\theta$ once around, from 0 to $2\pi$.

questions.prompt: Find the moment of inertia of the ball about a vertical axis through its center, in t·m² (keep the mass in tonnes and the radius in meters).
hints: The squared distance to the vertical axis is $x^2+y^2=\rho^2\sin^2\phi$.
You should find $I=\tfrac25MR^2$; use $M=660$ t and $R$ from part (a).
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: A cross-section of the ball through the vertical z-axis, shaded orange by squared distance from the axis, darkest at the left and right edges. A point at distance rho and angle phi is joined to the axis by a segment labeled rho sin phi. Notes give the squared distance x squared plus y squared equals (rho sin phi) squared, and the integral for I.
hintFigure.caption: The steel farthest from the vertical axis counts most: each bit adds $\delta\,(\rho\sin\phi)^2\,dV$, which is where the extra $\sin^2\phi$ comes from.

questions.prompt: How far below the center of the ball, in meters, is the center of mass of its lower half? Give a positive distance.
hints: Use $\pi/2\le\phi\le\pi$; the depth below the center is $-z=-\rho\cos\phi$.
The $\phi$-integral $\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}(-\cos\phi)\sin\phi\,d\phi$ equals $\tfrac12$. Divide the depth moment by the half-ball volume $\tfrac23\pi R^3$.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: A cross-section of the ball with its lower half shaded. A point in the lower half, at distance rho from the center and angle phi from the upward z-axis, has a vertical segment from its level up to z = 0 labeled depth minus rho cos phi. Notes give the limits pi/2 to pi for phi and the depth moment integral.
hintFigure.caption: In the lower half $\cos\phi\le0$, so the depth $-\rho\cos\phi$ is positive. Integrate it over the half-ball, then divide by the half-ball volume.

solution: Radius: $V=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^\pi\!\int_0^R\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta=\tfrac43\pi R^3$. Setting $7850V=660{,}000$ kg gives $R=\big(\tfrac{3\cdot660{,}000}{4\pi\cdot7850}\big)^{1/3}\approx2.72$ m, so the ball is about 5.4 m across.

Moment of inertia: the squared distance to the vertical axis is $x^2+y^2=\rho^2\sin^2\phi$, which is where the extra $\sin^2\phi$ comes from. Then $I=\delta\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^\pi\!\int_0^R(\rho\sin\phi)^2\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta=\delta\cdot2\pi\cdot\tfrac43\cdot\tfrac{R^5}{5}=\tfrac25MR^2\approx1950$ t·m$^2$.

Lower half: it is $0\le\rho\le R$, $\pi/2\le\phi\le\pi$, $0\le\theta\le2\pi$. Its depth moment is $\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\!\int_0^R(-\rho\cos\phi)\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta=2\pi\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{R^4}4=\tfrac{\pi R^4}{4}$. Dividing by the volume $\tfrac23\pi R^3$ gives $\tfrac38R\approx1.02$ m below the center.
Interpretation: $\tfrac38R$ is less than $R/2$, as a good prediction says, because the half-ball is widest near the center, so more of its steel lies near the center than near the bottom.

Reconciliation: all three answers are positive. A ball about 5.4 m across is more than a story tall but fits within the five stories between the 87th and 92nd floors. The assumption that matters most is the solid ball: the real weight is a stack of plates with a flat top, so its true size and moment of inertia differ somewhat from these estimates.
problems.reflection: The real damper is a stack of steel plates of different diameters, not a smooth solid ball. How would you set up its volume as a sum of cylinders, and why would the answer differ slightly from the ball’s?
problems.discussionSolution: Treat each plate as a short cylinder, with volume π(radius)²(thickness), and add up the cylinders. The result is a stepped solid that only approximates a sphere: the corners of the steps add or remove a little steel compared with the smooth ball, so the volume, and hence the radius that gives 660 t, differs slightly from the solid-ball estimate.

data: Mass of the pendulum weight: $660$ t ($660{,}000$ kg)
Hangs between the 87th and 92nd floors
Height of the tower: $508$ m
assume: The weight is a solid ball of uniform steel. Its density, $7850$ kg/m$^3$, is a typical handbook value for steel, not a published figure for this damper.
The real weight is a stack of steel plates with a flat top, so the ball only approximates its shape.
model: The ball is $\rho\le R$ in spherical coordinates, with $R$ (m) its radius, its center at the origin, and the $z$-axis pointing up
$I$ (t·m²) is the moment of inertia about the vertical $z$-axis: how hard the ball is to start spinning about that axis
The lower half is the part with $z\le0$

Right: a graph of slice area pi (R squared minus d squared) against depth d below the center, largest at the center and shrinking to zero at the bottom, with the same two depths marked.

weeks.title: Paths, work, and what depends on the route
weeks.subtitle: The Road Not Taken (Doesn’t Matter)
skills: Parametrize curves, including hanging cables, and compute their speed
Compute length, weight, and centroids with $ds$, independent of parametrization and direction
Compute work and circulation with $\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$ and $P\,dx+Q\,dy$, and explain their signs
Test for path independence, find potentials in 2D and 3D, and use the fundamental theorem
Recognize when equal cross-partials still fail to give a potential
formulas: $\int_C f\,ds=\int_a^b f(\mathbf c(t))\,\|\mathbf c^{\prime}(t)\|\,dt$ (the same in either direction of travel)
$\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_C P\,dx+Q\,dy=\int_a^b\mathbf F(\mathbf c(t))\cdot\mathbf c^{\prime}(t)\,dt$ (reversing $C$ flips the sign)
$\int_C\nabla f\cdot d\mathbf r=f(\mathbf c(b))-f(\mathbf c(a))$ for any path $C$ from $\mathbf c(a)$ to $\mathbf c(b)$
If $(P,Q)=\nabla f$, then $\partial P/\partial y=\partial Q/\partial x$; the converse holds on a domain with no holes

problems.title: Weighing the Golden Gate’s main cable
problems.context: Each of the Golden Gate Bridge’s two main cables is a bundle of 27,572 steel wires. Between the two towers, 1,280 m apart, each cable hangs in a smooth curve. Its sag is the drop from where it meets the towers to its lowest point at midspan. Because the cable curves, it is longer than the span, and its weight depends on that length. How long is one cable between the towers, how much does that stretch of cable weigh, and how high above its lowest point does it balance?
problems.model: The span, sag, and cable weight are published; the parabolic shape and a constant weight per meter of cable are modeling assumptions.
work: Sketch the cable for $-640\le x\le640$ and mark where it is flat and where it is steepest: where does one meter of span hold the least cable, and where the most? Parametrize it as $\mathbf c(t)=(t,y(t))$ and give its $t$-interval.
Check that $\Psi(u)=\big(k\sinh u,\ \tfrac k2\sinh^2u\big)$, $k=12800/9$ m, traces the same curve. Give its $u$-interval and show $\|\Psi^{\prime}(u)\|=k\cosh^2u$.
Parametrize the reversed cable, from the Marin tower to the San Francisco tower, and explain why all three parametrizations give the same length and the same $\int_C y\,ds$.
Predict before (b): is the cable a few meters, tens of meters, or hundreds of meters longer than the 1,280 m span?
After (b): estimate the weight $\int_C\lambda\,ds$ of the main-span cable, and explain why $\int\lambda\,dx$ would underestimate it.
After (c): the flat region between the cable and the line joining its two tops has centroid height $3h/5=86.4$ m. Explain why the cable’s centroid is so much lower.

questions.prompt: Enter the speed $\|\mathbf c^{\prime}(t)\|$ of $\mathbf c(t)=(t,\,9t^2/25600)$ as a function of $t$.
hints: The speed is the length of the velocity vector $\mathbf c^{\prime}(t)$.
Differentiate: $\mathbf c^{\prime}(t)=(1,\,9t/12800)$. Then take its length.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: Left: the parabolic cable with two velocity arrows, a horizontal one at the lowest point and one tilted up along the cable at t = 480. Right: a right triangle with horizontal leg 1, vertical leg 9t/12800, and the speed as its hypotenuse
hintFigure.caption: The velocity $\mathbf c^{\prime}(t)$ always moves 1 m to the right per unit of $t$ and rises by $9t/12800$, so the speed is the hypotenuse of the triangle on the right.

questions.prompt: Find the length $L=\int_C ds$ of the main-span cable, from tower to tower, in meters to two decimal places.
hints: Each short piece of cable has length $ds=\|\mathbf c^{\prime}(t)\|\,dt$, so $L$ is the integral of the speed from part (a), from $t=-640$ to $t=640$.
Substituting $t=k\sinh u$ turns the integrand into $k\cosh^2u\,du$; a calculator’s numerical integral also works. Your answer is in meters and must be more than 1,280.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: Graph of the speed against t from -640 to 640: a curve that equals 1 at t = 0 and rises slightly toward both ends; the area under it is shaded, split into a 1 by 1,280 rectangle and a thin orange sliver on top that is thickest near the towers
hintFigure.caption: $L$ is the whole shaded area under the speed graph: the $1\times1280$ m rectangle plus a thin sliver, thickest near the towers, where the cable is steepest.

questions.prompt: Using part (b), find $\bar y$, the height in meters of the cable’s centroid above its lowest point.
hints: Compute $\int_C y\,ds$ along the cable and divide by the length $L$ from part (b).
Along $\Psi$, $y\,ds=\tfrac{k^2}{2}\sinh^2u\cosh^2u\,du=\tfrac{k^2}{8}\sinh^2(2u)\,du$. Expect a little more than $h/3=48$ m.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: The parabolic cable with 31 dots spaced at equal lengths along it, crowding slightly toward the towers, and a dashed horizontal line at the average height over x, h/3 = 48 m
hintFigure.caption: Each dot marks an equal length, and so an equal weight, of cable; $\bar y=\int_C y\,ds/L$ is the average height of the dots, and their crowding near the towers lifts it a little above $h/3=48$ m.

solution: Parametrization: with the origin at the cable’s lowest point, $y=144(x/640)^2=9x^2/25600$, so $\mathbf c(t)=(t,9t^2/25600)$, $-640\le t\le640$. Then $\mathbf c^{\prime}(t)=(1,9t/12800)$, and the speed is $\sqrt{1+(9t/12800)^2}$. It grows from 1 at midspan to $\sqrt{1.2025}\approx1.097$ at the towers, so one meter of span holds the least cable at midspan and the most at the towers.

Same curve, three parametrizations: the reversed cable $\mathbf c_2(t)=(-t,9t^2/25600)$, $-640\le t\le640$, has the same speed at each point, so every integral with respect to $ds$ is unchanged. For $\Psi$, $y=\tfrac k2\sinh^2u=(k\sinh u)^2/(2k)$ and $2k=25600/9$, so $\Psi$ traces the same parabola for $|\sinh u|\le9/20$, that is, for $|u|\le U=\operatorname{arcsinh}(9/20)$. Its velocity $\Psi^{\prime}=(k\cosh u,k\sinh u\cosh u)$ has length $k\cosh u\sqrt{1+\sinh^2u}=k\cosh^2u$. Each parametrization traces the cable exactly once, so $ds$ is the same arc-length element in all three.

Length: \[L=k\int_{-U}^{U}\cosh^2u\,du=k\,(U+\sinh U\cosh U)\approx1321.97\text{ m},\] about 42 m (3%) more than the 1,280 m span. So the prediction’s answer is tens of meters, not hundreds, because the cable is nearly flat over most of the span.

Weight: $\int_C\lambda\,ds=48.7\times1321.97\approx64{,}380$ kN, about 6,560 t. The estimate $\int\lambda\,dx=48.7\times1280\approx62{,}340$ kN is too small because $dx<ds$ wherever the cable slopes, so it misses the extra length near the towers.

Centroid: \[\int_C y\,ds=\frac{k^2}{8}\int_{-U}^{U}\sinh^2(2u)\,du=\frac{k^2}{8}\Big(\frac{\sinh4U}{4}-U\Big)\approx65047\text{ m}^2,\] so $\bar y\approx65047/1321.97\approx49.20$ m. By symmetry, $\bar x=0$.

Why the cable’s centroid is low: the flat region is widest at the top, so most of its area sits high and its centroid is at $3h/5=86.4$ m. The cable’s weight is spread almost evenly in $x$, and most of the span is low, so its centroid is near the average height $h/3=48$ m.

Reconciliation: one main-span cable is about 1,322 m long, weighs about 64,400 kN, and balances about 49 m above its lowest point. All three are positive and sensible: $L$ exceeds the span, as it must since $ds\ge dx$, and it is more than half of the published 2,332 m length of the whole cable, which runs from anchorage to anchorage. The assumption that matters most is how to read the published 48.7 kN/m. Per meter of cable it gives 64,380 kN; per horizontal meter it gives 62,340 kN. The two differ by only 3%, so the weight is known to about that accuracy.
problems.reflection: The source gives the cable’s weight per horizontal meter. If the weight per meter of cable is constant, is the weight per horizontal meter also constant? If not, where along the span is it largest?
problems.discussionSolution: No. The weight per horizontal meter is $\lambda\,ds/dx=\lambda\sqrt{1+(y^{\prime})^2}$. It equals $\lambda$ only at midspan, where the cable is horizontal, and grows to about $1.097\lambda$ at the towers, where the cable is steepest. (For a real suspension bridge it is the deck’s load per horizontal meter that is nearly constant, which is why the cable hangs as a parabola.)

data: Main span (tower to tower): $1280$ m, published
Half-span: $640$ m, half the published main span
Maximum sag of the main cable: $h=144$ m, published
Cable weight: $48.7$ kN per horizontal meter, published
Diameter of one main cable, with wrapping: $0.92$ m, published
assume: The main-span cable hangs as a parabola, lowest at midspan. A cable carrying an evenly spread deck load hangs very nearly in this shape
The weight per meter of cable is constant, $\lambda=48.7$ kN/m. This matches the published value at midspan, where the cable is horizontal; near the towers the two readings differ by up to about 10%
The cable is a curve: its 0.92 m thickness is ignored, which is fair because it is tiny next to the 1,280 m span
model: Coordinates in meters, origin at the cable’s lowest point: $x$ is the horizontal distance from midspan and $y$ the height above the lowest point. Cable: $y=144\,(x/640)^2$, $-640\le x\le640$
$ds$ (m): the length of a short piece of cable. $\lambda$ (kN/m): the weight of one meter of cable
Weight (kN) and centroid height (m): $W=\int_C\lambda\,ds$, $\ \bar y=\dfrac{\int_C y\,ds}{\int_C ds}$, the height at which the cable would balance

figure.alt: Side view of the Golden Gate main span: two towers, a parabolic main cable that sags 144 m between them, vertical suspenders, and the deck
figure.caption: The model: the main cable as the parabola $y=144\,(x/640)^2$ between the towers at $x=-640$ and $x=640$, with its lowest point at the origin and sag $h=144$ m. The vertical scale is doubled.

solutionFigures.alt: Graph of the cable’s weight per horizontal meter across the span, 48.7 kN/m at midspan rising to 53.4 kN/m at the towers; the rectangle of height 48.7 holds 62,340 kN and a thin orange sliver on top brings the total to about 64,380 kN
solutionFigures.caption: The weight per horizontal meter, $\lambda\,ds/dx$, grows from $48.7$ kN/m at midspan to $53.4$ kN/m at the towers; $\int\lambda\,dx$ counts only the rectangle and misses the orange sliver.

solutionFigures.alt: The flat region between the cable and the line joining the tower tops, shaded, with its centroid marked at 86.4 m, and the cable’s centroid marked at about 49.20 m, just above the dotted line h/3 = 48 m
solutionFigures.caption: The flat region is widest at the top, so its centroid sits at $3h/5=86.4$ m; the cable’s weight is spread almost evenly in $x$, so $\bar y\approx49.20$ m sits near $h/3=48$ m.

problems.title: Sailing around Antarctica: with or against the current?
problems.context: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current flows eastward all the way around Antarctica, driven by strong westerly winds (winds that blow from the west). A ship sailing around Antarctica can go east with the current or west against it. How strongly the water swirls around a closed loop is measured by its circulation: add up, all the way around the loop, the part of the water’s velocity that points along the loop. This is the line integral of the velocity around the loop. How large is the circulation around a voyage that circles Antarctica, how much time does riding the current save, and why does turning the ship around change some totals but not others?
problems.model: The average current speed is published; the route along latitude 60° S, the uniform eastward speed, and the small northward drift are assumptions.
work: Sketch the map: Antarctica, the circle $C$, and $\mathbf u$ at eight points of $C$. Show that the eastward part of $\mathbf u$ turns clockwise and the drift points away from the pole. Mark the westward direction of travel.
Parametrize the westward voyage (counterclockwise on the map) and give its $t$-interval.
Predict before (b): from your sketch, not an integral, will the westward circulation be positive or negative? Explain why the drift adds nothing to $\oint_C\mathbf u\cdot d\mathbf r$.
After (c): explain why reversing the voyage flips the sign of $\oint_C\mathbf u\cdot d\mathbf r$ but not of $\oint_C ds$ or $\oint_C\|\mathbf u\|\,ds$.
At speed $V$ through the water, a ship takes time $\oint_C ds/(V+\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf T)$, with $\mathbf T$ the unit tangent. Show that this is about $L/V-(\oint_C\mathbf u\cdot d\mathbf r)/V^2$.
Estimate the hours an eastward voyage at $V=20$ km/h saves over a westward one.

questions.prompt: Find the length $L=\oint_C ds$ of the voyage around $C$, in km.
hints: Parametrize the circle as $\mathbf c(t)=(\rho\cos t,\rho\sin t)$, $0\le t\le2\pi$, and integrate the speed.
The speed $\|\mathbf c^{\prime}(t)\|$ is constant, equal to $\rho=3185.5$ km. Since $\cos60^\circ=1/2$, expect about half the length of the equator, $2\pi R\approx40{,}000$ km.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: Left: a cut through Earth along its axis, with radius R drawn to the 60 degree south latitude and the horizontal distance rho from the axis to that point. Right: the voyage circle seen from above the South Pole, with a short highlighted arc ds subtending a small angle dt and an arrow showing counterclockwise (westward) travel
hintFigure.caption: Left: the $60^\circ$ S circle has radius $\rho=R\cos60^\circ$. Right: on $\mathbf c(t)=(\rho\cos t,\rho\sin t)$, a small step $dt$ covers the arc $ds=\rho\,dt$.

questions.prompt: Find the circulation $\oint_C\mathbf u\cdot d\mathbf r$, in km²/h, for the westward voyage, which runs counterclockwise on the map seen from above the South Pole.
hints: On a short piece of the voyage, $\mathbf u\cdot d\mathbf r$ is the current’s signed speed along the direction of travel times the distance sailed. The drift is perpendicular to $\mathbf c^{\prime}(t)$, so it gives zero.

Integrate $\mathbf u(\mathbf c(t))\cdot\mathbf c^{\prime}(t)$ from $0$ to $2\pi$. The eastward part gives the constant $\frac{1.8}{\rho}(\rho\sin t,-\rho\cos t)\cdot(-\rho\sin t,\rho\cos t)$. Expect a negative answer: the ship fights the current.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: Left: the voyage circle with black travel arrows pointing counterclockwise outside it, teal current arrows pointing clockwise inside it, and minus signs all around. Right: at one point, the travel direction points up, the eastward part of the current points down, and the drift points sideways at a right angle
hintFigure.caption: Going west (counterclockwise on the map), $\mathbf c^{\prime}(t)$ points against the eastward part of $\mathbf u$ at every point of $C$, while the drift is perpendicular to $\mathbf c^{\prime}(t)$.

questions.prompt: Find $\oint_C\|\mathbf u\|\,ds$, in km²/h, for the same westward voyage.
hints: On the circle $\|\mathbf u\|$ is constant: the eastward part and the drift are perpendicular, with sizes $1.8$ and $0.18$ km/h.
Multiply $\|\mathbf u\|$ by the length from part (a). This scalar integral takes no sign from the direction of travel.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: Left: the voyage circle with equal-length current arrows at eight points, each tilted slightly outward. Right: a right triangle with a long leg of 1.8 km/h along the circle, a short leg of 0.18 km/h outward (drawn 2.5 times longer), and the size of u as the hypotenuse
hintFigure.caption: At every point of $C$ the current is the same right triangle: $1.8$ km/h along $C$ and $0.18$ km/h straight out, with $\|\mathbf u\|$ as its hypotenuse, which never takes a sign.

solution: Orientation and length: seen from above the South Pole, Earth turns clockwise, so eastward is clockwise on this map. The westward voyage is $\mathbf c(t)=(\rho\cos t,\rho\sin t)$, $0\le t\le2\pi$, with $\rho=6371\cos60^\circ=3185.5$ km. Its speed is $\|\mathbf c^{\prime}(t)\|=\rho$, so $L=\oint_C ds=2\pi\rho=6371\pi\approx20{,}015$ km.

Circulation: on the circle the drift $(0.18/\rho)(x,y)$ points straight out and $\mathbf c^{\prime}(t)$ is tangent, so their dot product is zero at every point. The eastward part gives $\frac{1.8}{\rho}(\rho\sin t,-\rho\cos t)\cdot(-\rho\sin t,\rho\cos t)=-1.8\rho$, so \[\oint_C\mathbf u\cdot d\mathbf r=-1.8(2\pi\rho)=-11467.8\pi\approx-36{,}027\text{ km}^2/\text{h}.\] It is negative, as the sketch predicts: going west, the ship moves against the current at every point. Going east (clockwise) gives $+36{,}027$ km$^2$/h, because reversing $\mathbf c^{\prime}$ flips the sign of each dot product.

Scalar integral: $\|\mathbf u\|=\sqrt{1.8^2+0.18^2}=1.8\sqrt{1.01}$ km/h everywhere on the circle, so $\oint_C\|\mathbf u\|\,ds=1.8\sqrt{1.01}\,(6371\pi)\approx36{,}207$ km$^2$/h in either direction. The scalar integral counts the drift and ignores direction. The line integral ignores the drift and keeps direction.

Time saved: since $1/(V+w)\approx1/V-w/V^2$ for small $w=\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf T$, the time is about $L/V-\frac{1}{V^2}\oint_C\mathbf u\cdot d\mathbf r$. The circulation is $+36{,}027$ km$^2$/h going east and $-36{,}027$ km$^2$/h going west, so going east saves about $2(36{,}027)/20^2\approx180$ hours. The exact times $L/(V\pm1.8)$ differ by about 182 hours. A ship that rides the current around Antarctica arrives roughly a week sooner than one that fights it.

Reconciliation: the signs make sense. Going with the current gives a positive circulation and a shorter trip; going against it gives a negative circulation and a longer one. The voyage takes about $L/V\approx1000$ hours, roughly six weeks, so a week is a real but modest saving. The approximation is good because the current is under a tenth of the ship’s speed. The assumption that matters most is the uniform 1.8 km/h: the time saved is proportional to the average current along the route, and the published speeds range from about 10 to 100 cm/s (0.36 to 3.6 km/h).
problems.reflection: The line integral $\oint\mathbf u\cdot d\mathbf r$ has units of area per time (here km²/h). Why is it a natural measure of how strongly water swirls around a loop, while $\oint\|\mathbf u\|\,ds$ is not?
problems.discussionSolution: Because the line integral adds up only the part of the flow along the loop, with a sign. Flow that goes around the loop adds up, while flow that crosses the loop or reverses direction cancels. $\oint\|\mathbf u\|\,ds$ counts every bit of motion as positive, so water drifting straight across the loop or sloshing back and forth would also make it large.

data: Average speed of the Antarctic Circumpolar Current: $50$ cm/s, published; converted, $1.8$ km/h
Range of speeds around Antarctica: about $10$ to $100$ cm/s, published
The current flows from west to east (the West Wind Drift)
Earth’s mean radius: $R=6371$ km, published
assume: The voyage follows latitude $60^\circ$ S exactly, a circle centered on the pole. A real route need not
Along the voyage the current flows due east at its published average, $1.8$ km/h. The real speed varies from place to place
The current also drifts north, away from the pole, at $0.18$ km/h (0.05 m/s), a tenth of the eastward speed. This drift is a modeling choice, not a measurement; it shows which integrals notice it
model: Map: Earth seen from directly above the South Pole, origin at the pole, $x,y$ in km. The $60^\circ$ S circle appears at its true radius $\rho=R\cos60^\circ=3185.5$ km
Surface current near the voyage, in km/h: $\mathbf u(x,y)=\dfrac{1.8}{\rho}(y,\,-x)+\dfrac{0.18}{\rho}(x,\,y)$. The first term is the eastward current; the second is the drift
$C$: the voyage circle $x^2+y^2=\rho^2$
