problems.reflection: A planet orbits twice as far from the Sun as Earth does. Without computing a new integral, what irradiance does it receive, and which part of your work justifies the answer?
problems.discussionSolution: About 340 W/m², one quarter of S. The flux through every sphere centered on the Sun is the same luminosity L, so at distance 2d the irradiance is L/(4π(2d)²) = S/4. Part (a) justifies this: the flux does not depend on the radius, because nothing between the spheres absorbs light.

data: Total solar irradiance at Earth’s distance, measured by satellites at the 2008 solar minimum: $S=1360.8$ W/m$^2$ (it varies by about $0.1\%$ over a solar cycle)
Mean Earth–Sun distance: $d=149.6\times10^6$ km
Earth’s volumetric mean radius: $R=6371$ km
Published luminosity of the Sun (for checking): $382.8\times10^{24}$ W
assume: Sunlight spreads out equally in all directions, and nothing between the Sun and Earth absorbs it. This would fail if gas or dust along the way absorbed light.
Near Earth the rays are parallel. This is reasonable because Earth’s radius is less than a twenty-thousandth of its distance from the Sun.
Earth is a perfect sphere. The real Earth is slightly flattened at the poles, which changes the answers only slightly.
Earth absorbs all the sunlight that reaches it. Any reflection would lower the absorbed power.
model: Sunlight (W/m$^2$), with the Sun at the origin: $\mathbf F(\mathbf r)=Sd^2\,\dfrac{\mathbf r}{|\mathbf r|^3}$, where $\mathbf r$ (m) is the position measured from the Sun’s center and $|\mathbf F|=S$ at distance $d$
Near Earth, with Earth’s center at the origin and the Sun in the $+z$ direction: $\mathbf F=(0,0,-S)$; Earth is the sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=R^2$

Power absorbed per square meter at a day-side point ($z\ge0$): $-\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n=Sz/R$ W/m$^2$, where $\mathbf n$ is Earth’s outward unit normal; $z/R$ is the slant factor, $1$ where the Sun is overhead and $0$ at the day–night line

photo.alt: The full disk of the Sun in ultraviolet light from NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory, with bright active regions and glowing magnetic loops

figure.alt: Left: the Sun at the center of two concentric circles, labeled a1 and a2, crossed by the same straight rays pointing outward. Right: Earth as a circle with parallel vertical sunlight arriving from above; the upper half is highlighted as the day side, z at least 0, and the lower half is labeled night side
figure.caption: The model. Left: the same radial rays cross every sphere of radius $a$ around the Sun, so each sphere catches the same total power. Right: near Earth the rays are parallel, $\mathbf F=(0,0,-S)$, and they light only the day hemisphere $z\ge0$.

solutionFigures.alt: Earth in vertical sunlight with a flat disk of radius R drawn edge-on just above it. The rays that pass through the disk are exactly the rays that hit Earth; rays outside it miss. Text: absorbed power = (S/R) pi R cubed = S pi R squared, about 1.735 times 10 to the 17 watts
solutionFigures.caption: Earth absorbs exactly the sunlight crossing its shadow disk: $S\pi R^2\approx1.735\times10^{17}$ W.

solutionFigures.alt: Left: a thin hemispherical shell cut by equally spaced horizontal lines, with its center of mass marked at height a/2; bands of equal height have equal area. Right: a solid half-ball with its center of mass at 3a/8, below the a/2 level, because most of its volume sits near the base
solutionFigures.caption: The thin shell’s center of mass is at $a/2$, higher than the solid half-ball’s $3a/8$.

problems.title: How much sunlight do Noor’s mirrors catch?
problems.context: Noor Ouarzazate I, in the Moroccan desert, is a 160 MW solar power plant that uses no solar panels. Instead, long curved mirrors called parabolic troughs track the Sun. Each trough’s cross-section is a parabola, so it focuses sunlight onto a pipe running along its focal line. The plant’s mirror field is published by its aperture area, 1,308,000 m$^2$. The aperture of a trough is the flat opening across its top. How much solar power do the mirrors catch, and why is it the aperture area, not the mirror area, that sets this power?
problems.model: The plant’s size, aperture area, and trough dimensions are published; the strength of direct sunlight, perfect tracking, and the absence of losses are assumptions.
work: Sketch the cross-section $z=x^2/6.8$, $|x|\le2.88$, with the focus, three vertical sunbeams, and the upward unit normal at $x=0$ and at the rim. Mark where sunlight hits the mirror most nearly head-on.
After (a): Write $\cos\alpha$ as a function of $x$.
Before (b): Write $\iint_S f\,dS$ over one 12 m module as a double integral over its shadow, including the factor $\sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}$, and spot the cancellation before integrating.
Predict: is the mirror area $\iint_S1\,dS$ of one module larger or smaller than the $5.76\times12$ m$^2$ aperture? Set it up and justify your answer without evaluating.
Decide whether $\iint_S1\,dS$ could ever be the volume of the trough, and say why.

questions.prompt: For the mirror $z=g(x,y)=x^2/6.8$, enter the upward vector area element $(-g_x,-g_y,1)$, the vector that multiplies $dA$ in $d\mathbf S$.
hints: Differentiate $g$ with respect to $x$ and to $y$; the trough is straight along $y$.
$g_y=0$, so only $g_x$ needs simplifying; keep $+1$ as the third component for the upward orientation.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: Left: the right half of the trough cross-section z = x squared over 6.8, with a dashed tangent line at x = 1.7, a slope triangle with run 1 and rise g_x, and an orange arrow (minus g_x, 1) perpendicular to the curve. Right: a view along the trough, where the mirror height at the bottom, at x = 1.7, and at the rim are horizontal lines: the height does not change with y
hintFigure.caption: Across the trough the slope is $g_x$ and $(-g_x,1)$ is perpendicular to the mirror; along the trough the height never changes, which tells you $g_y$.

questions.prompt: Direct sunlight of $900$ W/m$^2$ arrives along every trough’s axis of symmetry. Using the published aperture area of $1{,}308{,}000$ m$^2$, find the total solar power reaching all the mirrors of Noor I, in megawatts.
hints: For one small strip of mirror, $f\,dS=900\cos\alpha\,dS$, and $\cos\alpha\,dS$ is the area of the strip’s shadow: the cosine cancels the area factor.
So the power is $900$ W/m$^2$ times the shadow area, which is the aperture area, summed over the whole field. Expect an answer of order a thousand MW.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: The right half of the trough cross-section with vertical sunbeams falling on one short strip of mirror, highlighted in orange. Directly above the strip, its shadow on the aperture line is a short dark segment labeled dA = cos alpha dS. Labels give the sunlight as 900 W per square meter straight down and the power on the strip as 900 cos alpha dS
hintFigure.caption: Each strip of mirror gets $900\cos\alpha\,dS$ watts, and its shadow on the aperture has area $dA=\cos\alpha\,dS$.

questions.prompt: Sunlight is the field $\mathbf F=(0,0,-900)$ W/m$^2$, and $D$ is the shadow of one module in the $xy$-plane. Which integral gives the solar power, in watts, that hits that module’s mirror?
hints: The vector $(-g_x,-g_y,1)\,dA$ already equals $\mathbf n\,dS$: it includes the area factor.
The option with the length of $\mathbf F$ ignores the angle, so it counts light at full strength even where it strikes the mirror at a slant.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: A small tilted patch dS of the mirror above its flat shadow dA. From the patch rise two arrows in the same direction: the long vector N = (minus g_x, minus g_y, 1), whose vertical part is 1, and the unit normal n of length 1. Text: the length of N is the square root of 1 + g_x squared + g_y squared, the patch area is dS = that square root times dA, so N dA = n dS
hintFigure.caption: $\mathbf N=(-g_x,-g_y,1)$ has length $\sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}$, the same factor that turns $dA$ into $dS$, so $\mathbf N\,dA=\mathbf n\,dS$.

solution: Normal and $\cos\alpha$: $g_x=2x/6.8=x/3.4$ and $g_y=0$, so $(-g_x,-g_y,1)=(-x/3.4,0,1)$. Dividing by its length gives the upward unit normal $\mathbf n$, so $\cos\alpha=\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf k=1/\sqrt{1+x^2/11.56}$. This is $1$ at the bottom, where sunlight strikes the mirror head-on, and about $0.76$ at the rim.

Weighted integral: For one module, \[\iint_S f\,dS=\int_0^{12}\!\!\int_{-2.88}^{2.88}\frac{900}{\sqrt{1+x^2/11.56}}\sqrt{1+\frac{x^2}{11.56}}\,dx\,dy=900(5.76)(12)\approx62.2\text{ kW}.\] The cosine cancels the area factor: a tilted piece of mirror receives less light per square meter by exactly the factor by which it has more area than its shadow.

Mirror area: The mirror area is $\iint_S1\,dS=12\int_{-2.88}^{2.88}\sqrt{1+x^2/11.56}\,dx\approx76.67$ m$^2$. Prediction check: it is larger, about $11\%$ more than the $69.12$ m$^2$ aperture, because the square-root factor exceeds $1$ away from $x=0$. It is an area in m$^2$, never a volume.

Choosing the flux formula: Flux uses $\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S=\mathbf F\cdot(-g_x,-g_y,1)\,dA$ with no extra square root. Here that is $-900\,dA$. The flux of downward light through the upward-oriented mirror is negative, so the minus sign in front turns it into absorbed power. The option with an extra root counts the area factor twice. The one with $\|\mathbf F\|$ gives $900$ W/m$^2$ times the mirror area. The one that divides by the root uses the unit normal but leaves out the area factor in $dS$.

Whole field: Summing over all modules, the power is $900$ W/m$^2$ times the total aperture area, $900\times1{,}308{,}000$ W $=1177.2$ MW. The collected power depends only on the aperture, which is why the aperture area is the number that matters.

Check: The power is positive and about seven times the $160$ MW turbine rating. A gap is expected: the model ignores every loss, and the turbine turns only part of the collected heat into electricity. The assumption that matters most is the $900$ W/m$^2$ arriving along each trough’s axis: the power is proportional to it, and light tilted along the trough lowers it (see the discussion).
problems.reflection: A trough turns about a single axis, its long axis, so the sunlight usually arrives at an angle $\beta$ to the trough’s axis of symmetry, tilted along the trough’s length. Should the collected power then go up, go down, or stay the same, and which factor in your integral changes?
problems.discussionSolution: It goes down, by the factor $\cos\beta$. With the light tilted along the trough, $\mathbf F=900(0,\sin\beta,-\cos\beta)$ W/m$^2$, and since $g_y=0$, $-\mathbf F\cdot(-g_x,-g_y,1)=900\cos\beta$: the constant $900$ in the integrand becomes $900\cos\beta$. Only the component of sunlight along the aperture’s normal is collected. This “cosine loss” is the one that turning about a single axis cannot remove.

data: Turbine capacity of Noor I (electric output): $160$ MW
Solar-field aperture area of Noor I: $1{,}308{,}000$ m$^2$
SENER trough aperture width (2007 design): $5.76$ m
SENER trough focal length: $1.70$ m
SENER collector module length: $12$ m
assume: Every trough is a perfect parabolic cylinder with the published SENER dimensions. That Noor I uses exactly this 2007 geometry is not confirmed.

Direct sunlight of $900$ W/m$^2$, an assumed round value, arrives along each trough’s axis of symmetry (perfect tracking). A trough turns about one axis only, so real light usually arrives tilted along its length.
Gaps, shading, dust, and reflection losses are ignored, so the result is an upper limit on the power collected.
model: Mirror of one module: $z=g(x,y)=\dfrac{x^2}{4(1.70)}=\dfrac{x^2}{6.8}$ over $-2.88\le x\le2.88$, $0\le y\le12$ (meters; $x$ across the trough, $y$ along it, $z$ up)
Sunlight: $\mathbf F=(0,0,-900)$ W/m$^2$, pointing straight down; the focus is $1.70$ m above the vertex
Sunlight per square meter of mirror: $f=900\cos\alpha$ W/m$^2$, where $\alpha$ is the angle between the upward unit normal and the vertical; $\cos\alpha$ is the cosine factor

photo.alt: Rows of parabolic trough mirrors of Noor Ouarzazate I and II stretching across the desert near Ouarzazate, Morocco

figure.alt: Cross-section of the parabolic trough, a U-shaped curve 5.76 m wide, with vertical sunbeams that reflect off the curve to the focus above its center. Orange arrows show the unit normal at the center, pointing straight up, and at the right rim, tilted toward the center; a small arc marks its angle alpha from the vertical
figure.caption: Cross-section of one trough, to scale in meters: the mirror $z=x^2/6.8$, the $5.76$ m aperture, and the focus $1.70$ m above the vertex. Vertical sunbeams reflect to the focus. The orange arrows are upward unit normals $\mathbf n$; at the rim, $\mathbf n$ tilts away from the vertical by the angle $\alpha$.

solutionFigures.alt: Graph across the trough, x from minus 2.88 to 2.88 m: the area factor rises from 1 to 1.31 at the rims, cos alpha falls from 1 to 0.76, and their product is the flat dashed line at 1
solutionFigures.caption: The cosine factor and the area factor cancel exactly, so every strip gets $900$ W per m$^2$ of shadow: $900(5.76)(12)\approx62.2$ kW per module.

solutionFigures.alt: The trough cross-section above two bars: the aperture, 5.76 m wide, giving 69.12 square meters per 12 m module, and the mirror unrolled flat, 6.39 m wide, giving 76.67 square meters per module
solutionFigures.caption: Unrolled, the mirror is $6.39$ m wide against the $5.76$ m aperture: $76.67$ m$^2$ of mirror per module versus $69.12$ m$^2$ of aperture.

problems.title: Walk or run to class in the rain?
problems.context: A winter storm rolls in off Monterey Bay just as you leave a UC Santa Cruz lecture hall. Your next class is 100 m away, and you have no umbrella. Should you walk or run? Physicists still publish on this question. In 2012, F. Bocci showed that the best strategy depends on the shape of the moving body and on the wind. Flux integrals answer the question when there is no wind. How much rain lands on you, as a function of your speed, and does running keep you drier?
problems.model: Typical heavy-rain intensity and drop speed are published; the cylindrical body, still air, and constant speed are assumptions.
work: Sketch your body (the cylinder) from the side and from above, with the rain velocity $(-v,0,-u)$ that you see. Mark where rain comes in ($\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n<0$, outward $\mathbf n$).
With (a): Give the domain of $\Phi(\theta,z)$, decide whether $\Phi_\theta\times\Phi_z$ points outward or inward, and say what listing the parameters as $(z,\theta)$ does.
Compute the flux of $\mathbf F$ through the top disk with the upward normal, and explain its sign.
After (b): On the front half ($\cos\theta>0$), water lands at $g=\rho v\cos\theta$ m$^3$ per m$^2$ of shirt per second. Compute $\iint g\,dS$ there and compare with (b).
Explain why the outward flux of $\mathbf F$ through the whole side is $0$, and why that is not the amount of water you collect.
Predict before (c): running three times as fast, do you collect a third as much water, the same, or something in between? Why?

questions.prompt: For the side parametrized by $\Phi(\theta,z)=(0.15\cos\theta,0.15\sin\theta,z)$, enter $\Phi_\theta\times\Phi_z$ as a function of $\theta$.
hints: Differentiate $\Phi$ with respect to $\theta$ and to $z$, then take the cross product in the order $\Phi_\theta\times\Phi_z$.
$\Phi_\theta=(-0.15\sin\theta,0.15\cos\theta,0)$ and $\Phi_z=(0,0,1)$.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: Left: side view of the body cylinder with a point at height z on its side and an orange arrow Phi_z pointing straight up. Right: the cylinder from above, with x and y axes, a point at angle theta on the circle, and an orange arrow Phi_theta tangent to the circle in the counterclockwise direction; at the point, Phi_z points up, out of the page
hintFigure.caption: $\Phi_z$ points straight up and $\Phi_\theta$ is tangent to the circle, counterclockwise seen from above. Their cross product is perpendicular to both.

questions.prompt: Walking at $v=1.5$ m/s, find the outward flux of $\mathbf F$ (normal pointing away from the cylinder’s axis) through the front half of the side ($\cos\theta\ge0$), in milliliters per second ($1$ m$^3=10^6$ mL).
hints: On the side, $\mathbf F\cdot(\Phi_\theta\times\Phi_z)=-0.15\rho v\cos\theta$; integrate over $-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2$ and $0\le z\le1.7$.
Use $\rho=R/u$ with $R=0.0152/3600$ m/s and $u=6.7$ m/s, then convert m$^3$ to mL. Expect a negative answer smaller than $1$ mL/s in size.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: Left: the cylinder from above, with the front half highlighted from theta = minus pi/2 to pi/2, horizontal rain arrows (minus v) arriving from the right, and outward normals on the front; the label says F dot n is negative there. Right: the front half unrolled into a rectangle, theta from minus pi/2 to pi/2 across and z from 0 to 1.7 m up, shaded darkest in the middle where cos theta is largest, with a small cell dS = 0.15 dtheta dz
hintFigure.caption: On the front half the rain comes in, so $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n<0$, most strongly at $\theta=0$. Integrate over $-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2$, $0\le z\le1.7$.

questions.prompt: You cross the $100$ m at constant speed $v$ (in m/s). Counting only the top disk and the front half of the side, find the total volume of water that lands on you, in mL, as a function of $v$.
hints: The trip takes $100/v$ seconds; multiply the water landing on you per second by this time.
Per second, $R$ times the disk area lands on the top, and $\rho v\cdot2(0.15)(1.7)$ lands on the front. At walking speed expect a few tens of mL.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: Side view of the whole 100 m trip, not to scale: a dashed outline of your body at the start and a solid one at the end. A long blue slab between them is the rainy air your front sweeps through, 100 m long, 2(0.15) m wide and 1.7 m tall, with water fraction rho. Rain falls on the top at rate R on area pi (0.15) squared for 100/v seconds
hintFigure.caption: Two contributions: the top catches rain at rate $R$ for $100/v$ seconds, and the front sweeps through a slab of rainy air $100$ m long.

solution: Picture and signs: In your frame the rain slants down and backward, toward $-x$. It comes in through the top disk and the front half of the side ($\cos\theta>0$), where $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n<0$ for the outward normal. The back half faces away from it.

Orientation: On the domain $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, $0\le z\le1.7$, $\Phi_\theta=(-0.15\sin\theta,0.15\cos\theta,0)$ and $\Phi_z=(0,0,1)$, so $\Phi_\theta\times\Phi_z=(0.15\cos\theta,0.15\sin\theta,0)$. At $\theta=0$ it is $(0.15,0,0)$, which points away from the axis, so it is outward. Listing the parameters as $(z,\theta)$ gives $\Phi_z\times\Phi_\theta=-(\Phi_\theta\times\Phi_z)$, the inward normal; to keep the outward orientation you would have to negate it.

Top disk: The water fraction is $\rho=R/u=(0.0152/3600)/6.7\approx6.30\times10^{-7}$, so rain is less than a millionth water by volume. The top disk has upward normal $\mathbf k$, and $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf k=-\rho u=-R$, so its flux is $-R\pi(0.15)^2\approx-0.298$ mL/s at any speed. It is negative because the rain moves down through a disk oriented up.

Front half: On the side, $\mathbf F\cdot(\Phi_\theta\times\Phi_z)=-0.15\rho v\cos\theta$. Over the front half, \[\int_0^{1.7}\!\!\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}-0.15\rho v\cos\theta\,d\theta\,dz=-2(0.15)(1.7)\rho v\approx-0.482\text{ mL/s}\] at $v=1.5$ m/s. It is negative because the rain enters your body through the outward-oriented front.
Scalar integral: With $dS=0.15\,d\theta\,dz$, $\iint g\,dS$ over the front half gives $+0.482$ mL/s. It has the same size as (b) but is positive, because a scalar integral carries no orientation.

Whole side: The back half has outward flux $+0.482$ mL/s, so the whole side gives $0$: without your body, the rain entering through the front would leave through the back. But your body blocks the rain, so the back stays dry and only the inward flux through the front wets you.

Total water: The trip takes $100/v$ seconds, so \[W(v)=\frac{100}{v}\big(R\pi(0.15)^2+2(0.15)(1.7)\rho v\big)\times10^6=\frac{29.85}{v}+32.14\text{ mL}.\] Walking ($v=1.5$ m/s) collects about $52$ mL and running ($v=5$ m/s) about $38$ mL, so running helps, but only partly. The front term does not depend on speed: you sweep out the same rainy volume however fast you go. Running only shortens the time the top is exposed.

Check: $W(v)$ is positive and falls as $v$ grows, but never below the $32$ mL front term. Prediction check: running three times as fast gives something in between, less water but far more than a third. A few tens of milliliters, a small splash over your head and shirt, fits a short dash through heavy rain. The assumption that matters most is still air: with wind, the front term depends on your speed (see the discussion).
problems.reflection: A 2 m/s tailwind blows the rain forward, in your direction of travel. At what running speed does the front of your shirt stay dry, and what does this suggest about Bocci’s finding that shape and wind matter?
problems.discussionSolution: At 2 m/s. In your frame the rain’s horizontal velocity is 2 − v m/s, which is zero at v = 2 m/s, so only the top gets wet. Running faster wets your front, and running slower wets your back. With wind there can be a best speed, and how much it helps depends on the ratio of top area to front area, that is, on the body’s shape.

data: Heavy rain, intensity (typical value, USGS): $1.52$ cm/h
Heavy rain, median drop diameter (typical): $2.05$ mm
Heavy rain, fall velocity of the drops (typical): $6.7$ m/s
assume: Your body is a vertical cylinder of radius $0.15$ m and height $1.7$ m. This is a crude stand-in: only the top area and the front’s width times height will matter.
The air is still: rain falls straight down at $u=6.7$ m/s. Wind changes the answer (see the discussion).
You move in the $+x$ direction at constant speed $v$, ignoring starting and stopping.
Rain lands only on surfaces moving into it: any drop that would cross your back half has already hit your front, so the back half stays dry.
Your class is $100$ m away.
model: Rain rate $R=0.0152/3600$ m/s: the depth of water that would collect in a flat pan each second
Water fraction of the air (m$^3$ of water per m$^3$ of air): $\rho=R/u$
In your frame the rain velocity is $(-v,0,-u)$ m/s, and the water-flux field is $\mathbf F=\rho\,(-v,0,-u)$ (m$^3$ of water crossing each m$^2$ per second)
Body: side $x^2+y^2=0.15^2$, $0\le z\le1.7$, and top disk at $z=1.7$ (meters)

photo.alt: A rain-soaked footbridge through misty redwood and oak forest on the UC Santa Cruz campus

figure.alt: Left, side view: a tall cylinder 1.7 m high representing your body, moving to the right, with rain arrows slanting down and to the left; the top and the right-hand (front) side are highlighted. Right, view from above: a circle with rain arrows arriving from the right, the front half highlighted and the back half labeled sheltered
figure.caption: The model in your frame: you move in the $+x$ direction, and the rain arrives with velocity $(-v,0,-u)$. The top disk and the front half of the side, where $\cos\theta>0$ (teal), get wet; the back half is sheltered.

solutionFigures.alt: Two views from above at walking speed. Left, with no body: rain passes straight through the cylinder, the front has outward flux minus 0.482 mL/s and the back plus 0.482 mL/s, so the whole side gives 0. Right, with your body: the front still takes in 0.482 mL/s but the back stays dry, so you collect 0.482 mL/s
solutionFigures.caption: Without a body the side’s outward flux is $-0.482+0.482=0$ mL/s; your body blocks the rain, so the back stays dry and you collect $0.482$ mL/s.

solutionFigures.alt: Graph of the water collected, W(v) = 29.85/v + 32.14 mL, for speeds from 1 to 8 m/s. The curve falls toward the dashed line at 32.14 mL, the front term. Walking at 1.5 m/s gives about 52 mL; running at 5 m/s gives about 38 mL
solutionFigures.caption: $W(v)=29.85/v+32.14$ mL: running at $5$ m/s collects about $38$ mL instead of $52$, but never less than the $32$ mL front term.

problems.title: How fast is the universe making room?
problems.context: Distant galaxies are moving away from us, each at a speed proportional to its distance. This is Hubble’s law, and the constant of proportionality is the Hubble constant $H_0$, measured in km/s per megaparsec (one megaparsec, Mpc, is about $3.09\times10^{22}$ m). Two precise measurements of $H_0$ disagree, a puzzle called the “Hubble tension.” The Planck satellite’s map of the cosmic microwave background gives $67.4$ km/s/Mpc, while Cepheid stars and supernovae (the SH0ES team) give $73.04$. Picture a region of space whose boundary moves with the galaxies. How fast does it gain volume, and would an observer in another galaxy measure the same rate?
problems.model: The values of the Hubble constant are published; treating the galaxies as a smooth fluid that moves exactly with the Hubble flow is an assumption.
work: Sketch $W$ with a few velocity arrows on its dome and base. Mark where they cross the boundary outward and where they run along it.
Before (a): Give the outward unit normal on the dome and on the base, and compute $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n$ on each without parametrizing.
Before (b): Explain why the base contributes nothing even though the galaxies on it are moving.
After (b): Say what the ratio of total outward flux to volume means for a region carried along by the flow.
Predict before (c): does a sphere of radius $a$ about another galaxy at $\mathbf p$ have more, less, or the same outward flux as one about us?
After (c): Write $\mathbf v=H(\mathbf r-\mathbf p)+H\mathbf p$, and use symmetry to explain your answer and check your prediction.

questions.prompt: Find the outward flux of $\mathbf v$ (normal pointing away from the Milky Way) through the dome of $W$ (the curved part only): the volume per billion years that the flow carries out through the dome, in Mpc$^3$/Gyr, as a function of $a$.
hints: On the dome $\mathbf n=\mathbf r/a$, so $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n=Ha$ everywhere: on each small patch, $Ha\,dS$ is the volume per Gyr leaving through it.
Multiply by the hemisphere’s area $2\pi a^2$. Units check: Mpc/Gyr times Mpc$^2$ gives Mpc$^3$/Gyr.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: Cross-section of the half-ball W with the Milky Way at the center of the base. Grey velocity arrows v = H r point straight out from the dome, all the same length; a small patch dS on the dome carries the outward normal n = r/a. Text: on the dome the length of r is a, and the dome area is 2 pi a squared
hintFigure.caption: On the dome $|\mathbf r|=a$, so every arrow $\mathbf v=H\mathbf r$ has the same length and points along $\mathbf n=\mathbf r/a$.

questions.prompt: Find the total outward flux of $\mathbf v$ through the boundary of $W$ (dome and base) divided by the volume of $W$, in Gyr$^{-1}$.
hints: On the base the outward normal is $(0,0,-1)$, and $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n=-Hz=0$ there.
The half-ball’s volume is $\tfrac23\pi a^3$. The ratio has units of Gyr$^{-1}$, so $a$ must cancel.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: Cross-section of the half-ball W. Plus signs line the dome, where v dot n is positive. On the base, orange outward normals point straight down, n = (0, 0, minus 1), and grey velocity arrows lie flat along the base, so v dot n = minus H z = 0. The volume of W is two thirds pi a cubed
hintFigure.caption: Outward $\mathbf n$ on the base points down, and $\mathbf v$ lies along the base, so only the dome contributes. The volume of $W$ is $\frac23\pi a^3$.

questions.prompt: Find the outward flux of $\mathbf v$ (normal pointing away from $\mathbf p$) through the sphere of radius $a$ centered on another galaxy at position $\mathbf p$, in Mpc$^3$/Gyr, as a function of $a$.
hints: On this sphere $\mathbf n=(\mathbf r-\mathbf p)/a$, so $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n=Ha+H\,\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf n$.
The constant field $H\mathbf p$ has zero net flux through the sphere, because $\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf n$ changes sign between opposite points.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: Two copies of a circle centered on another galaxy at p. Left: the part H(r minus p) of the velocity, arrows pointing radially out from p, just as they do about the Milky Way. Right: the constant part H p, parallel arrows all pointing the same way; the half of the circle they leave through is marked plus and the opposite half minus, with outward normals n and minus n at two opposite points
hintFigure.caption: Split $\mathbf v=H(\mathbf r-\mathbf p)+H\mathbf p$: the first part is radial from $\mathbf p$; the constant part $H\mathbf p$ leaves through one half of the sphere and enters through the other.

solution: Dome: The arrows point straight away from the Milky Way, so they cross the dome outward everywhere and run along the base. On the dome $\mathbf n=\mathbf r/a$, so $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n=H\,\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf r/a=Ha$, a constant. The flux is $Ha\cdot2\pi a^2=2\pi Ha^3\approx0.433\,a^3$ Mpc$^3$/Gyr with $H=0.0689$ Gyr$^{-1}$.

Base: On the base $z=0$ the outward normal points down, $\mathbf n=(0,0,-1)$, so $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n=-Hz=0$. Galaxies in that plane move along it, not across it. The total outward flux is therefore $2\pi Ha^3$.

Flux per volume: Dividing by the volume $\tfrac23\pi a^3$ gives $3H\approx0.207$ Gyr$^{-1}$, whatever the value of $a$. So a region carried along by the flow gains volume at about $21\%$ per billion years at today’s rate.

Another center: On the sphere about $\mathbf p$, $\mathbf n=(\mathbf r-\mathbf p)/a$ and $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n=Ha+H\,\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf n$. The first term gives $Ha\cdot4\pi a^2=4\pi Ha^3$. The second integrates to zero because opposite points of the sphere have opposite $\mathbf n$. So the flux is $4\pi Ha^3$. Prediction check: it is the same as for a sphere centered on the Milky Way: every galaxy sees the same expansion, and the flow singles out no center.

Check: The fluxes through the dome, the whole boundary, and the sphere are all positive, as they must be when every galaxy moves away from every other. The ratio $3H$ is the same for the half-ball and for both spheres, whatever $a$ and whatever the center. The assumption that matters most is the value of $H$: the SH0ES value raises every answer by about $8\%$ (the ratio becomes $3\times0.0747\approx0.224$ Gyr$^{-1}$). The smooth-flow assumption fails for small regions, where galaxies have motions of their own.
problems.reflection: Compare the ratio of outward flux to volume for the half-ball in (b) and for the sphere in (c). Guess the ratio for a cube of side $s$ centered on us, check it face by face, and say which general theorem this previews.
problems.discussionSolution: The same ratio, 3H, as for the half-ball and the sphere. For the cube centered on us, the face x = s/2 has v · n = Hs/2 and area s², so it contributes Hs³/2; the six faces give 3Hs³, and dividing by the volume s³ gives 3H, which is div v. This previews the Divergence Theorem: the outward flux through any closed surface equals the integral of div v over the enclosed volume.

data: Planck 2018: $H_0=67.4\pm0.5$ km/s/Mpc
Conversion: $100$ km/s/Mpc $=(9.777752$ Gyr$)^{-1}$, so $67.4$ km/s/Mpc $\approx0.0689$ Gyr$^{-1}$
assume: Galaxies move exactly with the Hubble flow, with no local motions of their own, and the Milky Way is at the origin. This describes only regions large enough that local motions average out.
The Planck value $H=0.0689$ Gyr$^{-1}$ is used; lengths are in Mpc and times in Gyr. The SH0ES value would raise every answer by about $8\%$.
model: Velocity field: $\mathbf v=H\mathbf r=H(x,y,z)$ Mpc/Gyr, where $\mathbf r$ (Mpc) is a galaxy’s position and $H$ (Gyr$^{-1}$) is the Hubble constant, the expansion rate
Region $W$: the half-ball $x^2+y^2+z^2\le a^2$, $z\ge0$, of radius $a$ (Mpc), bounded by a dome and a flat base disk in the plane $z=0$

photo.alt: The Hubble Ultra Deep Field: thousands of distant galaxies of many shapes and colors scattered across a black sky
photo.credit: NASA and the European Space Agency

figure.alt: Cross-section of the half-ball region: a semicircular dome on a flat base, with the Milky Way at the center of the base. Velocity arrows point straight out from the center and get longer farther away; the arrows on the base lie along it
figure.caption: Cross-section of the region $W$: the dome, the base $z=0$, and the Hubble-flow arrows $\mathbf v=H\mathbf r$, which grow with distance from the Milky Way at the center. On the base the arrows lie along it, not across it.

solutionFigures.alt: Three nested half-balls of different radii sharing the Milky Way at the center of the base. Text: dome flux 2 pi H a cubed, about 0.433 a cubed Mpc cubed per Gyr; base flux 0; volume two thirds pi a cubed; ratio 3H, about 0.207 per Gyr, for every a
solutionFigures.caption: Flux and volume both grow like $a^3$, so every half-ball gains volume at the same rate, $3H\approx0.207$ Gyr$^{-1}$.

solutionFigures.alt: Two copies of the same square grid of galaxies. Left: velocity arrows as seen from the Milky Way at the center, all pointing away from it and longer farther out. Right: the same galaxies seen from another galaxy at p, with its velocity subtracted; the arrows now point away from p in exactly the same pattern
solutionFigures.caption: Seen from the galaxy at $\mathbf p$, the relative velocities $H(\mathbf r-\mathbf p)$ form the same pattern, so the flux about $\mathbf p$ is again $4\pi Ha^3$.

problems.title: Saharan dust across the Atlantic
problems.context: Every year winds carry dust from the Sahara west across the Atlantic. Using NASA’s CALIPSO satellite observations from 2007 to 2013, scientists estimated how much dust crosses imaginary vertical “curtains” of air at fixed longitudes, and how much falls on the Amazon basin, where it feeds the rainforest’s plants. How much dust crosses each square meter of a curtain, does tilting the curtain change the total, and how much dust falls into the ocean between two curtains?
problems.model: The yearly dust totals are published multi-year averages; the curtain size, horizontal westward motion, and steady state are assumptions.
work: Sketch the $15^\circ$W curtain and the closed box from it to the $35^\circ$W curtain. Mark each outward normal and whether dust goes in or out.
Predict before (b): does tilting the curtain increase, decrease, or keep the dust flux through it? Why?
Before (b): For the tilted curtain $x=g(y,z)=-z/5$ with $\Phi(y,z)=(g(y,z),y,z)$, compute $\Phi_y\times\Phi_z$, say whether it points east or west, and write the westward vector area element.
After (b): Check your prediction, and explain it using the curtain’s shadow on the plane $x=0$.
Before (c): Write the dust budget for the closed box face by face (east, west, bottom, top, sides), and explain why in steady state its total outward flux is zero.

questions.prompt: Find the average westward dust flux through the $15^\circ$W curtain, that is, the mass of dust crossing an average square meter of the curtain each year, in kilograms per square meter per year.
hints: The average flux is the yearly mass divided by the curtain’s area; $182$ million tonnes is $1.82\times10^{11}$ kg.
The curtain is $3000$ km by $5$ km; convert both to meters before dividing. Expect roughly ten kilograms per square meter per year.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: The 15 degrees west curtain seen from the east, drawn as a long rectangle 3000 km wide (south to north) and 5 km tall, not to scale. Symbols show dust moving away from the viewer, westward. One small orange square marks a single square meter. Text: 182 million tonnes per year cross the whole curtain; 1 km = 1000 m and 1 tonne = 1000 kg
hintFigure.caption: The average flux is the yearly mass through the whole curtain divided by its area; convert km to m and tonnes to kg first.

questions.prompt: Find the westward flux of dust (normal pointing west, toward South America) through the tilted curtain $x=-z/5$ (same $y$ and $z$ ranges), in millions of tonnes per year.
hints: With the westward element $(-1,g_y,g_z)\,dy\,dz$, $\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S=f(y,z)\,dy\,dz$.
Compare this integrand and its $(y,z)$ rectangle with the vertical curtain’s.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: View from the south, x east and z up in km. The vertical curtain x = 0 is dashed; the tilted curtain x = minus z/5 leans 1 km west at its top, 5 km up. Horizontal dust arrows F = (minus f, 0, 0) cross both. An orange westward normal points out of the tilted curtain toward the west. Text: Phi(y, z) = (minus z/5, y, z) over the same (y, z) rectangle
hintFigure.caption: The tilted curtain $x=-z/5$ uses the same $(y,z)$ rectangle as the vertical one; take its normal pointing west and compare the integrands.

questions.prompt: Using the closed box between the $15^\circ$W and $35^\circ$W curtains, find how much dust per year falls into the ocean between them, in millions of tonnes.
hints: Outward flux: $-182$ through the east face (dust enters) and $+132$ through the west face.
The bottom’s outward normal points down; the top and sides carry nothing in the model.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: Cross-section of the closed box between the curtains, with orange outward normals on all four drawn faces. Dust arrows enter through the east face (15 degrees west, outward flux minus 182) and leave through the west face (35 degrees west, outward flux plus 132). The top carries 0, and the bottom carries the unknown D, outward meaning down into the ocean. Text: steady state, total outward flux = 0
hintFigure.caption: Add the outward fluxes face by face: $-182$ (east), $+132$ (west), $0$ (top and sides), and $D$ (bottom). In steady state they sum to zero.

solution: Average flux: $182$ million tonnes per year is $1.82\times10^{11}$ kg per year. The curtain’s area is $(3\times10^6)(5\times10^3)=1.5\times10^{10}$ m$^2$, so the average flux is the total divided by the area, about $12.13$ kg per m$^2$ per year.

Tilted curtain: For $\Phi(y,z)=(-z/5,y,z)$, $\Phi_y=(0,1,0)$ and $\Phi_z=(-\tfrac15,0,1)$, so $\Phi_y\times\Phi_z=(1,0,\tfrac15)$, which points east. The westward element is therefore $(-1,0,-\tfrac15)\,dy\,dz$. With $\mathbf F=(-f,0,0)$, $\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S=f\,dy\,dz$: the same integrand over the same rectangle as for the vertical curtain, so the flux is still $182$ Mt/yr.

Prediction check: Tilting keeps the flux the same. The dust moves horizontally, so only the curtain’s shadow on the plane $x=0$, perpendicular to the flow, matters. The tilted curtain and the vertical one have the same shadow.

Box budget: Dust flows in through the east face and out through the west face and the bottom. The outward fluxes are $-182$ Mt/yr through the east face (dust entering), $+132$ Mt/yr through the west face, and $0$ through the top and sides by assumption. The bottom, whose outward normal points down, carries the deposition $D$. In steady state no dust is created or stored inside, so the total outward flux is zero: $-182+132+D=0$, which gives $D=50$ Mt/yr.

Interpretation: Of the $182$ Mt/yr that crosses $15^\circ$W, about $50$ Mt/yr falls into the ocean before $35^\circ$W. Farther west, about $27.7$ Mt/yr ($15\%$ of $182$) falls on the Amazon basin, and about $43$ Mt/yr travels past $75^\circ$W to the Caribbean.

Check: $D=50$ Mt/yr is positive, as a deposition must be, and it is a little over a quarter of the dust entering the box. The assumption that matters most is that nothing crosses the top or the sides: any dust leaving that way would be wrongly counted as falling into the ocean.
problems.reflection: Compare your answers for the vertical and the tilted curtain. What assumption about the dust’s motion decided that comparison, and would it still hold if the dust were also settling downward?
problems.discussionSolution: The assumption that the dust moves horizontally. The vertical curtain, the tilted curtain, the 1 km wide strip joining their top edges, and the two triangular ends enclose a thin wedge. With horizontal flow no dust crosses the top strip or the ends, and in steady state none is created or stored inside, so the two curtains carry the same flux. If the dust also settles downward, this fails: dust falls into the wedge through the top strip and leaves through the tilted curtain, so the tilted curtain carries slightly more than the vertical one.

data: Dust carried past $15^\circ$W: $182$ million tonnes per year (CALIPSO-based average, 2007–2013)
Still airborne at $35^\circ$W: $132$ million tonnes per year
Falling on the Amazon basin: $27.7$ million tonnes per year
Traveling past $75^\circ$W toward the Caribbean: about $43$ million tonnes per year
NASA reports these in “tons,” read here as metric tonnes
assume: The curtain at $15^\circ$W is a vertical rectangle $3000$ km wide (north–south) and $5$ km tall. Its size is assumed, and only part (a) depends on it.

Dust moves horizontally westward, so nothing crosses the top or the north and south sides of the box between $15^\circ$W and $35^\circ$W. Dust that falls out is counted only where it leaves through the box’s bottom.
Steady state: the yearly averages do not change with time, so no dust piles up inside the box.
model: $x$ east, $y$ north, $z$ up (km); curtain: $x=0$, $0\le y\le3000$, $0\le z\le5$
Dust mass flux: $\mathbf F=(-f(y,z),0,0)$, pointing west, where $f(y,z)\ge0$ is the dust mass crossing a unit area of curtain per year; $\iint f\,dy\,dz=182$ Mt/yr over the curtain
Tilted curtain: $x=-z/5$ over the same $y$, $z$ rectangle

figure.alt: Schematic of the tropical Atlantic with West Africa on the right and South America on the left. Two vertical curtains, at 15 degrees west and 35 degrees west, bound a closed box. Westward dust arrows are labeled 182 and 132 million tonnes per year, arrows from the box floor mark an unknown deposition, and a dashed arrow labeled 27.7 points to the Amazon
figure.caption: Schematic, not to scale: the curtains at $15^\circ$W and $35^\circ$W with the published yearly dust totals ($182$ and $132$ million tonnes), and the closed box between them. The deposition through the box’s bottom is the unknown.

solutionFigures.alt: View from the south of the thin wedge between the vertical and the tilted curtain. Each horizontal dust arrow crosses both curtains once, and nothing crosses the top strip, so both curtains carry 182 Mt/yr: they have the same shadow on the plane x = 0
solutionFigures.caption: Every horizontal dust path crosses both curtains once, so the tilted curtain carries the same $182$ Mt/yr.

solutionFigures.alt: Dust budget drawn as bands with widths to scale between the 15 degrees west and 35 degrees west lines: a band of 182 Mt/yr enters from the east, a band of 132 Mt/yr continues west, and a band of 50 Mt/yr turns down into the ocean. Equation: minus 182 + 132 + D = 0
solutionFigures.caption: Steady state: $-182+132+D=0$, so $D=50$ Mt/yr falls into the ocean between $15^\circ$W and $35^\circ$W.

weeks.title: Boundaries that know the inside
weeks.subtitle: It’s Not Easy Being Green
skills: Orient boundaries positively, including boundaries of regions with holes
Verify Green’s theorem edge by edge, and use it to avoid hard line integrals
Find areas and centroids from boundary data (ellipses, polygons, planimeters)
Excise a small circle around a singularity, and decide when a circulation is zero
Review sphere symmetry for surface integrals and flux (Quiz 3)
formulas: $\oint_{\partial D}P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\Big(\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}\Big)dA$, $\partial D$ positively oriented (region on the left), $P,Q$ continuously differentiable on an open set containing $D$
Area, with $\partial D$ positively oriented: $A=\oint_{\partial D}x\,dy=-\oint_{\partial D}y\,dx=\tfrac12\oint_{\partial D}x\,dy-y\,dx$

Flux form, with $\mathbf n$ the outward unit normal: $\oint_{\partial D}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds=\oint_{\partial D}F_1\,dy-F_2\,dx=\iint_D\Big(\dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial F_2}{\partial y}\Big)dA$

problems.title: Measuring the Bermuda Triangle from its edges
problems.context: A 1964 magazine article drew a “Bermuda Triangle” between Miami, Bermuda, and San Juan and blamed it for vanished ships and planes. NOAA finds no evidence that disappearances happen there more often than anywhere else, but the triangle still makes a good test shape. Before computers, chart-makers measured areas with a planimeter: an instrument with an arm whose tracer point you run once around a boundary while a small wheel rolls along the paper. The wheel’s roll gives the area. Mapping software today does the same job from boundary coordinates alone. How can one trip around the edge tell you the area inside, and where the region’s center is?
problems.model: The three station positions are published; the flat chart, the rounded vertices, and the idealized planimeter are modeling choices.
work: Sketch $T$, order M, S, B counterclockwise, and parametrize each edge for $0\le t\le1$. Mark which edges run north ($dy>0$).
Before (b): Check the hypotheses of Green’s theorem for the planimeter field. Why must $|y|<L$ hold on all of $T$?
Before (b): Show that the wheel roll is $A/L$ for any traced region. What does a clockwise trace show?
Before (c): Predict the sign of $\oint_{\partial T}x^2\,dy$ from your sketch.
After (c): Check (c) with $\iint_T2x\,dA$, then find $\bar x=\frac1{2A}\oint_{\partial T}x^2\,dy$ and mark the centroid.
Review: Compute $\int x\,ds$ along the edge from M to S.

questions.prompt: Before tracing the triangle, an operator checks (calibrates) the planimeter on a shape whose area is known exactly. Use $A=\tfrac12\oint x\,dy-y\,dx$ to find the area, in cm$^2$, of the calibration ellipse $x=6\cos t$, $y=4\sin t$ (in cm), $0\le t\le2\pi$, traced counterclockwise.
hints: Substitute the parametrization: $dx=-6\sin t\,dt$ and $dy=4\cos t\,dt$.
The integrand simplifies to $x\,dy-y\,dx=24\,dt$. Integrate over $0\le t\le2\pi$, then halve. Size check: the ellipse fits in a 12 cm by 8 cm box, so expect about three quarters of 96 cm$^2$.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: The calibration ellipse x = 6 cos t, y = 4 sin t, with semi-axes 6 cm and 4 cm, arrows showing counterclockwise travel, and the points t = 0, pi/2, pi, and 3pi/2 marked. A thin shaded wedge from the origin to a short piece of the ellipse is labeled with area one half of (x dy minus y dx). Beside it are dx = −6 sin t dt and dy = 4 cos t dt.
hintFigure.caption: Each short step along the ellipse sweeps a thin wedge from the origin of area $\tfrac12(x\,dy-y\,dx)$. Going once counterclockwise, the wedges fill the ellipse exactly once.

questions.prompt: Using the planimeter model with $L=10$ cm, find the wheel roll, in cm, when the tracer goes once counterclockwise around the triangle $T$.
hints: Apply Green’s theorem with $P=-y/L$ and $Q=\sqrt{L^2-y^2}/L$. Since $Q$ depends on $y$ only, $Q_x-P_y=1/L$.
So the roll is $A/L$, with $A$ the area of $T$: half the cross product of the edge vectors from M to S and from M to B.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: Triangle T with vertices M at the origin, S at (14, −8), and B at (16, 7), its edges arrowed counterclockwise M to S to B. The edge vectors from M to S, (14, −8), and from M to B, (16, 7), are highlighted, and a dashed parallelogram they span has twice the area of T. Dotted lines at y = 10 and y = −10 mark how far the tracer can go from the rail.
hintFigure.caption: Since $Q_x-P_y=1/L$, the roll is $A/L$. The area $A$ is half the parallelogram spanned by the edge vectors from M, and the whole triangle lies inside $|y|<L$.

questions.prompt: With $\partial T$ positively oriented (counterclockwise), compute $\oint_{\partial T}x^2\,dy$ edge by edge, in chart units, so the answer is in cm$^3$.
hints: Split $\partial T$ into the edges M to S, S to B, and B to M, and parametrize each for $0\le t\le1$.
For example, on S to B, $x=14+2t$ and $dy=15\,dt$, so that piece is $15\int_0^1(14+2t)^2\,dt=3380$. The other two edges are negative.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: Triangle T with each edge labeled by its parametrization for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1: M to S is (14t, −8t) with dy = −8 dt, S to B is (14 + 2t, −8 + 15t) with dy = 15 dt, and B to M is (16 − 16t, 7 − 7t) with dy = −7 dt. The two edges running south are drawn in one color, and the single edge running north in another.
hintFigure.caption: Only the east edge S to B runs north ($dy>0$), and it is also where $x^2$ is largest. The other two edges run south and contribute negative amounts.

solution: Orientation and area: The counterclockwise order is M $\to$ S $\to$ B $\to$ M, because $(14,-8)\times(16,7)=14\cdot7+8\cdot16=226>0$. So the area of $T$ is $A=\tfrac12(226)=113$ cm$^2$.
Calibration ellipse (a): $x\,dy-y\,dx=(6\cos t)(4\cos t)\,dt-(4\sin t)(-6\sin t)\,dt=24\,dt$, so $A=\tfrac12\int_0^{2\pi}24\,dt=24\pi\approx75.40$ cm$^2$.

Hypotheses: Green’s theorem needs a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth simple closed boundary, and $P,Q$ continuously differentiable on an open set containing the region. Here $P=-y/L$ and $Q=\sqrt{L^2-y^2}/L$. At $|y|=L$ the derivative $Q_y$ blows up, and beyond it $Q$ is undefined (the arm cannot reach that far from the rail), so we need $|y|<L$. With $L=10$ cm and $-8\le y\le7$ on $T$, the hypotheses hold.

Wheel roll (b): Green’s theorem gives roll $=\iint_T(0+\tfrac1L)\,dA=A/L=113/10=11.3$ cm, and the same argument gives $A/L$ for any region the tracer can reach. The awkward $\sqrt{L^2-y^2}\,dy$ term never needs integrating. On the calibration ellipse the wheel should roll $24\pi/10\approx7.54$ cm, which is how the operator checks the instrument. Tracing clockwise reverses the boundary, so the wheel reads $-11.3$ cm.

Edge by edge (c): $\int_0^1(14t)^2(-8)\,dt=-\tfrac{1568}3$, then $\int_0^1(14+2t)^2(15)\,dt=15(196+28+\tfrac43)=3380$, and $\int_0^1(16-16t)^2(-7)\,dt=-\tfrac{1792}3$. The total is $3380-1120=2260$ cm$^3$. It is positive, as the sketch predicts: the only north-running edge, S to B, is also the edge farthest east, where $x^2$ is largest.

Double-integral check and centroid: With $P=0$ and $Q=x^2$, Green’s theorem gives $\oint_{\partial T}x^2\,dy=\iint_T2x\,dA=2A\bar x$, so $\bar x=2260/226=10$ cm. This matches the average of the vertices’ $x$-coordinates, $(0+14+16)/3=10$, which is the centroid of any triangle. Similarly $\bar y=(0-8+7)/3=-\tfrac13$ cm.
Review: On M to S, $\mathbf c(t)=(14t,-8t)$ has speed $\sqrt{260}$, so $\int x\,ds=\int_0^1 14t\sqrt{260}\,dt=7\sqrt{260}\approx112.9$ cm$^2$.

On the map: The area came out positive because the trace ran counterclockwise. $113$ cm$^2$ on the chart is $1.13$ million km$^2$. The spherical triangle through the three stations has about $1.15$ million km$^2$, so the flat chart and the rounded vertices together lose only about 2 percent. What matters most is the choice of vertices: later writers drew larger boundaries enclosing $1.3$ to $3.9$ million km$^2$. The centroid $(10,-\tfrac13)$ cm lies about 1,000 km east of Miami and about 30 km south of it.
problems.reflection: Writers have given the Triangle areas from 1.3 to 3.9 million km². What does that range tell you, and what would you need before trusting a claim that the region is unusually dangerous?
problems.discussionSolution: The range shows that the “Triangle” has no agreed boundary: its area depends on which vertices a writer picks, so it is a story, not a measurement. Before believing a claim of danger you would need a fixed boundary, a count of incidents, and the amount of shipping and air traffic inside it, compared with other busy regions. NOAA finds no evidence that disappearances there are more frequent than elsewhere.

data: Virginia Key (Miami) tide station: $25.73^\circ$ N, $80.16^\circ$ W (NOAA, rounded to two decimals)
Bermuda (St. Georges Island) tide station: $32.37^\circ$ N, $64.70^\circ$ W (NOAA, rounded)
San Juan (La Puntilla) tide station: $18.46^\circ$ N, $66.12^\circ$ W (NOAA, rounded)
Vertices of the 1964 triangle (Gaddis): Miami, San Juan, Bermuda
assume: The chart is flat: distances east and north in km, measured at latitude $25.5^\circ$ N and drawn at 1 cm $=100$ km. This ignores Earth’s curvature, which you check at the end.
Each vertex is rounded to the nearest 100 km (1 cm on the chart). This keeps the arithmetic in whole numbers and moves each vertex by at most about 70 km.

The planimeter is an idealized linear one: the foot of the arm (length $L=10$ cm) slides along a rail on the $x$-axis, and the wheel at the tracer rolls only by the tracer’s motion perpendicular to the arm. It works only while the tracer stays within $L$ of the rail.
model: Chart coordinates in cm, $x$ east and $y$ north, Miami at the origin. Triangle $T$: M $=(0,0)$, S $=(14,-8)$, B $=(16,7)$, with area $A$ (cm$^2$)

The wheel roll (cm), how far the wheel turns when the tracer goes once around a loop $C$: $\dfrac1L\oint_C-y\,dx+\sqrt{L^2-y^2}\,dy$, where $L=10$ cm is the arm length. The planimeter field is $(P,Q)=\big(-y/L,\ \sqrt{L^2-y^2}/L\big)$.
Calibration ellipse: $x=6\cos t$, $y=4\sin t$ cm, $0\le t\le2\pi$

photo.alt: A Keuffel and Esser polar planimeter, with its tracing arm and measuring wheel, in a green-lined case in front of a map

figure.alt: Chart of triangle T with vertices M (Miami) at the origin, S (San Juan) at (14, −8), and B (Bermuda) at (16, 7). A planimeter rail runs along the x-axis, an arm of length 10 cm joins a point on the rail to the tracer on the edge from S to B, and a half-size calibration ellipse sits at the lower right.
figure.caption: The chart model (1 cm $=100$ km): the triangle $T$ and the idealized planimeter. The foot of the arm (length $L$) slides along the rail $y=0$, and the wheel at the tracer rolls by the tracer’s motion perpendicular to the arm. The calibration ellipse is drawn at half size.

solutionFigures.alt: Triangle T with each edge labeled by its contribution to the integral of x squared dy: M to S gives −1568/3, about −522.7 cubic cm; S to B gives +3380; B to M gives −1792/3, about −597.3. The total is 3380 − 1120 = 2260 cubic cm.
solutionFigures.caption: The three edge contributions to $\oint_{\partial T}x^2\,dy$ (cm$^3$): the north-running east edge outweighs the two south-running edges.

solutionFigures.alt: Triangle T with its three medians dashed, meeting at the centroid (10, −1/3) cm, marked with a dot and a dotted vertical line at x-bar = 10, with the note that it lies about 1,000 km east of Miami.

problems.title: Every seat in the Roman theatre at Orange
problems.context: The Roman theatre at Orange, in southern France, still has its stone seating: a half-ring of rows wrapped around the orchestra, the semicircular floor in front of the stage. A surveyor’s software can measure a region like this using only its boundary, and you will do the same with Green’s theorem. How much seating area is there, and how far from the front of the stage does the average spectator sit?
problems.model: Both diameters are published; the exact half-ring, the rounded radii, and the flat plan view are assumptions.
work: Sketch $D$, mark its four boundary pieces, and orient each so $D$ is on the left. Why does the inner arc run clockwise?
Mark the sign of $-\tfrac12y^2\,dx$ on each piece. Why do the straight pieces add nothing?
Before (a): Use Green’s theorem to turn the area and first-moment integrals into double integrals in polar coordinates.
Before (c): Predict: is $\bar y$ more or less than the middle radius, $33.5$ m? Why?
After (c): Check the outer-arc piece directly with a parametrization.
Find $\bar y=M/A$, and estimate the capacity at $0.5$ m$^2$ per spectator.

questions.prompt: Find the seating area $A$ of the model region $D$, in m$^2$.
hints: Green’s theorem turns $\tfrac12\oint_{\partial D}x\,dy-y\,dx$ into $\iint_D1\,dA$.
In polar coordinates this is $\int_0^\pi\int_{15}^{52}r\,dr\,d\theta$. Size check: the whole half-disk of radius 52 m is about 4,250 m$^2$, and the orchestra takes away a little.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: The half-ring seating region between radii 15 m and 52 m above the stage line, with a radius ray, an arc showing theta running from 0 to pi, and one small polar box shaded and labeled dA = r dr dtheta.
hintFigure.caption: In polar coordinates $D$ is $15\le r\le52$, $0\le\theta\le\pi$, and a small piece has area $dA=r\,dr\,d\theta$.

questions.prompt: With $\partial D$ positively oriented (so $D$ stays on your left), find the inner arc’s contribution to $-\tfrac12\oint_{\partial D}y^2\,dx$, in m$^3$.
hints: Keeping $D$ on the left, the inner arc runs clockwise, from $(-15,0)$ to $(15,0)$.
Use $x=15\cos t$, $y=15\sin t$ with $t$ going from $\pi$ down to $0$. Then $-\tfrac12y^2\,dx=\tfrac{15^3}{2}\sin^3t\,dt$, and $\int_0^\pi\sin^3t\,dt=\tfrac43$.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: Left: the boundary of the half-ring with arrows: along the stage line from 15 to 52, counterclockwise around the outer arc, along the stage line from −52 to −15, and clockwise around the inner arc, so the region is always on the left. Right: a close-up of the inner arc from (−15, 0) at t = pi, through t = pi/2 at the top, to (15, 0) at t = 0, with dx > 0.
hintFigure.caption: Keeping $D$ on the left makes the inner arc run clockwise, from $(-15,0)$ to $(15,0)$: use $x=15\cos t$, $y=15\sin t$ with $t$ running from $\pi$ down to $0$.

questions.prompt: Find the first moment of the seating about the stage line (area weighted by distance from that line), $M=-\tfrac12\oint_{\partial D}y^2\,dx=\iint_D y\,dA$, in m$^3$.
hints: Green’s theorem with $P=-y^2/2$ and $Q=0$ gives $Q_x-P_y=y$.
In polar coordinates $y\,dA=(r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta$, so $\iint_Dy\,dA=\int_0^\pi\sin\theta\,d\theta\int_{15}^{52}r^2\,dr$.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: The half-ring shaded from light near the stage line to dark at the back, showing that the weight y grows with distance from the stage line. One small piece dA is marked with a dashed vertical segment showing its distance y = r sin theta from the line.
hintFigure.caption: The first moment weights each small piece $dA$ by its distance $y=r\sin\theta$ from the stage line, so $M=\iint_D y\,dA$ separates into a $\theta$ integral and an $r$ integral.

solution: Orientation: $D$ is $15\le r\le52$, $0\le\theta\le\pi$. Its positive boundary is the segment from $(15,0)$ to $(52,0)$, the outer arc counterclockwise to $(-52,0)$, the segment to $(-15,0)$, and the inner arc clockwise back to $(15,0)$. Along the inner arc the region lies outside the small circle, so keeping it on the left means going clockwise.
Area (a): By Green’s theorem, $A=\iint_D1\,dA=\int_0^\pi\!\int_{15}^{52}r\,dr\,d\theta=\tfrac\pi2(52^2-15^2)=1239.5\pi\approx3894.0$ m$^2$.

Boundary pieces (b): On the two segments $y=0$, so $y^2\,dx=0$. On the outer arc, $x=52\cos t$, $y=52\sin t$, $0\le t\le\pi$, which gives $-\tfrac12\int_0^\pi52^2\sin^2t\,(-52\sin t)\,dt=\tfrac{52^3}2\cdot\tfrac43=\tfrac23(52^3)$. The inner arc is the same computation with radius $15$ and $t$ running from $\pi$ to $0$, so its piece is $-\tfrac23(15^3)=-2250$ m$^3$. The signs fit the sketch: the outer arc runs toward negative $x$ ($dx<0$) and adds, while the inner arc runs toward positive $x$ ($dx>0$) and subtracts.

First moment (c): By Green’s theorem, $M=\iint_D y\,dA=\int_0^\pi\sin\theta\,d\theta\int_{15}^{52}r^2\,dr=\tfrac23(52^3-15^3)\approx91{,}488.7$ m$^3$, which matches the sum of the two arcs. So $\bar y=M/A\approx23.5$ m, less than the middle radius $33.5$ m: a seat at radius $r$ sits only $r\sin\theta$ from the stage line, and seats near the two ends of the half-ring are almost on that line.

In the theatre: $M$ is positive because all the seating lies on the side $y>0$, and $\bar y\approx23.5$ m lies between the inner and outer radii, as it must. So the average spectator sits about $23.5$ m back from the front of the stage. At $0.5$ m$^2$ per person the model seats $3894/0.5\approx7800$ spectators, above both published capacities, 5,850 and 7,300. The assumption that matters most is the evenly filled half-ring: aisles and stairs, ignored in the model, take up part of the plan area.
problems.reflection: Real Roman seating rises in stone steps away from the stage. Is the plan-view area you found more or less than the actual stone seat surface, and is $\bar y$ the same as the average distance from a seat to the actors?
problems.discussionSolution: Less, and no. The plan-view area is a projection, so the stepped stone surface (seat tops plus risers) is larger. $\bar y$ is only the average horizontal distance from the stage line; the distance to the actors also includes each seat’s sideways offset and the height of the upper rows.

data: Seating diameter: $103.63$ m (Ancient Theatre Archive)
Orchestra diameter: $29.9$ m (same source)
Seating capacity: 5,850 or 7,300 (two published figures)
assume: In plan view the seating is a flat, exact half-ring, with radii rounded to $15$ m and $52$ m, half the published diameters. Other descriptions give somewhat different diameters, so the rounding is well within the uncertainty.
The front of the stage is the line $y=0$ through the center of the orchestra, so all the seating lies on one side of it.
Aisles and stairs are ignored, and spectators fill the seating area evenly. This overstates the area people can actually sit on.
model: $D$: $15\le r\le52$, $0\le\theta\le\pi$ (meters), in polar coordinates centered on the orchestra

Seating area $A$ (m$^2$) $=\tfrac12\oint_{\partial D}x\,dy-y\,dx$; first moment about the stage line $M$ (m$^3$) $=-\tfrac12\oint_{\partial D}y^2\,dx$; average distance from the stage line $\bar y=M/A$ (m)

photo.alt: Wide view of the Roman theatre at Orange: curved rows of stone seating wrap around the semicircular orchestra, facing the tall stage wall

figure.alt: Plan view of a half-ring seating area between radii 15 m and 52 m, above a horizontal line marking the front of the stage; the semicircular orchestra fills the inside of the ring.
figure.caption: Plan view of the model seating $D$ ($15\le r\le52$ m, $0\le\theta\le\pi$), with the front of the stage along $y=0$ and the orchestra inside the inner arc.

solutionFigures.alt: The oriented boundary of the half-ring with each piece labeled: the two straight pieces on the stage line give 0, the outer arc (dx < 0) gives +2/3 times 52 cubed, about 93,738.7 cubic m, and the inner arc (dx > 0) gives −2/3 times 15 cubed = −2250 cubic m.
solutionFigures.caption: The pieces of $-\tfrac12\oint_{\partial D}y^2\,dx$ (m$^3$): the straight pieces add nothing, the outer arc adds, and the clockwise inner arc subtracts.

solutionFigures.alt: The half-ring seating with a dashed horizontal line at y-bar of about 23.5 m and a dotted arc at the middle radius 33.5 m, which rises above the line, with the note that seats near the ends sit close to the stage line.
solutionFigures.caption: The average distance from the stage line, $\bar y\approx23.5$ m, is less than the middle radius $33.5$ m because seats near the ends of the half-ring sit close to $y=0$.

problems.title: Circulation around Typhoon Haiyan
problems.context: Typhoon Haiyan struck the central Philippines in November 2013. At its peak, the Japan Meteorological Agency reported 10-minute average winds of 65 m/s and storm-force winds out to 150 km from the center. A simple model treats the wind outside the eye as an ideal vortex: the air circles the eye, and its speed falls like $1/r$ with distance $r$ from the center. The circulation around a closed loop measures how much spin the wind carries around it: it adds up the part of the wind that blows along the loop. How much circulation does the storm carry around a loop that encloses the eye, would a lopsided loop give a different answer, and what about a loop that misses the eye?
problems.model: The peak wind and the wind radii are published; the ideal-vortex model, its calibration at 150 km, and the loops are assumptions.
work: Sketch the wind and the three loops, mark where $\mathbf v$ is undefined, and compute $Q_x-P_y$ for $r>0$.
Before (a): Explain why Green’s theorem on the disk $r\le150$ km would wrongly predict zero.
Before (b): Predict: is the ellipse’s circulation larger in size than the circle’s, smaller, or equal?
Before (b): Excise a small circle $C_\varepsilon$ about the center, orient the boundary of the region between it and the ellipse positively, and conclude without parametrizing.
After (c): Explain part (c) with Green’s theorem.
Check the model: its speed at the gale radius, $460$ km, and where it reaches $65$ m/s. What do these say about $1/r$?

questions.prompt: Find the circulation of the wind counterclockwise (seen from above) around the circle $r=150$ km centered on the eye, in km$^2$/h.
hints: On this circle the wind blows along the loop, counterclockwise, at the calibrated 90 km/h, so each kilometer of the loop contributes 90 km$^2$/h.
For a tangent wind of constant speed, circulation $=$ speed $\times$ length of the loop. Size check: expect km$^2$/h and a value near 100,000.
questions.label: a

hintFigure.alt: The circle of radius 150 km around the eye, with wind arrows of equal length all pointing counterclockwise along the circle. One short piece ds of the circle is highlighted with the note that the wind along it, at 90 km/h, adds 90 ds.
hintFigure.caption: On this circle the wind is tangent and has the same speed, $90$ km/h, everywhere, so $\mathbf v\cdot d\mathbf r=90\,ds$ on every piece of the loop.

questions.prompt: Find the circulation of the wind around the ellipse $x^2/300^2+y^2/200^2=1$, traversed clockwise (seen from above), in km$^2$/h.
hints: Between the ellipse and a small circle around the eye the curl is zero, so by Green’s theorem the two loops, both taken counterclockwise, have equal circulation.
Traversing the ellipse clockwise reverses the sign.
questions.label: b

hintFigure.alt: The ellipse with semi-axes 300 km and 200 km, arrowed counterclockwise, and a small circle C epsilon around the eye arrowed clockwise. The region R epsilon between them is shaded and labeled with zero curl.
hintFigure.caption: The region $R_\varepsilon$ between the ellipse and a small circle $C_\varepsilon$ avoids the eye and has $Q_x-P_y=0$. Its positive boundary is the ellipse counterclockwise plus $C_\varepsilon$ clockwise.

questions.prompt: Find the circulation of the wind counterclockwise around the circle of radius $100$ km centered at $(420,0)$ km, in km$^2$/h.
hints: Check whether this circle encloses the eye.
The field is smooth on the disk this circle bounds, and its curl is zero there.
questions.label: c

hintFigure.alt: Wind arrows circling the eye, which is marked with an x where the wind is undefined. The circle of radius 100 km centered 420 km east is shaded; it lies 320 km from the eye and does not contain it.
hintFigure.caption: The disk bounded by the loop in (c) stays $320$ km away from the eye, so $\mathbf v$ is smooth on the whole disk and Green’s theorem applies.

solution: Curl and hypotheses: For $r>0$, with $P=-\tfrac{\Gamma}{2\pi}\tfrac{y}{x^2+y^2}$ and $Q=\tfrac{\Gamma}{2\pi}\tfrac{x}{x^2+y^2}$, both $Q_x$ and $P_y$ equal $\tfrac{\Gamma}{2\pi}\tfrac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}$, so $Q_x-P_y=0$. But the field is undefined at the center, which lies in every disk around the eye. So Green’s theorem does not apply on the disk $r\le150$, and its prediction of zero is wrong.

Circle (a): On $r=150$ the wind is tangent with speed $\Gamma/(2\pi\cdot150)=90$ km/h, so the circulation is $\Gamma=2\pi(150)(90)=27000\pi\approx84{,}823$ km$^2$/h. The same computation gives $\Gamma$ on every circle centered on the eye.

Excised region (b): Let $R_\varepsilon$ be the region between the ellipse and $C_\varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon<200$. Its positive boundary is the ellipse counterclockwise plus $C_\varepsilon$ clockwise. The field is smooth on $R_\varepsilon$ with zero curl, so Green’s theorem gives $\oint_{\text{ellipse, ccw}}=\oint_{C_\varepsilon,\text{ccw}}=\Gamma$. Clockwise, the circulation is $-27000\pi\approx-84{,}823$ km$^2$/h. So the larger, lopsided loop has a circulation of the same size as the circle: the extra area between them has zero curl and adds nothing.
Loop that misses the eye (c): The disk $(x-420)^2+y^2\le100^2$ does not contain the center, so Green’s theorem applies and gives $\iint0\,dA=0$.

Model check: At $460$ km the model gives $90\cdot150/460\approx29$ km/h $\approx8$ m/s, but JMA reported gale winds ($\ge15$ m/s) that far north, so the real winds fall off more slowly than $1/r$. The model reaches $65$ m/s at $r=150\cdot25/65\approx58$ km, and closer in it predicts ever faster winds without limit. The ideal vortex is only a rough description of the winds outside the core. The circulation is positive counterclockwise because the model wind turns counterclockwise, and its size, near $85{,}000$ km$^2$/h, is pinned only by the 150 km calibration. The assumption that matters most is the $1/r$ falloff: it is what makes every loop around the eye give the same answer.
problems.reflection: The model check shows that the real winds fall off more slowly than $1/r$. What if the speed fell off like $1/\sqrt r$ instead: would the circle in (a) and the ellipse in (b) still have circulations of the same size, and would the loop in (c) still give zero?
problems.discussionSolution: No, and no. Around a circle of radius $r$ centered on the eye the circulation would be $2\pi r\,v(r)$, which now grows like $\sqrt r$, so bigger loops carry more. Equivalently, for a wind of speed $v(r)$ circling the center, $Q_x-P_y=\frac1r\frac{d}{dr}\big(r\,v\big)$, which is zero for $v\propto1/r$ but positive everywhere outside the eye for $v\propto1/\sqrt r$. So by Green’s theorem the ellipse, which encloses the circle plus a band of positive curl, has a circulation of larger size, and the loop in (c) encloses positive curl and has positive circulation.

data: Maximum 10-minute wind: $65$ m/s (JMA best track)
Central pressure: $895$ hPa
Storm-force winds ($\ge25$ m/s $=90$ km/h) out to $150$ km from the center
Gale winds ($\ge15$ m/s) out to $460$ km north and $330$ km south of the center
assume: Outside the eye, the wind is an ideal counterclockwise vortex, calibrated so that its speed is $90$ km/h at $r=150$ km. How well $1/r$ fits farther out is checked against the gale radius.
The model does not apply in the eye, because the speed $\Gamma/(2\pi r)$ grows without limit as $r\to0$; the field is undefined at the center.
The map is flat, in km, with the eye at the origin, and the wind is a snapshot that stays fixed while each loop is traced.
model: $\mathbf v(x,y)=\dfrac{\Gamma}{2\pi}\,\dfrac{(-y,\ x)}{x^2+y^2}$ km/h for $(x,y)\ne(0,0)$, with speed $\Gamma/(2\pi r)$ at distance $r$ km from the eye
$\Gamma$ (km$^2$/h): the vortex strength, a constant fixed by the $90$ km/h wind at $150$ km
Loops: the circle $r=150$; the ellipse $x^2/300^2+y^2/200^2=1$; the circle of radius $100$ about $(420,0)$

photo.alt: Typhoon Haiyan seen from the International Space Station: a vast spiral of cloud over the western Pacific, with part of the station at the edge

figure.alt: Wind arrows circling counterclockwise around the eye. Three loops are drawn: the dashed circle of radius 150 km around the eye, a larger ellipse around the eye with an arrowhead showing clockwise travel, and a small circle to the east that does not enclose the eye.
figure.caption: The ideal-vortex model outside the eye (arrows) and the three loops: (a) the circle $r=150$, (b) the ellipse, traversed clockwise, and (c) the circle of radius $100$ about $(420,0)$, which does not enclose the eye. Map in km.

solutionFigures.alt: Two graphs against r in km. Left: the model wind speed 13500/r km/h falls steeply, passing 90 km/h at 150 km. Right: the circulation 2 pi r times the speed is a flat line at 27000 pi, about 84,823 square km per hour.
solutionFigures.caption: On circles centered on the eye the speed falls like $1/r$ while the loop length grows like $r$, so every such circle has circulation $\Gamma=27000\pi\approx84{,}823$ km$^2$/h.

solutionFigures.alt: Graph of the model wind speed 13500/r km/h against distance from the eye. Marked: the calibration point, 90 km/h at 150 km; the model value 29 km/h at 460 km, well below the reported gale winds of at least 54 km/h there; and the reported peak of 234 km/h, which the model reaches at 58 km.
